title: A Multi-view, Hybrid, Hypergraph Learning Framework with Causal Perturbation for Early Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.This work is the first to systematically integrate NPI-derived EC with multi-view features and hybrid hypergraph learning. 2.The overall framework (Fig. 1) is logically well-structured, with each step supported by clear motivation, mathematical formulation, and implementation details. 3.Comprehensive baseline comparisons are given. Ablation studies quantitatively validate the contribution of each component, and interpretability analyses are highly consistent with known pathological characteristics of AD. 4.In early screening scenarios for CN vs. MCI, the method achieves a good balance between sensitivity and specificity, provides interpretable biomarkers, and shows strong potential for real-world clinical translation.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient details on NPI/EC extraction: in Section 2.2 only Equation (1) is provided, but key implementation details such as the architecture of the surrogate ANN, training hyperparameters, perturbation intensity settings, and post-processing of the EC matrix (e. g. , thresholding/normalization) are lacked. 2.Superedge K-value definition: The authors set the number of learnable superedges to K=10 to fill the gap between Schaefer 7 and 17 networks. It is suggested that the authors supplement this with a sensitivity analysis of the K-value (e. g. , K= {5, 10, 15, 20}) to demonstrate the stability of this parameter selection. 3.Overly brief description of the multi-view encoders: The “dedicated encoder” for the five additional views is only mentioned in one sentence, without details on network architecture, parameters, feature dimensions, or preprocessing steps. 4.Lack of statistical significance analysis: Although in Table 1 clear performance gaps are showed compared to baselines, no p-values or other statistical test results are reported. 5.Table 2 formatting is slightly disorganized; reformatting is recommended. 6.Some long sentences (e. g. , at the end of the Introduction and in Section 2.3) could be split to improve readability. 7.The hyperedge degree (De) should be explicitly defined before Equation (4). 8.The future work plan is too general and does not specify any concrete directions for expansion. 9.Computational efficiency: Considering that the model integrates CNN, Transformer, and hypergraph convolution, how are its parameter count and inference speed? It is recommended to supplement the FLOPs or runtime comparison of the main comparison models in the reply or body text.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Incorporation of effective connectivity beyond standard FC. Most rs-fMRI-based methods rely exclusively on undirected functional connectivity, which captures correlation but not directionality. This paper introduces effective connectivity via Neural Perturbational Inference alongside FC, providing a richer characterization of inter-regional relationships. The ablation in Table 2 confirms that the connectivity view contributes substantially to performance. 2.Multi-view complementary information utilization. The design of extracting multiple complementary views from the same rs-fMRI data — spanning temporal, spectral, connectivity, and topological domains — is well-motivated. The Adaptive Reliability Fusion module provides a principled mechanism for combining these views while accounting for heterogeneous noise across subjects, and the ablation demonstrates that each view contributes non-redundantly. 3.Hypergraph modeling is well-suited for brain network complexity. The human brain exhibits complex, high-order interactions that extend beyond pairwise connections. Hypergraphs, where a single hyperedge can connect multiple nodes simultaneously, are a natural formalism for capturing such multi-region co-activation patterns. The hybrid design combining neuroscientific priors with learnable hyperedges is a thoughtful approach that balances biological grounding with data-driven flexibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.Overcomplicated pipeline with unclear marginal contributions. The framework integrates six feature views, six dedicated encoders, sample-wise quality networks, global learnable weights, prior and learnable hyperedges, orthogonal regularization, multi-layer hypergraph convolution, dual-path attention pooling, focal loss with label smoothing, diversity regularization, and supervised contrastive loss. While each component is individually motivated, the sheer number of interacting modules makes it extremely difficult to identify where the performance gain truly originates. The ablation in Table 2 removes components in coarse groups but never isolates closely coupled elements — for instance, EC versus FC within the connectivity view, or prior versus learnable hyperedges within the hypergraph module. Without finer-grained ablations, the reader cannot determine whether the improvement comes from the causality modeling, the multi-view fusion, the hypergraph structure, or simply from having more parameters and loss terms. 2.Insufficient description of the six feature views and brain parcellation. The paper does not adequately explain what each of the six feature views concretely represents, how each is computed, or why these particular six were chosen over other possible representations. For instance, how are the time-frequency statistics extracted? What specific graph-theoretic topology metrics are used? How is nodal Shannon entropy defined and computed on the fMRI signal? The paper provides references but offers almost no inline description, significantly increasing the barrier to understanding and reproducibility. 3.Key structural details of the hypergraph are underspecified. Several critical quantities governing the hypergraph structure are not clearly defined. How many hyperedges are there in total (the paper mentions 7 prior + 10 learnable = 17, but this is not stated explicitly)? How many nodes does each hyperedge connect — is this uniform or variable? For the learnable hyperedges, the temperature-scaled similarity in Eq. 3 produces soft membership values, but it is unclear whether a threshold or top-k selection is applied to sparsify the incidence matrix, or whether all nodes belong to all learnable hyperedges with varying weights. For the prior hyperedges, are the Schaefer 7-network assignments binary and non-overlapping? These details are essential for understanding the model’s actual computational graph and for reproducibility. 4.The “causal” claim is overstated. The paper repeatedly positions causality as a core contribution, but the effective connectivity derived from NPI is based on virtual perturbations of a surrogate neural network trained on observational fMRI data. This captures directed statistical dependencies under the model’s learned dynamics, not true causal effects in the interventionist sense. Confounding pathways, indirect effects, and hemodynamic delays inherent to BOLD fMRI are not explicitly addressed. The paper should more carefully qualify this as “directed” or “model-inferred effective connectivity” rather than broadly claiming causal inference. 5.The claimed directionality is not preserved through the architecture. The paper emphasizes directional (causal) interactions as a key motivation, yet the downstream architecture does not maintain this directionality. Specifically, the Transformer blocks in the encoder allow every node to attend to every other node symmetrically via self-attention, effectively erasing the asymmetry present in the EC matrix. Furthermore, the hypergraph convolution in Eqs. 4–5 updates node features by symmetric aggregation – information flows from nodes to hyperedges and back without any directional distinction. This means that even though the EC input encodes that ROI i causally drives ROI j but not vice versa, this asymmetry is lost once the features pass through the Transformer and hypergraph layers. The paper does not discuss this architectural tension, nor does it demonstrate that the directional information in EC survives to influence the final classification. A directed message-passing scheme or an asymmetry-preserving attention mechanism would be needed to substantiate the claim that directionality is meaningfully exploited.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The overall idea is interesting. The paper combines effective connectivity, multi-view fusion, and hypergraph learning in a single framework for early AD diagnosis. 2.The multi-view setting is a strength. Using several complementary rs-fMRI feature types, together with adaptive fusion, is well motivated for handling noisy and heterogeneous data.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The novelty is somewhat incremental. The paper combines several existing directions—effective/causal connectivity analysis, hypergraph learning, and multi-view fusion/transformer-based modeling. In that sense, the main contribution is more a new integration of prior ideas than a clearly new methodological concept. 2.The validation is still limited. The experiments are conducted only on ADNI and only on the CN vs. MCI task. There is no external dataset, cross-site evaluation, or more realistic clinical setting, so the generalizability of the method is still unclear.3.The performance gain is not very large. In Table 1, the proposed model improves over the strongest baselines, but the margin is still relatively modest considering the complexity of the framework. This makes it harder to judge whether all proposed components are necessary in practice.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the AC and R1/R2/R3.Our work targets CN-vs-MCI early AD screening by integrating NPI-derived directed EC, multi-view rs-fMRI, and hybrid hypergraph learning to capture directional and higher-order changes beyond standard FC/GNN pipelines. [M1: NPI details; AC,R1,R2] Following Luo et al. (Nat. Methods), our implementation trains an MLP surrogate to predict BOLD x(t+1) from x(t-2:t) by one-step MSE. We train it only on CN subjects as a healthy reference, then perturb all CN/MCI subjects, so EC reflects subject-specific deviation from healthy dynamics. For each source ROI, an impulse increase is injected; EC_ij is the L2 deviation between perturbed and baseline predictions of ROI j, averaged over time, row-wise min-max normalized, and 99th-percentile clipped, approximating the surrogate Jacobian. [M2: multiview features; AC,R1,R2] EC is in M1, and FC is standard. R2 asked about other views: raw time series uses Conv1D+2-layer Transformer over time; time-frequency statistics are 16-D/ROI, including time-domain stats (mean/std/skewness) and Welch-PSD features (slow-band power/spectral centroid); graph topology on top-20% |FC| includes degree, betweenness, clustering, local efficiency, participation coefficient, and within-module z-score (Schaefer 7-net); nodal Shannon entropy is H_i=-sum_j p_ij log p_ij, where p_ij comes from sliding-window dFC variability. Each view is mapped to a shared latent dimension before ARF. [M3: causality; R2] We agree to qualify “causal” as “directed/model-inferred EC” rather than interventionist causality. NPI was validated against ground-truth generative EC and CCEP propagation, and moves beyond undirected FC. Directionality is not erased: the Transformer attends over time, not ROI pairs, so it does not symmetrize EC. EC is encoded row-wise; thus ROI i’s embedding carries its outgoing profile (EC_ij != EC_ji). Hypergraph convolution aggregates these direction-aware embeddings, with directionality residing in node features rather than edge operators. In finer ablations omitted for space, removing EC while keeping FC caused larger degradation than removing FC while keeping EC, supporting that directed EC reaches the classifier. [M4: hypergraph details; AC,R1,R2] Total hyperedges = 17: seven fixed Schaefer 7-network prior hyperedges plus ten learnable hyperedges. Prior incidence is binary/non-overlapping, with each ROI assigned to one Schaefer network. Learnable incidence in Eq. 3 is soft during training; at inference, top-k node selection per hyperedge yields sparse binary incidence. In Eq. 4, D_e=sum_i H(i,e), which we will define before the equation. K=10 bridges Schaefer 7- and 17-network granularities while allowing AD-specific reorganization. K in {5,10,15,20}: performance rose then fell, peaking at K=10.[M5: validation; R1,R2,R3] Table 2 groups six views into three semantic categories as a presentation choice within the page limit. The key fine-grained clarification is in M3: EC contributes beyond FC, addressing R2’s concern on whether directionality matters. The gain is not due to model size: HyperBrainNet has ~0.51M parameters and ~0.10 GFLOPs, lighter than BrainNetTransformer. The small 5-fold std in Table 1 indicates stable gains; paired tests on existing folds show significant improvements. ADNI is a multi-site/multi-phase consortium; external-cohort validation was conducted but omitted for space. Minor revisions: reformat Table 2; split long sentences; define D_e; clarify NPI/multi-view/hypergraph details; specify future work. Code will be released after acceptance. Given R1/R3’s support, we invite R2/AC to reconsider: 1) we qualify causality and use a CN-only surrogate to define disease-deviation EC; 2) the Transformer attends over time (not ROI pairs) and row-wise EC preserves EC_ij != EC_ji asymmetry; 3) fine-grained ablations support EC’s value beyond FC; 4) the lighter-than-BrainNetTransformer budget rules out parameter inflation as the source of observed gains.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper presents HyperBrainNet, consisting of Adaptive Reliability Fusion for multiview representations. including neural perturbational inference, Hybrid Hypergraph Learning, and Hierarchical Attention Pooling. While the method presents some novelty, several critiques have been raised that need to be addressed in the rebuttal. For example, details of NPI, multiview features, causality, and hypergraph need to be provided. The significance of validation needs to be discussed as well. | Reviewers’ critiques focused on the n details of NPI, multiview features, causality, hypergraph setting, and validation, which were addressed by the authors’ rebuttal. The remaining confusion of causality and directionality need to be further clarified in the final version of the paper. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The work is clinically relevant and technically coherent, and two reviewers support acceptance. Although Reviewer #2 raises a valid concern that the causal/directional claim is overstated and not fully preserved by the downstream architecture, the rebuttal reasonably clarifies that the method should be interpreted as using model-inferred directed EC rather than interventionist causality. The authors also address several missing details regarding NPI, multi-view features, hypergraph construction, K sensitivity, statistical testing, and computational cost. I believe the paper is marginally above the acceptance threshold, provided that the final version incorporates the rebuttal clarifications and substantially tones down the causal claims. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The authors provide additional clarifications regarding the reviewers concerns but not fully. Issues remain regarding some technical details and overclaims, but majority of reviewers lean towards accepting the paper. Contents from the rebuttal must be explicitly incorporated into the final manuscript.

title: Age Conditional Longitudinal Forecasting of Adolescent Functional Connectivity via Brownian Bridge Diffusion Models
reviewer_1_strengths: 1) Using Brownian bridge diffusion for reconstructing the follow-up data from the baseline data is interesting, and the motivation of this model design is straightforward.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1) The presentation of the paper is very bad. The method section does not provide definitions of many notations (e. g. , h, o(), a, W, N(i) in Eq. 1 and m_t, S in Eq. 5, age_diff, age_ratio), as well as the GAT structure, without any preliminaries, which makes it difficult to understand the equations, loss functions, and the model structures. 2) How did the $k=30$ of top-k connections selected? The paper lacks an ablation study on $k$. Does it affect the generated connectivity patterns under the same experimental conditions? If so, which ROIs were significantly affected and why is that so? 3) Only one dataset and three baseline methods (DDPM, GAN, Flow-based model) were used for comparison, which significantly limits the scope of the experimental validation. 4) In section 3.5, the paper provides a comparison between the raw early-age and raw late-age FC differences vs. the raw early-age and generated late-age FC differences. Table 4 shows that the similarity between the generated late-age and the raw early-age FC is higher than that of the raw late-age and raw early-age FC. These results mean that the generated FC looks similar to the raw early-age FC, but it does not guarantee any “physiological” plausible changes over time. How does the proposed method ensure that the generated FC reflects physiologically plausible temporal progression, rather than merely retaining features of the early-age FC?
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper studies a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem, and its endpoint-conditioned latent-space formulation is well matched to paired longitudinal FC prediction. 2.The empirical study is reasonably comprehensive, with multiple baselines, quantitative metrics, ablations, cross-atlas analysis, and an initial biological plausibility analysis.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The top-k graph construction used by the GAT encoder would benefit from clearer specification. In particular, it is not clear from the manuscript whether the graph is built per sample, whether symmetrization is applied, or how graph undirectedness/consistency is handled when top-k neighbors are selected at the node level. 2.The Brownian bridge formulation is not fully transparent in the paper. In particular, the role of fθ is described inconsistently across the manuscript (e.g., as a reverse time drift, a gradient term, and a correction term), while Eqs. (4) and (6) appear to suggest a more specific residual. In addition, the derivation of the reverse-time update in Eqs. (9)–(10) is not sufficiently explicit, and the form of λ2(t) does not seem right. 3.Train/val/test splitting and subject-level separation are not specified; risk of data leakage is non-negligible in paired longitudinal designs and must be clarified. 4.In comparative experiments, baselines are restricted to generic generative models; missing strong FC forecasting baselines. 5.No statistical significance testing across methods; reported gains (e.g., PCC 0.63 vs. 0.61) may not be significant.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Novel problem formulation: age-conditioned FC-to-FC longitudinal forecasting. Instead of doing cross-sectional analysis or generic connectome generation, the paper tackles the harder task of predicting a subject’s future functional connectivity from earlier FC plus target age, which is a meaningful and relatively underexplored formulation for developmental neuroscience. This is interesting because it directly addresses sparse and irregular longitudinal sampling. Interesting technical combination of graph learning and Brownian Bridge diffusion. The method combines a GAT-based autoencoder with Brownian Bridge diffusion in latent space. The novelty is not just using diffusion, but using a bridge process anchored by source and target domains rather than standard pure-noise diffusion. That makes it well suited to paired developmental prediction, where the task is to transform early-age FC into late-age FC in a stable, conditioned way. Well-executed ablation study. The ablations test key design choices: removing the AE, replacing AE with VAE, varying sampling steps, latent dimension, and noise schedule. This is valuable because it shows which components actually matter, especially the importance of the autoencoder and the Brownian-Bridge-specific variance design. Use of real longitudinal developmental data. The study uses the CCNP longitudinal cohort and constructs within-subject scan pairs across ages 6–18.That is a practical strength because truly longitudinal data are harder to obtain and make the task more convincing than purely synthetic or cross-sectional setups.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The “Brownian Bridge for longitudinal neuroimaging forecasting” angle is not entirely new. A close prior example already exists in neuroimaging: Stoyanov et al. (2025) proposed a conditional Brownian Bridge diffusion model for cortical-thickness trajectory forecasting. That does not make this paper uninteresting, but it does narrow the novelty claim: the distinctive part here is specifically functional-connectivity forecasting with age conditioning, not Brownian-Bridge-based neuroimaging trajectory prediction as a whole. The train/test protocol is not described clearly enough to rule out optimistic results. The dataset is expanded from 393 scans into 1,380 within-subject scan pairs, but the paper does not clearly state whether the split is performed at the subject level or only at the pair level. If pairs from the same individual appear in both training and test sets, performance could be inflated because the model would effectively see very similar subject-specific patterns during training. Clinical feasibility is not really demonstrated. All experiments are on a single healthy developmental cohort from CCNP, spanning ages 6–18, with no external validation cohort, no neurological or psychiatric patient group, and no downstream clinical endpoint such as diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment response. So while the work is scientifically interesting, any implication of clinical usefulness is still premature. Robustness across parcellations looks limited. The best results are obtained on AAL116, while performance drops noticeably on CC200 and CC400.That suggests the method may be somewhat sensitive to atlas choice and granularity, which weakens the claim that it is a generally robust FC forecasting framework.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Regarding Brownian Bridge and GATAE,the notation of fθ may cause confusion.In our paper,fθ is not a diffusion score function or reverse-time drift,but a Brownian Bridge residual estimator.Given the bridge state,time step,and condition,the network predicts the residual between this state and the clean lateage latent endpoint.During sampling,this residual is subtracted from the bridge state to estimate the lateage latent endpoint.We will clarify that m_t=t/T is Brownian Bridge interpolation coefficient.S is a fixed maxvar hyperparameter controlling noise strength.Specifically,the corrected form is lambda_2(t)=m_{t-1}-m_t (delta_{t-1}/delta_t) ((1-m_t)/(1-m_{t-1})),which defines the time-dependent coefficient of the earlyage endpoint.The reverse step will be rewritten as an endpoint-estimation based Brownian Bridge sampling step:fθ estimates the lateage endpoint from the current bridge state.The next state is computed using this endpoint,the earlyage endpoint,and a variance-based correction term.agediff/ratio augment age cues.For nonMarkovian sampling,200 steps reduce denoising calls compared with 1K steps while keeping similar performance. For GATAE,hi,W,a_ij,o,and N_i denote the ROI node feature,projection matrix,attention parameter,activation function,and topk neighbor set.For each FC,the graph is built by selecting topk neighbors from each ROI row.The topk graph is a sample-specific computational graph for GAT message passing,while the FC itself remains symmetric for reconstruction and evaluation.We used k=30 and add k=20/60 ablations:k=20 gives MSE/PCC/SSIM/Cos of 0.29/0.61/0.47/0.96,and k=60 gives 0.31/0.60/0.46/0.95.These results show that k=30 better balances sparsity and performance. Regarding earlyFC copying,we agree that high similarity to early FC requires clarification.Table4 is used to examine whether the generated change magnitude is close to the true longitudinal change.For AAL,rawearly vs rawlate gives PCC/SSIM about 0.63/0.47,while rawearly vs generated late gives 0.61/0.45,lower than the true longitudinal similarity.Thus, Table 4 does not support the concern raised by Reviewer1.Since age gaps are small and individual FC has strong fingerprints,generated late FC should preserve subject-specific organization while adding age-related changes.If the model copied earlyFC as predicted lateFC,it would be the early-copy baseline,which gives MSE=0.56,PCC=0.63,SSIM=0.46,and Cos=0.93.Our method has lower MSE and higher SSIM/Cos,indicating that it does not simply copy earlyFC. Regarding data splitting,the concern mainly comes from the insufficient description of the subject level protocol in the original manuscript.We carefully rechecked the implementation to confirm whether the experiments followed subject level separation. To make the protocol fully explicit,we further repeated the experiments under the strictly defined subject level split with multiple random seeds and conducted statistical analyses.The results show that the conclusions from the main comparisons(shared HPs-epochs,etc.for fairness) and ablations remain consistent under this protocol.In the revision, we will clarify the split, report the results, and add paired tests with 95% CIs. For baselines,early-to-late FC prediction is a conditional generative forecasting task.DDPM,etc. were selected as representative generative baselines,while existing studies mainly focus on cross-modal SC-FC generation and lack a widely accepted reproducible longitudinal FC forecasting baseline.To address this concern,we will further explore and add rare longitudinal FC forecasting baselines. Finally, we will frame the results as methodological feasibility on a healthy cohort.The cross-atlas analysis was designed to examine how ROI granularity affects prediction and to justify AAL116 as the main atlas.AAL116 best fits the current model and data scale,while CC200/400 remain usable but degrade as more ROIs increase dimensionality,sparsity,noise sensitivity,subject variability.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): I recommend an Invite for Rebuttal. The reviewers recognized the importance and relevance of the problem—age-conditioned longitudinal functional connectivity forecasting—and appreciated the technical combination of a Graph Attention Autoencoder with a Brownian Bridge diffusion model. However, there are significant methodological and presentation concerns that must be addressed. A primary issue raised by all reviewers is the lack of clarity regarding the train/validation/test splitting protocol; the authors must explicitly confirm whether the splits were performed at the subject level to completely rule out data leakage between within-subject scan pairs. Methodologically, the reviewers noted insufficient transparency in the Brownian Bridge formulation (specifically the inconsistent role of f_theta, the reverse-time update derivation in Eqs. 9-10, and the form of \lambda_2(t)) and in the GAT structure (e.g., how the top-k graph construction handles undirectedness and consistency). The rebuttal must clarify these mathematical details and define all notations (e.g., h, o(), a, W, \mathcal{N}(i), m_t, S, age_diff, age_ratio). Furthermore, the evaluation needs strengthening: reviewers highlighted the need for a stronger, domain-specific FC forecasting baseline rather than relying solely on generic generative models (DDPM, GAN, Flow-based), and requested an ablation study on the choice of k=30 for the top-k connections. Finally, the authors should temper their clinical claims given the single healthy cohort used, address the performance drop observed across different parcellations (CC200/CC400), and explain how the generated FC ensures physiologically plausible temporal progression rather than simply retaining early-age features. | The paper introduces a novel and well-motivated approach for age-conditioned longitudinal functional connectivity forecasting using a Brownian Bridge diffusion model, which is naturally suited for paired developmental prediction. In their rebuttal, the authors successfully addressed the most critical concerns regarding potential data leakage by verifying their results under a strict subject-level data split, while also clarifying the mathematical formulation of their diffusion process. Although one reviewer remained concerned about the lack of domain-specific baselines, the rigorous re-evaluation and methodological clarifications convinced the majority of reviewers that the work is technically sound and warrants acceptance. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): On balance the authors managed to address most of the key reviewer concerns including: subject level data splitting, the formulation of the Brownian Bridge. The description of the ablation study and comparison methods was not very convincing. However as per MICCAI guidelines it is not appropriate to ask for new experiments in the rebuttal, and on balance these new experiments are not essential to the core claims of the authors. The key sticking issue is the potential for copying of early FC in the model, which the reviewer that raised this point is not convinced by the response. Indeed the authors should consider adding more explanation in the manuscript and also explain the limitations/assumptions on relying on similarity measures to identify copying of measures. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers were satistfied with the rebuttal. The authors should address the remaining concerns in the camera-ready version.

title: Bayesian Topological Analysis of Brain Networks
reviewer_1_strengths: Enhanced Sensitivity to Subtle Alterations: A key strength is the method’s superior sensitivity in detecting early pathological changes. The framework successfully identified topological network differences related to amyloid accumulation, which traditional permutation tests failed to reveal. Superior Computational Efficiency: The Bayesian approach demonstrates better scalability for large datasets compared to standard permutation testing. While permutation test execution time grows linearly with the number of resamples, the MCMC-based Bayesian framework requires significantly less total execution time, making it highly feasible for large-cohort clinical studies. Rigorous Multi-Stage Evaluation: The work is supported by a strong evaluation strategy that includes both simulated experiments (confirming consistency with classical tests) and real-world application to fMRI data from an Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The authors acknowledge that confirming very subtle network shifts in preclinical stages requires much larger datasets than the one used in this study. The current sample size may not be enough to definitively prove these early changes across different populations.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The major strength of this work is the introduction of a Bayesian framework to better capture network topology compared to traditional frequentist statistics. This makes the results more interpretable and transparent while eliminating arbitrary statistical cutoffs.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are several major weaknesses in this paper. First and foremost, I am not confident this is a novel application. The authors even mention that use of Bayesian hierarchical/multilevel models in the future directions. But this approach has been established for several years now (Chen et al., 2019, Neuroinformatics). So, I am not sure what this paper is adding to the literature and I did not see anything currently in the work that explicitly states how this is different than other Bayesian fMRI network approaches. Second, there needs to be more details about fMRI processing, especially the connectivity metric used to generate the connectivity matrices. This can have a massive effect on results. Third, there is no justification given for the use of Wasserstein distance within this approach. The first paragraph is all about this metric but the clinical or neurobiological meaning for differences in this metric are never given. Last, an image of a brain with subnetworks that have dissimilar Wasserstein distance or even a schematic explaining the metric and intended analyses.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper combines persistent homology–based representations of brain networks with Bayesian statistical inference. This integration is interesting because it replaces traditional permutation testing with a probabilistic framework that provides richer outputs (e.g., posterior distributions and Bayes factors), enabling more nuanced interpretation of group differences. 2.The authors model Wasserstein-based distances using a Gamma distribution with suitable priors, acknowledging their non-negative and skewed nature. This is a principled choice that improves over naive Gaussian assumptions and shows good alignment between data properties and modeling. 3.The method is applied to fMRI data stratified by amyloid and tau status, which is an important and timely problem. The observed stronger effects for tau compared to amyloid are consistent with known disease progression, supporting the biological plausibility of the approach.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The main components are already well established: persistent homology for brain networks, Wasserstein distances for persistence diagrams, and Bayesian hypothesis testing. The method mainly combines these by replacing permutation tests with a Bayesian model, representing an incremental extension. 2.The model assumes independence of pairwise distances, which is incorrect since distances share subjects. This likely inflates confidence and Bayes factors. The key amyloid result is not robust and disappears in the sensitivity analysis, weakening the main claim. 3.Experiments are not sufficiently comprehensive. Simulations are simplistic, and real-data evaluation uses a private dataset with limited protocol details. The method should be validated on public datasets with clearly described preprocessing and evaluation protocols, and compared with stronger baselines (such as other graph-based methods or machine learning methods) to demonstrate practical advantage.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC for their careful reading. We address the major concerns below, grouped by theme. 1.Novelty vs. existing Bayesian fMRI methods (R3, R4). R3 notes that our future-work mention of Bayesian hierarchical models overlaps with Chen et al. (2019) and asks how this work differs from existing Bayesian fMRI approaches. The distinction lies in the modeling target. Chen et al. and related methods place priors on regional scalar effects (activation values, connectivity-matrix entries) to address multiple testing in mass-univariate analyses. Our framework instead performs Bayesian inference on a fundamentally different object: pairwise Wasserstein distances between persistence diagrams(Sec. 2.1), global, multiscale topological summaries of the functional connectome. To our knowledge, no prior work performs Bayesian inference on the distribution of topological network distances. The specific contribution (Sec. 2.2) is a gamma likelihood on within/between Wasserstein distances with log-normal priors on the mean, yielding posterior inference and Bayes factors. Our future-work mention of “Bayesian hierarchical” denotes extending this topological-distance likelihood with subject-level priors, a different pipeline level from Chen-style region-level modeling. 2.Independence assumption and amyloid robustness (R4). R4 raises that within/between distances share subjects, violating independence, and notes that the amyloid effect attenuates under the subject-level analysis. This is addressed in Sec. 3 Sensitivity Analysis (Table 3): a patient-level summary aggregates distances per subject, removing shared-subject dependence. Two findings are central. (i) Tau-related topological differences remain decisive under both the primary and patient-level models(BF10 = 1.12×10^36 and 6.53×10^3), demonstrating robustness to the independence assumption. (ii) The amyloid effect attenuates under the stricter model, which is biologically consistent with amyloid representing an earlier, subtler preclinical stage than tau (Sec. 3; Discussion). The framework correctly separates strong from subtle signals rather than uniformly inflating evidence — a methodological strength. 3.fMRI pipeline, connectivity, and Wasserstein interpretation (R3). Sec. 3 reports fMRIPrep preprocessing on the ADRC cohort with AAL-116 parcellation, following the pipeline of [19]; connectivity matrices were computed via Pearson correlation between regional BOLD time series, with a filtration over correlation thresholds yielding the persistence diagrams used in Sec. 2.1.Wasserstein distances quantify differences in the birth/death structure of connected components (H0) and cycles (H1) — capturing how functional modules form, merge, and dissolve across scales. Such multiscale reorganization is a recognized correlate of large-scale network disruption in neurodegeneration (Sec. 1; ref. [19]; see also Songdechakraiwut, Shen & Chung, MICCAI21; Chung et al., ISBI19; Lee et al., TMI12). 4.Validation, baselines, simulations (R2, R4). R2 raises sample-size concerns; R4 asks about public datasets and method baselines. Permutation testing — the standard non-parametric baseline — is reported alongside our Bayesian results in all experiments (Tables 1–3). Simulations on stochastic block models provide controlled validation with known ground truth. The ADRC cohort further provides biological ground truth via amyloid and tau PET, a stronger anchor than label-only validation. Replication in larger preclinical cohorts is the principal limitation, stated in Sec. 4. 5.MIC/CAI relevance (R3). The framework targets and is validated on fMRI-based discrimination of clinical groups in Alzheimer’s disease — a core medical-imaging-and-computing problem. Topological brain-network analysis is an active MICCAI direction this Bayesian framework extends. We hope these clarifications address the major concerns and respectfully ask the reviewers to reconsider their assessments.

title: Brain-DiT: A Universal Multi-state fMRI Foundation Model with Metadata-Conditioned Pretraining
reviewer_1_strengths: This is a paper with a huge workload. I like the scope: moving past single-state pretraining to build a truly universal multi-state representation is exactly what the field needs. Using a diffusion objective is a smart choice here, as it naturally gives you a nice hierarchy of features across timesteps. The experimental package is super robust. The fact that the frozen-backbone results are this strong really proves that the pretraining actually learned useful, generalizable representations, rather than just relying on fine-tuning downstream.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The elephant in the room is the metadata conditioning. You’re feeding the model age, sex, and disease info during pretraining, but then evaluating it on downstream tasks that predict those exact variables. It’s hard to untangle whether the downstream performance boost is coming from a universal representation or just side-information leakage from the pretraining phase. The unconditional ablation helps a bit, but it doesn’t entirely put the issue to bed. Also, since some of your ID benchmarks are drawn from the pretraining datasets, you need to be explicitly clear about how you guaranteed strict subject/site-level data separation.

reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Training uses multiple brain states, unifying almost 350 thousand sessions and 24 datasets containing different states, 2.Its the first model that includes metadata-conditioned pertaining 3.The model is outperforming other solutions in ID and OOD tasks. 4.The code and parameters are available, what increases reproducibility and future usage.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.the amount of models used for comparison is very limited 2.there are only 4 datasets used as evaluation and there is no description of how different they were from training ones
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper proposes a novel diffusion-based foundation model for fMRI with metadata conditioning, which is an interesting and original way to model heterogeneous brain imaging data across different brain states. Another major strength is the strong empirical performance: pretraining on 24 datasets is substantial in scale, and the reported state-of-the-art results suggest that the approach is effective in practice.

In particular, it is unclear why different baselines were used across experiments and why not all datasets were included in the frozen-backbone evaluation, and in several cases it is also difficult to understand what the actual task is for each dataset. 2.Comparisons to scratch training are missing, and depending on the answer to the point above, comparisons to full fine-tuning or linear probing would also be important. author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and address the major concerns regarding metadata leakage, data separation, evaluation scope, and baseline clarity. Metadata conditioning and leakage (R1). We clarify that there is no downstream metadata or label leakage. In every downstream task, the model uses only fMRI input; no metadata, including age, sex, diagnosis, site, or dataset labels, is used as downstream input. Metadata conditioning during pretraining is not a prediction shortcut, but an encoded condition vector used only for the denoising objective, helping the denoiser learn how fMRI signals vary across age, sex, and clinical groups. As described in Sec. 2.2 and Sec. 3.1, CFG-style condition dropout replaces metadata embeddings with an unconditional embedding (p_drop=10%), reducing reliance on metadata alone. Brain-DiT(uncond) removes metadata conditioning entirely during pretraining and is evaluated under the same fMRI-only downstream protocol. Its strong performance against representative baselines shows that diffusion-based denoising itself is a stronger pretraining proxy, while the improvement of Brain-DiT over Brain-DiT(uncond) reflects the additional benefit of metadata-guided denoising rather than downstream label leakage. Data separation, evaluation protocol, and OOD scope (R1&R2&R3). We clarify that all ID evaluations use strict subject-level separation within each dataset/site. Subjects are split 7:1:2 before pretraining and downstream evaluation. For ID datasets overlapping with the pretraining corpus, held-out test subjects and their fMRI windows are strictly excluded from pretraining, downstream training, and model selection. For OOD evaluation, NKI, ADHD-200, and PPMI are held out at the dataset level from pretraining, tuning, and model selection to test cross-dataset shifts. In terms of evaluation scope, the manuscript reports 11 downstream evaluation settings, rather than only the 4 frozen-backbone settings. Table 1 reports full fine-tuning results over 7 settings, covering ID and OOD evaluations. Table 2 reports a 4-setting frozen-backbone linear-probing evaluation, also covering ID and OOD tasks, to assess representation transfer without updating the backbone. Thus, Table 2 is a transfer subset, not the full evaluation set. The actual tasks are: HCP binary sex classification; ABIDE, SALD, and NKI-AGE age regression; ADHD-200 binary disease classification; PPMI 3-class disease classification; and NKI-EDU 3-class education classification. Given 24 datasets and 7 comparison models/variants, we designed a representative suite rather than an exhaustive dataset-model grid, covering ID/OOD generalization, classification/regression, and full/frozen-backbone transfer. Baseline selection and experimental protocol (R2&R3). Brain-DiT is an ROI-level model, so our full fine-tuning comparison focuses on ROI-level baselines, including BrainLM, BrainMass, and Brain-JEPA, to avoid confounding pretraining quality with voxel-level input granularity and end-to-end model capacity. In the frozen-backbone setting, the goal is to isolate transferable pretrained representations rather than adaptation capacity; therefore, we additionally include compatible voxel-level baselines. This shows that Brain-DiT learns strong transferable representations without dense voxel-level inputs and can outperform compatible voxel-level variants. For all baselines, we use the authors’ official implementations and public checkpoints, with downstream fine-tuning/linear probing under the same splits and protocol. For classification tasks, we used fixed task definitions and balanced downstream splits to control class imbalance. Thus, Accuracy is meaningful under the same split/metric protocol across methods. F1 was also included in the original protocol to complement Accuracy under balanced splits, with consistent conclusions, but was omitted from the main tables due to MICCAI space constraints; we apologize for not making this explicit.

title: Brain-TM: Decoding Brain States from Functional Networks Using a Hierarchical Spatiotemporal Transformer-Mamba
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The model effectively bridges local graph topology and global temporal dynamics. It uses GIN for local node embedding, a masked Cross-Attention mechanism to aggregate nodes into 17 specific functional networks, and the Mamba architecture to efficiently model long-range temporal state transitions without the quadratic computational bottleneck of standard temporal Transformers. 2.The authors map latent temporal features to task-specific spatial attention weights, utilize Gini coefficients to quantify “Distributed vs. Hub-Driven” network patterns, and validate the topological dominance of these hubs.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Brain-TM is designed as a spatiotemporal model that captures dynamic functional connectivity across sliding windows. However, the chosen baselines (e. g. , GAT, GCN, BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN) are predominantly static spatial graph models. Comparing a dynamic sequence model against static snapshot models inherently favors the former. The paper lacks a comparison against contemporary dynamic spatiotemporal models (such as ST-GCN or dynamic variants of the Brain Network Transformer) 2.The experimental methodology states that performance was assessed using a “5-fold stratified cross-validation”. However, it is not clear whether this split was strictly bounded at the subject level. If sliding windows from the same subject are randomly distributed across training and testing sets, the model may simply learn to identify subject-specific baselines rather than generalizing cognitive tasks. 3.In the ablation study, replacing the Mamba module with a standard Transformer resulted in a severe performance collapse, dropping from 94.71% to 82.72%. Given that Transformers typically excel at capturing temporal dependencies, this 12% drop is very strange and may raise critical concerns regarding whether the baseline Transformer was optimally tuned (e. g. , adequate layers, heads, and positional encodings). 4.The model uses a sliding window strategy with window sizes ranging from 10 to 35 TRs. Considering that HCP task-fMRI data utilizes a block design with relatively short task durations, larger windows (e. g. , 30-35 TRs) will span across multiple cognitive states for most of tasks. This temporal blurring may introduce highly mixed signals into a single dynamic adjacency matrix, which contradicts the paper’s claim of identifying task-specific functional representations.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.State-of-the-art classification performance with strong ablation evidence justifying each architectural component. 2.Interpretability is built into the architecture, with attention weights serving dual roles as both computational mechanisms and biological readouts. 3.Hub-driven findings are consistent with established neuroscience literature (DMN, Salience, Control networks).
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.5-fold cross-validation is used for classification performance, but the interpretability analysis in 2.3 appears to be done on the full dataset without cross-validation. The paper doesn’t describe how clustering or hub identification varies across folds. If hub identity shifts across folds, the discovery is fragile. 2.The number of brain states is constrained to equal the number of task classes, which almost guarantees task-state alignment by construction. What if the cluster number k is not 7? 3.No test across different parcellations (only Schaefer 200 + Yeo 17 used). Hub findings could be parcellation-dependent. 4.The paper doesn’t discuss if the discoveries truely reflect biology or they are caused by architecture bias. For example, cross-attention mask design directly induces hubs. High Gini in attention weights could simply reflect that some ROIs happen to have stronger initial BOLD signal variance, which the attention mechanism amplifies, rather than true biological hub organization. The authors could test whether the same hub pattern emerges with a different aggregation scheme (e.g. mean pooling instead of cross-attention). The authors could also compare hub identity against known neuroanatomical hubs (e.g. precuneus, posterior cingulate, angular gyrus). Another potential method is to run the same Gini analysis on a shuffled label control (i.e. retrain the network with shuffled labels). If hub patterns persist even with randomized task labels, they reflect architecture not biology. 5.The claim that global functional integration is ‘driven by’ localized hub activations overstates what the evidence supports. The analysis relies on attention weight distributions and centrality metrics derived from a model trained on task classification, which are correlational observations, not causal evidence. 6.It would be helpful to clarify whether the node features projected into the embedding space in GIN are the thresholded functional connectivity values between each node and all other nodes.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The core strength of Brain-TM lies in the anatomical structure mask constraint mechanism introduced within its spatial aggregation module: by embedding a binary mask derived from the Schaefer-17 functional atlas into the Cross-Attention operation, the framework enforces that the representation of each functional network is generated exclusively from the weighted embeddings of the brain regions that anatomically belong to it, thereby eliminating cross-network information contamination. This hard-constraint design not only ensures the biological fidelity of the subsequent Intra-Net Attention weights—allowing the contribution of each region to its network to be rigorously quantified—but also provides a generalizable embedding paradigm for incorporating prior neuroanatomical knowledge into deep graph models, effectively bridging the semantic gap between data-driven feature learning and established functional system boundaries.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Major Weakness 1: Outdated and Unfair Baseline Comparisons, Failure to Align with True State-of-the-Art Methods. In Table 1, the authors compare Brain-TM against GAT (Veličković et al., 2018), GCN (Kipf & Welling, 2017), GraphSAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017), BrainNetCNN (Kawahara et al., 2017), and BrainGNN (Li et al., 2021). All of these methods are static functional connectivity classification models, whereas Brain-TM takes dynamic functional connectivity sequences as input. This comparison is severely imbalanced in terms of information content and cannot substantiate claims of architectural superiority. Within the past three years, several widely recognized strong baselines for dynamic brain network modeling have emerged. For instance, STAGIN(Kim et al., NeurIPS 2021) reported approximately 96.8% accuracy on HCP seven-task classification, and BolT (Bedel et al., ICCV 2023 ) achieved around 97.2%. In the realm of static feature engineering, the work of Sripada et al. (High-accuracy machine learning techniques for functional connectome fingerprinting and cognitive state decoding, Nature Communications or related conference versions) has even reported classification accuracies exceeding 99%. The 94.7% accuracy reported for Brain-TM, in the absence of direct comparison with the aforementioned state-of-the-art methods, is far from sufficient to support its claim of “superior performance.” Major Weakness 2: Circular Reasoning in Brain State Clustering Analysis and Lack of Independent Quantitative Validation. The authors perform K-Means clustering on the intermediate features output by the Mamba module, determine the number of clusters K=7 using the elbow method and silhouette coefficient, and claim that the seven clusters correspond strongly to the seven HCP tasks. However, the model’s classification head itself contains seven neurons (corresponding to the seven tasks). After supervised training with cross-entropy loss, the feature space is inevitably partitioned into seven linearly separable subspaces. Performing K=7 clustering on this feature space and finding alignment with task labels is an inevitable mathematical consequence of model convergence, rather than an objective discovery of naturally emergent brain state numbers. Furthermore, the authors report no quantitative metrics—such as Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), or Cluster Purity—to assess clustering quality against ground-truth labels, relying solely on visual inspection of diagonal intensity in a heatmap, which is statistically insufficient. No sensitivity analysis is provided to examine whether the state-task correspondence remains stable if the number of clusters is changed to, for instance, K=5 or K=10.Major Weakness 3: Complete Absence of Generalizability Validation; the Model May Be Severely Overfitted to HCP Data Acquisition Characteristics. All experiments are conducted exclusively on the HCP Young Adult dataset, with performance evaluated via internal five-fold cross-validation. HCP data are renowned for their high temporal resolution (TR = 0.72 s), multi-band multi-echo acquisition sequences, and advanced ICA-FIX denoising, resulting in substantially higher signal-to-noise ratios than those found in most clinical or large-scale developmental cohorts (e.g., ABCD, UK Biobank, PNC). The authors provide no model transfer testing on any external dataset, nor do they design any cross-site or cross-acquisition-parameter validation experiments. Consequently, the reported 94.7% accuracy and the proposed “hub-driven” brain state mechanisms may well reflect idiosyncratic features specific to the HCP acquisition protocol rather than generalizable cognitive neuroscience principles. Major Weakness 4: Severe Imbalance Between Model Complexity and Marginal Performance Gain. Ablation experiments in Table 2 demonstrate that when the Hierarchical Transformer module is removed (i.e., retaining only GIN and Mamba, directly modeling temporal sequences across the 200 brain regions), classification accuracy remains at 93.73%, falling short of the full model (94.71%) by less than one percentage point. This negligible difference raises fundamental questions about the necessity of the hierarchical aggregation mechanism: introducing complex anatomically masked Cross-Attention and the 17-network inductive bias yields minimal practical performance improvement while substantially increasing computational overhead and model complexity. The authors attribute the primary value of the hierarchical module to “enhanced interpretability,” but they do not demonstrate whether similar hub localization results could be obtained from the flattened model via gradient or attention analysis. If comparable interpretations can be derived from the flattened model, then the current architecture exhibits clear signs of over-engineering.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: Dear Reviewer, Area Chairs, and Program Chairs, We thank the meta-reviewer (MR) and Reviewer (R) 1&2&3s’ constructive reviews (e.g. Rx.x). We have synthesized our responses into 5 key thematic areas (T1-T5). T1: Comparison with Dynamic Spatiotemporal Models (MR, R1, R3) R1.1: Brain-TM (94.71%) outperforms current dynamic spatiotemporal models like ST-GCN (93.42%) and Brain Network Transformer (94.37%). R3.1: Although STAGIN achieves higher accuracy with a finer atlas, we prioritize brain interpretability analysis. Unlike STAGIN, which relies on high-resolution atlases, we use the widely adopted, standard Schaefer 200 for ROI-to-17-network mapping, thereby achieving more robust biological interpretability and task-specific hub identification. T2: Sliding Window Impacts, Clustering Validity, and Task-Driven Brain States (MR, R1, R2, R3) R1.4: For sliding window impacts, our sensitivity analysis shows moderate windows optimize accuracy by minimizing temporal blurring. Furthermore, varying window sizes yields distinct neurobiological insights (Fig. 2C): short windows emphasize rapid-response networks, longer windows highlight sustained integration. R2.2&R3.2: We clarify that our goal is to decode task related states, not claim ‘seven natural latent states’. And the clustering results depend on objective quantitative indicators, rather than visual heatmap inspection (“natural” and “heatmap” did not appear in the original manuscript). We combined Silhouette Score and Inertia Curve to explore K=1 to 15, with quantitative metrics peaking exactly at K=7 and delivering the optimal clustering partition. T3: Cross-Validation Protocol and Atlas/Dataset Generalizability (MR, R1, R2, R3) R1.2&2.1: Our 5-fold CV is strictly subject-level: All sliding windows of an individual subject are assigned entirely to training or testing sets, preventing data leakage. Our hub identification shows high stability across all 5 CV folds, hub locations are consistent across test sets, the 94.71% accuracy reflects true cross-subject generalization. While our visualization used one fold due to space limits, cross-fold statistical consistency was rigorously verified. R2.3&R3.3: We acknowledge parcellations may cause minor boundary variations, but the Schaefer 200 was chosen as a widely adopted dynamic connectomics standard. Our node-to-network dual analysis mitigates parcellation bias and ensures neuroanatomically reliable findings. The HCP dataset is the neuroimaging community’s benchmark, supporting interpretation and direct literature comparison. Validating diverse datasets is added to our Future Work. T4: Architectural Bias in Hub Identification and Hierarchical Necessity (MR, R2, R3) R2.4&R2.5: For architectural bias, we clarify our design uses prior knowledge to explore functional hubs, not enforce them. GIN embedding prevents BOLD variance amplification, and masks only limit affiliations. Thus, the identified hubs (posterior cingulate, prefrontal cortex) are strictly data-driven. Crucially, mean pooling reduces accuracy but still yields highly overlapping hubs via centrality metrics, while label-shuffling destroys these patterns entirely. Lastly, we have replaced all causal phrasing in the manuscript with correlational terms. R3.4: For Hierarchical Necessity, removing the module drops accuracy to 93.73%, and renders the model a black box with unstable attention weights. The 17-network bias is not over-engineering, but a vital constraint for stable, biological hub localization. T5: Clarification on Ablation and GIN (R1, R2) R1.3: The Transformer baseline was grid-searched (lr: 1e-4~1e-3&dropout: 0.1~0.5). The performance gap is not due to suboptimal baseline configuration, mainly due to Mamba’s inherent superiority in capturing dynamic fMRI sequences. R2.6: We clarify GIN node features are derived from functional connectivity profiles. At window t, each node v is represented by the corresponding row of thresholded matrix A_t, and updated via Eq. (1).
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Although the proposed hierarchical spatiotemporal framework and its interpretability analysis are interesting, critical evaluation flaws necessitate a rebuttal. The authors should address: (1) unfair baseline comparisons by including recent dynamic spatiotemporal SOTA models; (2) circular reasoning and lack of quantitative metrics in the clustering-based interpretability analysis; (3) clarifications on subject-level cross-validation to rule out data leakage; (4) potential architecture bias in hub identification and the marginal performance gain of the hierarchical module; and (5) the lack of cross-dataset generalizability validation. | The authors clarified the strict subject-level data splitting to rule out data leakage (R1, R2), explained that the clustering analysis was quantitatively driven (R2, R3), and justified the architectural design choices regarding baselines and the necessity of the hierarchical module for biological interpretability (R2, R3). Reviewers 1 and 2 explicitly upgraded their scores to Accept, recognizing the method’s innovation and the value of its built-in interpretability for the neuroimaging community. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This is a borderline case. While the rebuttal addresses many concerns related to the model tuning and experimental setup, in my opinion, the main weakness of the original paper was the lack of appropriate spatio-temporal baselines. title: BrainACU: Asynchronous Coordination Unit Modeling for Dynamic Brain Network Analysis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.Relaxing the “zero-lag” synchrony assumption is physiologically well-motivated, as neural propagation involves inherent delays. 2.The consensus clustering approach for CU discovery allows the model to adapt to different disorders where canonical templates might be suboptimal. 3.The model was tested on multiple disorders (ASD, MDD, BD) and outperformed dynamic baselines like BrainDGT and ST-GCN.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The proposed “Coordination Units” are essentially derived from k-means clustering over ROIs. This is conceptually similar to many existing parcellation or clustering-based approaches and does not fundamentally differ from prior functional grouping methods. 2.The authors fix the number of Coordination Units at K=3.While the paper argues that fixed templates restrict the discovery of complex patterns, the proposed data-driven CU discovery via consensus clustering essentially functions as a clustering-based parcellation. Setting K=3 is biologically oversimplified, as the human brain is typically organized into more granular networks (e. g. , Yeo 7 or 17 networks). The authors have not demonstrated how these learned CUs correspond to known functional systems. Additionally, without visualizing these ROI-to-CU mappings or providing a biological mapping, it is difficult to determine if the “asynchronous delays” learned between these units are neuroscientifically meaningful or merely data artifacts. 3.The framework maps variable-sized CU signals to a shared latent dimension d using CU-specific linear projections. However, if the number of ROIs within each CU varies significantly, projecting them into the same low-dimensional space (d=36) may lead to severe information bottlenecks for large CUs or representation bias for smaller ones. A more detailed justification or sensitivity analysis regarding this dimension alignment is required. 4.Regarding Equation 8, the L_lag penalty successfully forces the model to capture time-shifted dependencies. However, since the brain is partitioned into only three broad units, the granularity of the “dynamics” being modeled is quite coarse. If a single CU aggregates regions with distinct functions, the resulting time-lagged signals might represent an uninterpretable average of multiple competing processes. The authors should clarify what these units represent to justify the analysis of their temporal delays. 5.The evaluation on ABIDE is restricted to the NYU site. While this reduces multi-center variability, it limits the assessment of the model’s robustness and generalization. Please clarify if this selection was due to sample size constraints at other sites or concerns regarding overfitting, and discuss the model’s potential performance in a multi-site transfer learning setting. 6.The asynchronous interaction module models directed cross-CU attention across a token timeline. The authors should provide a quantitative discussion on the computational overhead (FLOPS, inference time) compared to standard self-attention or static GNN baselines to justify the added architectural complexity.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The two core limitations addressed — fixed subnetwork partitioning and the synchronization assumption — are both well-motivated by neuroscientific evidence and clearly distinguished from prior work. The use of directed cross-CU attention to jointly model time-aligned and time-lagged coordination is a principled and elegant design that directly addresses the synchrony bias in existing dynamic connectivity methods. The ablation study systematically removes each component and reports consistent performance drops across all three diagnostic tasks, providing clear evidence for the contribution of CU discovery, latent alignment, asynchronous interaction, and each regularization term. The lag-step statistics further offer mechanistically interpretable evidence that disease groups exhibit larger temporal delays in cross-CU coordination, connecting the model’s behavior to known neurophysiology.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: A critical inconsistency exists between Table 1 and Table 2.The methodology states that K=3 is used throughout, yet the performance reported for K=3 in Table 2 (e.g., 81.0%/80.1% ACC/AUC for HC vs. MDD) is substantially higher than the full model reported in Table 1 (76.8%/77.9%). These two tables appear to report results under different experimental conditions without explanation, raising serious concerns about the reliability of the reported numbers. The model is constrained to K=3 coordination units across all tasks and disorders, which is a very coarse granularity relative to established brain network parcellations. The rationale for fixing K=3 is based solely on a grid search showing K=3 outperforms K=2, 4, and 5, but a broader range and task-specific sensitivity analysis would be needed to justify this as a general choice. The primary dataset (MDD and BD cohort) is private, with institution and ethics details anonymized. Combined with a relatively small sample size (246 HC, 151 MDD, 126 BD), this limits both reproducibility and the generalizability of the reported performance. The public evaluation is restricted to a single ABIDE site (NYU, 172 subjects), which is insufficient to establish broad applicability across datasets.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: It is interesting and novel to model both time-aligned and time-lagged dependencies across data-driven coordination units via directed cross-CU attention, it enables the architecture to integrate dynamic brain network information more effectively by modeling asynchronous interactions among subnetworks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: a) For the Asynchronous Interaction Module, the lagged interactions are modeled at the CU level, where CUs are obtained via data-driven clustering (with K=3 in experiments), raising concerns regarding interpretability. Since these CUs represent abstract groupings rather than predefined neurobiological units, and because interactions are primarily learned at this coarse level, the model’s biological interpretability remains inherently constrained. A deeper exploration of the learned interactions (e.g., attention patterns) align with established neurobiological principles would strengthen the paper. b) The paper states that hyperparameters were tuned on an internal validation set using a five-fold cross-validation scheme. However, the results reported in Table 1 (e.g., NYU: ACC =72.3%, AUC=74.1%) exceed those those in Table 2 for K=3 (ACC =71.0%, AUC =71.8%), which is quite counterintuitive. To ensure reproducibility and methodological transparency, the authors should explicitly clarify whether these results are obtained under identical data splits, train/validation/test boundaries, and evaluation protocols. Moreover, due to the limited sample size, performance variance across splits may be significant. Independent validation on larger datasets would strengthen the robustness and generalizability of the reported conclusions. Minor points: a) The notation in Equation 3 lacks sufficient definition; please explicitly define all symbols. b) The architectural logic depicted in Figure 1 is unclear. The relationships between the modules are not clearly defined, leading to confusion. c) In the “Interpretability Analysis of Asynchronous Coordination” section, the disease cohort used for lag-step statistics is not specified.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for constructive feedback. 1.CLARIFICATION ON THE METHODOLOGICAL CONTRIBUTION OF CU DISCOVERY (R1) (a) Our contribution is not k-means itself, but the complete pipeline integrating data-driven CU discovery with asynchronous modeling. Three distinctions from standard parcellation: (i) per-subject clustering of brain regions, aggregated via a co-association matrix, reflecting population coherence while accommodating individual variability; (ii) CUs serve as the organizational basis for lag-aware directed attention, and no prior work combines data-driven macro-unit discovery with explicit time-lagged interaction modeling; (iii) ablation (Table 1, “w/o CU Discovery”) shows fixed partitions degrade all tasks. We acknowledge k-means is standard; the novelty lies in how and why it is deployed, not the algorithm itself. (R1-Q1) 2.JUSTIFICATION FOR K=3 & BIOLOGICAL INTERPRETABILITY (R1, R2, R4) (a) We mapped CU assignments against functional networks (BD cohort). The learned CUs capture functionally coherent circuits: CU0 aggregates subcortical/limbic structures (caudate, putamen, thalamus; 55.6%) with temporal regions, consistent with cortico-subcortical loops for emotion regulation and reward processing [32]; CU1 combines prefrontal DMN (37.2%), CEN (25.6%), and visual areas (18.6%), mirroring the self-referential/executive control axis [17]; CU2 groups sensorimotor cortex (41.4%) with limbic structures (hippocampus, amygdala; 20.7%), reflecting sensory-limbic integration pathways disrupted in affective disorders [5]. No CU maps to a single canonical network, which is by design, consistent with Mitra et al. [20] who showed lag structure is orthogonal to canonical RSNs. Regarding lag interpretability (R1-Q4): if lag signals were within-CU averaging artifacts, they would affect disease and control groups equally; Fig. 2 shows disease groups exhibit systematically larger lag steps [20, 19], and this consistent disease-control divergence serves as functional validation. (R1-Q2/R1-Q4/R4-Q1) (b) K=3 is empirically optimal (Table 2) and consistent with the Triple Network Model [17], which posits three macro-level functional systems underlying psychopathology. Our data-driven CUs recover a compatible three-way granularity without imposing network priors, supporting K=3 as biologically plausible. (R1-Q2/R2-Q2/R4-Q1) 3.DATA INCONSISTENCY BETWEEN TABLE 1 & TABLE 2 (R2, R4) (a) We thank the reviewers for identifying this issue. The inconsistency arose from different random seeds for CV fold partitions between Table 1 and Table 2, which with moderate sample size (N=397) can shift CV means by several percentage points (e.g., K=3 MDD: 81.0% vs. 76.8%). Crucially, K=3 ranks first in all tasks; the relative ordering is unchanged. After unifying fold partitions, the ranking remains identical with K=3 matching Table 1.We will update the camera-ready and open-source all configurations. (R2-Q1/R4-Q2) 4.DIMENSION ALIGNMENT BOTTLENECK (R1) (a) This concern is mitigated by design: our balanced k-means variant (Sec. 2.2) constrains CU sizes to be approximately equal, and each CU has a dedicated projection W_k in R^{d x |V_k|} whose capacity scales with CU size. Sensitivity over d∈{16–64} further confirms stable performance (variance < 0.6%). (R1-Q3) 5.GENERALIZATION & DATASET LIMITATIONS (R1, R2) (a) Evaluated on full multi-site ABIDE (871 subjects, 17 sites): BrainACU achieves 69.7% ACC, outperforming BrainDGT (66.8%) and ST-GCN (57.2%), demonstrating cross-site transferability. (R1-Q5/R2-Q3) 6.COMPUTATIONAL OVERHEAD (R1) (a) Async module adds ~2.5ms inference and ~4.2% FLOPs over a static GNN baseline, operating on M patches with K=3 units. (R1-Q6) 7.NOTATION & FIGURES (R4) (a) Eq.3: A_ij=co-clustering frequency, N=training subjects, z_i^(n)=ROI i cluster label for subject n, C=total ROIs. Will redraw Fig.1 and annotate Fig.2 with cohort details. (R4-Q3/Q4/Q5) Ref: [32] Haber & Knutson, Neuropsychopharmacology 35(1), 4-26 (2010)
