title: BrainHTF: Learning Causal Graph Representation of Brain Connectome with Hyperbolic Transformer
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The integration of causality and hyperbolic geometry is conceptually well motivated for brain connectome analysis. 2.Both empirical performance and interpretability have been demonstrated to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Only two datasets have been used for validation. More brain network datasets should be included to further demonstrate the effectiveness of the method across different brain diseases. 2.Brain network datasets usually contain limited training samples. It is not clear whether the data can support the training of the complex hyperbolic Transformer architecture. 3.The review of existing literature is limited. More recent related works should be discussed.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper combines causal–bias disentanglement, hyperbolic modeling, and causal intervention into a coherent framework. Each component targets a key limitation, and together they enable more robust and meaningful graph representations. The method improves representation capacity via hyperbolic geometry while explicitly modeling causal structure for interpretability. This allows both strong predictive performance and identification of meaningful biomarkers. The model outperforms a wide range of baselines, including GNNs, transformers, and hyperbolic methods.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The mask generator operates at the level of individual edges, implicitly assuming that causal structure can be captured through pairwise interactions. However, real-world brain processes often involve multi-hop and higher-order dependencies, as well as region-level effects spanning groups of neighboring ROIs, which cannot be fully represented by one-step edge-level importance alone. The method identifies “causal” edges through a learned mask, but its stability across different folds or runs is not evaluated. This is important, since claims about causal patterns or biomarkers require some level of consistency; without it, it is difficult to tell whether the identified edges are truly meaningful or just artifacts of training variability.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper presents a clear motivation from limitations of prior work: weak edge-level interpretability and the difficulty of modeling hierarchical brain topology in Euclidean space. It has a clear idea of combining causal disentanglement and hyperbolic representation learning. 2.The empirical evaluation is reasonably convincing. It is supported by ablation studies showing that removing the hyperbolic component, mask disentanglement, or causal intervention reduces performance. 3.The paper is well written with clear overall diagram in Figure 1 and the visualization analysis in Figure 2.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Although the design is inspired by causality, what is presented in the paper is not strict biological causality. The input graph is built from Pearson correlations of fMRI signals, which are associative. Also, the intervention happens on learned latent representations, not on the brain or on an explicit structural causal model. So the claim of causality might be too strong in the paper. 2.Although the ablation studies show that replacing the hyperbolic transformer with a standard transformer reduces accuracy, the work does not thoroughly analyze when hyperbolic space is beneficial. Also, it is unclear why the curvature of the hyperbolic space is set to -3.It is also unclear how other hyperparameters are chosen. 3.Although this work proposes a new method for brain connectome analysis, the contribution is incremental and the components are not new. Hyperbolic transformers already existed in Hypformer, and causal-subgraph / intervention-based invariant graph learning was already established in graph machine learning.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: N/A
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): After reviewing the three reviews (one Weak Reject, two Weak Accept), I find that all reviewers agree the paper has clear strengths. The idea of combining causal disentanglement and hyperbolic geometry for brain connectome analysis is well motivated. The empirical results are convincing, with ablation studies supporting the design choices, and the paper is well written. However, several concerns prevent a stronger recommendation. The main issue is that the paper overclaims causality. The input graphs are built from Pearson correlations, which show associations, not true causes. The intervention happens on learned representations, not on the brain or a real causal model. The authors should soften their language. Reviewer 2 raises two important points. First, the mask generator only looks at individual edges, but real brain processes often involve complex patterns across multiple regions. Second, the stability of the identified causal edges across different training runs is not evaluated, so it is unclear whether the reported biomarkers are reliable. Reviewer 1 notes that only two datasets are used, and it is unclear whether the complex model can be trained effectively on the small sample sizes typical of brain network datasets. Reviewer 3 adds that the choice of hyperbolic curvature is not justified. Regarding novelty, the individual components are not new – hyperbolic Transformers and causal intervention learning already exist. However, combining them for brain connectome analysis is still interesting and can stimulate discussion. This is why I lean toward Weak Accept rather than Reject. In the final version of the paper, the authors should do three things: tone down the causality claims, evaluate the stability of the learned masks across multiple runs, and justify the curvature choice. Addressing these would strengthen the paper significantly.

title: BrainSTR: Spatio-Temporal Contrastive Learning for Interpretable Dynamic Brain Network Modeling
reviewer_1_strengths: (1) The paper addresses a highly meaningful problem. Explicitly targeting spatio-temporal interpretability—identifying both critical time phases and disease-relevant topological patterns—is a valuable and less explored direction in dynamic functional connectivity. (2) The overall design is technically sound and logically flows toward the stated objective. The modules are not disconnected; rather, the APP identifies informative temporal segments, the incremental structure generator extracts disease-related connectivities, and the contrastive objective constructs a discriminative semantic space. (3) The paper reports strong results across three distinct diagnostic tasks (MDD, BD, and ASD). BrainSTR achieves the highest reported ACC and AUC metrics across all tasks in Table 1, such as a notable +2.9% / +6.5% (ACC/AUC) improvement on the MDD dataset over the strongest dynamic baseline. (3) The ablation experiments successfully justify the proposed architecture. Removing the APP, the incremental structure update ($\Delta S$), the contrastive objectives, or the structure regularization terms all lead to performance degradation. (4) The paper goes beyond pure classification metrics. The case-level and group-level visualizations of important phases and retained subnetworks (e. g. , highlighting DMN-related patterns) make the contribution much more compelling than a standard performance-driven dynamic graph paper.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: (1) The contribution appears stronger at the level of framework integration than at the level of sharply novel technical principles. Individual components—such as adaptive temporal partitioning, graph structure masking, and contrastive learning—are closely related to existing ideas in the literature. (2) While the authors note that the Incremental Graph Structure Generator is designed to capture progressive topological changes, they do not empirically justify why this recursive formulation is superior to simpler, independent phase-wise structure learning strategies. Similarly, the APP module’s temporal modeling claims would be much more convincing if compared against simpler adaptive partitioning baselines. (3) The interpretability analysis is promising but predominantly qualitative. While the paper provides retained-connectivity ratios for representative subjects, the group-level findings lack rigorous statistical support. The paper would be significantly stronger with quantitative validation, such as the stability of discovered subnetworks across folds, reproducibility metrics, or statistical significance tests validating the differences between “important” and “non-important” phases. (4) The experimental section reports mean +- std for 5-fold cross-validation, but no statistical significance analysis (e. g. , p-values from t-tests) is provided. This is necessary to conclusively support the reported gains over strong baselines. (5) Broad claims regarding “robust cross-disorder generalization” should be phrased more cautiously, as the ASD experiments are conducted exclusively on the NYU site of the ABIDE dataset (74 ASD, 98 controls) to avoid multi-center variability. (6) The major performance claims on MDD and BD rely entirely on a private cohort of 246 controls, 151 MDD, and 126 BD subjects. Without public access to this dataset, the broader research community cannot independently verify the results or benchmark against them.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.This paper addresses the issue that disease-related signals are sparsely distributed in both time and topology, whereas irrelevant fluctuations and connectivity are pervasive. 2.To improve the interpretability of dynamic functional connectivity (FC), this paper employs a data-driven approach to partition phase boundaries with consistent states and identifies compact, diagnostically critical phases. 3.An incremental graph generator is proposed, which integrates multiple constraints to achieve stable and interpretable connectivity selection within each phase.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The introduction mentions that traditional contrastive learning methods are disturbed by irrelevant signals, which impairs semantic relevance. However, this discussion should be placed in the limitations section rather than in the context of proposing the solution, and should only be briefly addressed there. 2.The authors claim to learn natural boundaries of brain states through the model, yet they still use a sliding window approach for partitioning. As a result, the subsequent data-driven adaptation appears more like a secondary encoding of coarse-grained windows. Does this truly correspond to the switching points of real neural events? 3.The design logic of the proposed model is to first determine temporal boundaries and then select spatial topology within those boundaries. This raises a question: if the temporal phase selection is incorrect, how can the subsequent capture of connectivity patterns be corrected? 4.Adaptive phase partitioning essentially forces a unified timeline for all brain regions. However, brain network activity is not only synchronous but also asynchronous, generating signals at different times. How is this aspect accounted for? 5.How is the time-invariant component defined? The orthogonal approach mentioned can make two vectors uncorrelated, but this is a high-dimensional constraint, not a physiological constraint that ensures they truly represent stable brain states. 6.If the goal is merely to find abnormalities in connection density, such as in the default mode network (DMN), can the proposed method identify more specific patterns compared to ordinary change point detection? 7.Regarding experimental details, the data preprocessing is not clearly described—for example, whether any processing has been applied to the raw data.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Addresses an important problem of spatio-temporal interpretability in dynamic functional connectivity, going beyond standard classification-focused approaches. 2.Proposes a coherent framework that integrates temporal segmentation (APP), graph structure learning, and contrastive learning into a unified pipeline. 3.Introduces a data-driven temporal partitioning (APP) that moves beyond fixed sliding windows, aligning with recent trends in adaptive dFC modeling. 4.Explicitly models disease-relevant vs. irrelevant connectivity, providing a more interpretable and structured representation of brain networks. 5.Demonstrates consistent performance improvements across multiple datasets (MDD, BD, ASD), including strong baselines. 6.Provides both temporal and spatial interpretability, linking identified phases and subnetworks to known brain systems.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Insufficient positioning with respect to prior work. The introduction lacks a clear discussion of existing methods and their limitations, and the relationship between the proposed components and prior work is not well articulated. In particular, the APP module is closely related to adaptive temporal partitioning approaches (e.g., adaptive windowing in [5]), but this connection is not clearly discussed. 2.Unclear novelty of the APP module. Conceptually, APP performs data-driven temporal segmentation via change detection on learned representations, which is similar to existing adaptive segmentation approaches in dFC. The paper does not clearly explain what is fundamentally new beyond implementation details. 3.Design limitations of the incremental structure generator. The structure $S_t$ evolves with strong smoothness constraints and small fixed updates (e.g., $\alpha=0.0$), which may lead to near time-invariant masks and limit the ability to capture phase-specific connectivity. In addition, updates are based on a low-dimensional descriptor rather than the full connectivity $A_t$, potentially restricting expressiveness. 4.Heuristic and insufficiently justified contrastive formulation. The selection of important phases (e.g., threshold $\alpha_t >1/W$) is heuristic, and the contrastive objective introduces a non-standard formulation (e.g., subtracting similarity from $H^0$) without sufficient justification or ablation. 5.Limited experimental validation and analysis. While ablations are provided, they do not fully analyze key design choices (e.g., APP sensitivity, structure update formulation, contrastive components). In addition, experiments are restricted to a single ABIDE site (NYU), raising concerns about generalizability across sites.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank all reviewers and the AC for their constructive feedback and positive assessment. We will carefully revise the manuscript accordingly in the camera-ready version.

title: BrainWeaver: Weaving Dynamic Brain Networks with ROI-Guided Attention for Cognitive Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: Clear and well-structured paper The method, experiments, and ablations are easy to follow, and the overall structure is solid. Well-motivated design The combination of dynamic graphs, ROI priors, and contrastive learning is reasonable and fits the problem setting well. Good experimental coverage Evaluated on multiple cognitive tasks with a range of baselines. The ablation study is helpful and shows the contribution of each component. Interpretability The ROI importance and connectivity analyses are a nice addition and align with known neuroscience patterns.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Small performance gains Improvements over baselines are marginal and sometimes within standard deviation; no statistical significance analysis is provided. Overstated claims on stability The claim of “consistently lower standard deviations” is not fully supported by the results. Insufficient data description While the paper mentions the Neurograph benchmark, key details are missing (e. g. , number of subjects used, data splits, definition of prediction targets). Minor typos Minor writing issues (e. g. , Section 2.1: ‘an ROI-guided’ → ‘a ROI-guided’)
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Clinically valuable problem formulation. Continuous cognitive score regression across three cognitive domains is more informative and clinically actionable than binary classification. Predicting specific cognitive scores enables tracking of cognitive trajectory and early detection of decline, which has direct clinical utility beyond diagnostic labels. Principled use of neuroscience priors. The Multiple Demand (MD) system theory [Duncan, 2010] — which posits that diverse cognitive tasks share a core neural scaffold anchored in prefrontal and parietal cortex — provides well-established neuroscience grounding for the key ROI selection. The differential initialization (Eq. 5: key ROIs=1, non-key=ε) is an elegant compromise that preserves prior knowledge while allowing data-driven refinement, avoiding the brittleness of hard constraints. Comprehensive and convincing interpretability analysis. Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 together provide both node-level (regional importance) and edge-level (topological connectivity) interpretability across all three tasks. The distinct spatial patterns are neuroscientifically plausible: working memory shows a hub-centric pattern centered on left PFC with fronto-parietal connections; inhibitory control shows a balanced mesh topology between frontal eye fields, PFC, and parietal regions reflecting the attention network; general cognitive status shows widespread DMN and associative cortical involvement. These distinct patterns across tasks provide evidence that the model captures task-specific neural substrates rather than a generic signature. Large-scale evaluation with thorough baselines. HCP S1200 (~1200 subjects) is substantially larger than most brain network studies. The comparison against 11 baselines spanning both static (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE) and dynamic (ASTGCN, DySAT, EvolveGCN, TGCN, STAGIN, STNAGNN, Neurograph) architectures is thorough and well-organized. The consistent superiority of dynamic over static models validates the importance of temporal modeling.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: Improvements over SOTA are marginal and lack statistical significance testing — the most critical concern. BrainWeaver vs. Neurograph: Working Memory RMSE 13.40±0.34 vs. 13.60±0.49 (1.5% improvement — confidence intervals overlap); Inhibitory Control RMSE 10.26±0.28 vs. 10.30±0.25 (0.4% improvement — well within noise); General Cognitive Status RMSE 1.08±0.08 vs. 1.13±0.15 (4.4% improvement — more convincing but still moderate). No statistical significance tests (paired t-test, Wilcoxon, or bootstrap confidence intervals) are provided. Without p-values, the claimed SOTA cannot be substantiated. This is a critical omission for a paper whose primary claim is superior performance. The consistently lower standard deviations of BrainWeaver suggest improved stability, but stability alone does not constitute a sufficient contribution. Each component represents incremental variation of existing techniques. (a) The temporal attention fusion (Eq. 1-4) is an attention-weighted averaging over temporal graph snapshots, similar to DySAT [21] and STAGIN [14]. The specific attention computation differs in using separate graph-attention for query/key (Eq. 2), but this is a minor architectural variation. (b) The hierarchical graph representation (Eq. 5-6) uses prior-guided initialization followed by MLP-based importance learning and GAT-based clustering — conceptually similar to DiffPool with a prior-informed initialization. The paper does not compare against or discuss these related pooling methods. (c) The contrastive learning (Eq. 7) is standard symmetric InfoNCE without modification. The “clinical metadata” component raises a potential information leakage concern. The contrastive learning module aligns fMRI representations with “clinical metadata” (Section 2.3), but the specific variables constituting this metadata are never disclosed. If any cognitive-correlated variables (e.g., education level, other cognitive test scores, age) are included, the model gains access to information correlated with the prediction target during training, constituting information leakage. This must be clarified — it could fundamentally invalidate the entire experimental evaluation. Critical experimental details are missing, compromising reproducibility. (a) The key ROI set R is not listed — which specific brain regions from the Schaefer parcellation are designated as MD system nodes? (b) The number of temporal windows M, window size, and stride for dynamic graph construction are not stated. (c) Hyperparameters ε, τ, λ are not specified and have no sensitivity analysis. (d) Variable n in Eq. (2) is undefined. These omissions make independent reproduction impossible despite code availability. The ablation study reveals inconsistencies that are not discussed. Table 2 shows that removing the Fusion module barely affects General Cognitive Status performance (RMSE: 1.08 vs. 1.06 for full model — in fact, removing Fusion slightly improves RMSE). This suggests the temporal fusion module contributes inconsistently across tasks, contradicting the claim of a universally beneficial framework. The paper should honestly discuss task-dependent utility rather than claiming uniform superiority.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The hierarchical graph representation module (Section 2.2, Eq. 5–6) initializes ROI importance weights differently for multi-demand system nodes versus other ROIs. This is a specific and well-motivated design choice grounded in established cognitive neuroscience (Duncan, 2010). The ablation in Table 2 confirms this matters, where removing it causes the largest degradation across all three tasks (e.g., inhibitory control RMSE rises from 10.26 to 12.02). Overall, the ablation studies are thorough (Table 2). The authors remove each of the three components individually and results show all three contribute significantly to improving performance, with a clear ordering (Prior > CL > Fusion). The baselines are also thorough (Table 1), with comparing BrainWeaver against 11 methods from static GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT, GraphSAGE) to dynamic spatiotemporal models (EvolveGCN, DySAT, TGCN, ASTGCN, STAGIN, STNAGNN, Neurograph). Figure 2 shows distinct spatial importance maps per cognitive domain (fronto-parietal for working memory, distributed frontoparietal-salience for inhibitory control, DMN for general cognitive status). These align with known clinical literature on functional neuroanatomy. Figure 3 provides a complementary topological view. For reproducibility, the authors shared an anonymous code repository (including the weights of the trained BrainWeaver model).
reviewer_3_weaknesses: I couldn’t find the exact paradigm of fMRI used in the entire paper; the authors should explicitly state resting-state fMRI and refer to it as such. When you reference HCP datasets or mention dynamic, it’s very important to distinguish resting vs. task-based fMRI. Also mention the # of ROIs/parcellation used so readers do not have to go searching another paper. Looking at Table 1, the improvements shown between BrainWeaver and Neurograph are marginal (at most is the 4.4% RMSE drop for the general cognitive status task). There’s also no reported statistical significance testing, and considering the overlapping standard deviations between Brainweaver and some baselines, the differences in results could likely be noise. There are also inconsistent numbers between Tables 1 and 2.The full model row in Table 1 reports RMSE/MAE/MAPE of 13.40/10.67/10.73 for working memory and 1.08/0.85/2.97 for general cognitive status, while the full model row in Table 2 reports 13.38/10.66/10.77 and 1.06/0.81/2.85, respectively. These should be the same model. The discrepancy suggests different runs or seeds, and it is not explained. The experiments are limited to the HCP S1200 dataset with the Neurograph preprocessing pipeline and the Schaefer parcellation. The generalizability claim would hold a lot stronger where this study also examined on additional datasets, especially since healthy young adults from HCP are far from clinical populations with cognitive impairment. The contrastive learning module (Section 2.3) is unclear. What clinical metadata variables are included? Age, sex, education, handedness? How are they encoded? The projection heads for $u_i$​ and $v_i$​ are also not described architecturally nor is a dimension mentioned in the Implementation details. The temperature $\tau$ and weighting factor $\lambda$ in Eq. 8 are also not reported. While there is code, it’s not clear whether the arguments there are the final optimized hyperparameters vs. initialized parameters, hence why they should be reported for reproducibility and to evaluate whether the contrastive objective is well-calibrated. The cross-graph temporal attention fusion (Section 2.1, Eq. 2) is difficult to follow and potentially overcomplicated. For Eq. 2, why is this particular form of bilinear attention used over standard multi-head attention across temporal steps? There is no comparison to simpler temporal aggregation strategies (e.g., mean pooling, LSTM, standard transformer temporal attention) in the ablation. While removing the entire Fusion module is tested in Table 2, the ablation does not show whether this specific attention design outperforms simpler temporal fusion alternatives.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive comments. We appreciate the recognition of BrainWeaver’s clinically relevant problem formulation, neuroscience-grounded design, comprehensive baselines, ablation study, and interpretability analyses. We will revise the camera-ready version to improve clarity, reproducibility, and the positioning of our contributions. Regarding the concern about clinical metadata and potential information leakage, we clarify that cognition-related metadata have been deliberately excluded from the contrastive learning module. The metadata used in our framework does not include the target cognitive scores, other cognitive assessment scores, or variables directly derived from the prediction labels. It is used only for subject-level contrastive regularization rather than providing label-related information to the prediction head. We agree with the reviewers that statistical validation is important. In the camera-ready version, we will make our wording more precise and cautious, supplement missing implementation details to improve reproducibility, and correct minor textual issues, notation inconsistencies, and numerical discrepancies. Finally, we will better position BrainWeaver as an integrated neuroscience-guided dynamic graph framework rather than claiming novelty for each individual component. We will also discuss the task-dependent contribution of temporal fusion and the limitation that the current evaluation is based on healthy HCP subjects, with validation on clinical cohorts left as an important direction for future work.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): This paper presents a well-executed and clinically relevant framework for cognitive score prediction using dynamic fMRI, with strong experimental coverage and meaningful interpretability analysis. However, reviewers note that performance gains are modest and lack statistical significance, and the overall novelty is somewhat incremental. Important implementation details and the use of clinical metadata require clarification to ensure reproducibility and avoid potential concerns such as information leakage. With these revisions and clearer positioning of contributions, the paper meets the bar for acceptance.

title: CMD-AD: Cross-Modality Distillation from fMRI-EEG for Single-Modality Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: This paper designs a three-stage framework for cross-modal fusion and knowledge distillation to meet the demand for multi-modal diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease. It achieves efficient complementation between fMRI spatial structures and EEG temporal features, and transfers the capability of the fusion model to the single-modal encoder via distillation. The effectiveness of the proposed method is validated on eight multi-center datasets.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.Table 2 shows that performance drops significantly when the multi-scale hierarchical structure is removed, yet the correlation between the multi-scale hierarchy and pathological brain region characteristics in AD is not explained. 2.Experimental comparisons mainly focus on several traditional methods and unimodal models, lacking direct comparisons with representative multimodal state-of-the-art methods in recent years. 3.It is suggested to add modal weight analysis and interpretable visualization to improve the scientificity and credibility of the proposed method.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Addresses a clinically realistic and important problem: This work enables single-modality deployment while leveraging multimodal information during training, improving clinical feasibility. Comprehensive and convincing evaluation: The method is validated on eight multicenter datasets, including both single-modality and paired cohorts, which is relatively extensive for this domain.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The baseline selection is limited and not up-to-date. The comparisons are restricted to conventional single-modality brain network models (e.g., BrainNetCNN, BrainGNN), while more recent and stronger methods such as BrainNetTF [1], Alter [2], as well as multimodal or incomplete-modality learning approaches specifically designed for brain networks, are not included [3, 4, 5]. This raises concerns about the fairness and competitiveness of the reported performance gains. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2023.[4] Yang, Yanwu, et al. “Incomplete learning of multi-modal connectome for brain disorder diagnosis via modal-mixup and deep supervision.” Medical Imaging With Deep Learning. author_feedback: We appreciate all reviewers’ recognition of our technical novelty and practical value. Below, we concisely address the reviewers’ main concerns: 1) R1/R2/R4: clinical motivation and novelty. In clinical practice, paired fMRI-EEG provides complementary spatial-temporal information, but inference often has only fMRI or EEG. CMD-AD targets this bottleneck by leveraging paired fMRI-EEG during training while requiring only one modality at inference. Its main innovation is scale-wise cross-modality distillation: BCMF aligns fMRI and EEG at each scale to construct fused multiscale spatial-temporal features, which are distilled into each single-modality encoder. Compared with HC-GNN/MCSP, CMD-AD discards the fusion branch after training and requires only one modality at inference. It also avoids missing-modality synthesis as in R2-[5]. More importantly, instead of transferring only global latent knowledge (R2-[3,4]), CMD-AD distills per-scale fused features to capture hierarchical brain-network alterations induced by AD. 2) R2/R4: stronger and missing-modality baselines. Under the same subject-level splits and preprocessing, we additionally report R2-[1,2] and R2-[3-5]. R2-[1,2] are competitive at Base (Stage 1), yet CMD-AD exceeds them by 1.7/2.5 and 1.51.0 fMRI ACC/AUC points, and 3.0/5.0 and 2.0/3.0 EEG points. With CMD-AD distillation, R2-[1,2] further gain 4.5/5.2 and 4.7/5.7 fMRI points, and 7.0/8.5 and 6.3/7.5 EEG points. CMD-AD (Distill) also exceeds R2-[3-5] by 3.7/4.3, 2.7/3.7, and 3.7/5.0 fMRI points, and 2.0/3.0, 1.6/2.5, and 3.6/6.0 EEG points. These results show gains also come from scale-wise fusion and distillation, not backbone choice only. 3) R4: paired AD scarcity and Stage-2 sampling. We agree that paired AD subjects are limited, but CMD-AD does not learn the AD/NC boundary from paired data alone. Stage 1 trains disease-aware encoders on all labeled single-modality data. Stage 2 builds on these encoders to learn fMRI-EEG correspondence via BCMF and produce fused representations for Stage 3 distillation. Thus, paired data mainly support cross-modal alignment rather than for classification alone. Class balancing is applied only within the paired training split after subject-level splits are fixed, leaving validation/test distributions unchanged. 4) R2: hyperparameters and reproducibility. We apologize for omit hyperparameter search details. In Stage 3, η and κ weight feature- and logit-level distillation, while τ controls teacher-logit softness. We select them on held-out validation splits using AUC, searching η,κ∈{0.1,0.2,…,1.0} and τ∈{1,2,3,4}. The selected setting, η=0.5, κ=0.5, and τ=2, is fixed for all folds and modalities. We will add these details to Sec. 4.1.5) R1/R4: R1/R4: multiscale pathology and interpretability. We thank the reviewers for requesting clearer pathological interpretation and modal-weight analysis. AD-related FC alterations can occur at both system and regional levels, so coarse parcellations capture system-level disruption while finer parcellations preserve local ROI interactions. This explains why removing the multiscale hierarchy causes the largest performance drop. Fig. 2 supports this interpretation, as Grad-CAM consistently highlights association systems more strongly than primary sensory systems across scales. The learned scale-wise modality weights show greater reliance on fMRI at intermediate ROI scales, reflecting its spatial specificity, while EEG maintains complementary temporal contributions. Additional BCMF feature visualization shows tighter same-class fMRI-EEG alignment and larger AD-NC separation after fusion. 6) R4: harmonization and notation. We apologize for omit harmonization details due to space. FCNs are ComBat-harmonized before training, and all methods use the same harmonized inputs. For Eqs. (2) and (4), H^bar denotes the channel-aggregated feature used to compute attention context, which is then injected into each per-channel feature via the residual connection.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): While the motivation of exploiting multimodal complementarity is meaningful, the current submission has limitations that need to be addressed in the rebuttal including missing related works, evaluations, notations. | The paper addresses a clinically relevant problem and proposes a reasonable cross-modality distillation framework for single-modality AD diagnosis. However, the main concerns remain insufficiently resolved after rebuttal, particularly regarding limited novelty relative to existing incomplete-modality and cross-modal distillation methods, inadequate positioning against related work, missing or post-hoc baseline comparisons, and uncertainty about the reliability of the paired fMRI-EEG training data given the severe scarcity of AD-positive paired subjects. Although the rebuttal clarified several implementation details, these issues affect the strength and trustworthiness of the claimed contribution. Rejection is recommended. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): This manuscript is rejected due to multiple critical issues raised by all reviewers. First, the work only compares against traditional single-modality models and standard classifiers, while missing state-of-the-art multimodal, incomplete-modality learning and advanced brain network methods published in recent years, which undermines the fairness and persuasiveness of performance results. Second, the correlation between the core multi-scale hierarchical structure and pathological characteristics of Alzheimer’s disease is not elaborated, and modal weight analysis and reliable visual interpretation are absent. Third, closely related prior studies on incomplete multimodal learning and cross-modal distillation are not thoroughly discussed, and the unique advantages and incremental contributions of the proposed method are not clearly stated. Fourth, key hyperparameters lack detailed specifications, tuning strategies and selection criteria. Additionally, the training datasets suffer from severe imbalance with extremely limited AD-positive samples, raising doubts about the model’s capability to capture disease-related patterns. No effective harmonization or covariate adjustment is conducted for heterogeneous multicenter data, and minor inconsistencies exist in theoretical notations and formula definitions. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a unified feature distillation from fMRI-EEG for Single-Modality using their multi-site datasets. The reviewers’ critiques were mainly related to performance evaluation with state-of-the-art methods, discussion on experimental setting, and clarification on data harmonization. While those are important aspects, the paper demonstrates its novelty and incorporates intensive data harmization, which maintain its value.

title: Community-Aware Dynamic Graph Learning for Brain Disorder Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The paper presents a framework for brain disorder diagnosis by integrating lag-aware dynamic functional connectivity with community-aware graph learning. 2.The proposed dual-level modeling provides a multi-scale perspective for capturing both local and global brain dynamics. 3.The method is evaluated on multiple datasets, and includes basic interpretability analyses.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The claimed novelty is limited. The overall framework is conceptually similar to dFCExperts(Chen, Tingting, et al. “dfcexpert: Learning dynamic functional connectivity patterns with modularity and state experts. “ IEEE transactions on medical imaging (2025). ), with differences mainly in specific implementations. In addition, lag-based functional connectivity is not new. The method appears as a combination of existing techniques rather than being driven by a unified and well-justified research motivation. 2.The concatenation of zero-lagged matrices in Fig. 1(d) lacks clear explanation and justification. 3.The performance on ADNI is unusually high, especially for the CN vs. EMCI task, and is significantly higher than competing methods, raising concerns about fairness and possible data leakage. 4.The performance of baseline methods is generally low. Important related methods, particularly those based on dynamic FC and community detection, are missing from the comparison. 5.Fig. 3(a) lacks explanation. 6.The methodology behind the Visualization Analysis in Section 3.3 is not clearly described. 7.In Fig. 2, grouping the same metrics together would improve readability and comparison.
reviewer_1_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The shift from instantaneous (zero-lag) functional connectivity to lag-aware dynamic connectivity is well-motivated and better reflects the actual neurophysiological propagation of brain signals. 2.The experimental setup is very thorough. The authors validated their framework on four distinct datasets (ADNI, a local dataset, ABIDE, and ADHD-200) covering three different disorders. This demonstrates generalizability. 3.CaDGNN consistently outperforms a solid range of recent baselines (e.g., STA-GIN, BMR, BISTFormer) across multiple evaluation metrics, showing notable improvements in ACC and AUC.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.While the overall lag-aware framework and hierarchical design are novel, the downstream learning modules heavily rely on off-the-shelf components, such as standard Transformer encoders and Graph Attention Networks (GAT). The algorithmic contribution lies more in how the data is pre-processed and structured rather than in the neural network operators themselves. 2.The lag-aware network construction relies on a three-point parabolic interpolation of the cross-covariance function to estimate delays. The authors do not adequately discuss or ablate how robust this heuristic is against the typical noise and artifacts found in rs-fMRI data. 3.The title of Section 2.2 contains a clear typo: “Grpah Learning” should be corrected to “Graph Learning”.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The main strength of this paper is that its method is relatively complete. It does not only use static functional connectivity. It also does not rely on a simple temporal model. Instead, it combines lag information, community structure, and temporal learning in one framework. This gives the method some novelty. The experiments are also carried out on multiple datasets and tasks, including ADNI, ABIDE, ADHD-200, and a local MCI dataset. The results show that the method outperforms several baselines on some tasks. Another strength is that the paper includes an interpretation analysis of discriminative ROIs and connections, which makes the model more informative.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1 The lag values are estimated at the individual level. However, the manuscript does not show whether the learned lag patterns are robust to inter-site heterogeneity. Since multiple datasets and different preprocessing pipelines are involved, the reported lag effects may be influenced by site-specific acquisition or preprocessing differences. 2 The merging of clusters across different time points relies on the assumption that the same community label is directly comparable over time. This assumption is important, but it is not sufficiently validated in the current manuscript. The authors should provide evidence for cross-temporal label consistency, examine the effect of the temporal coupling parameter ω, and clarify how the method avoids artificial merging caused by label switching. 3 The study uses the Schaefer-500 atlas, which is a very high-resolution parcellation. This choice increases feature dimensionality and model complexity, and may also increase the risk of overfitting. The manuscript does not show whether the performance gain is robust across different atlas resolutions. Repeating the experiments with lower-resolution parcellations, such as Schaefer-100 or Schaefer-200, would strengthen the methodological validity. 4 The community-level graph is constructed with an all-ones adjacency matrix, so each time point is fully connected to all others. This design weakens the explicit modeling of temporal order and may bias the model toward global similarity rather than local temporal evolution. The authors should evaluate more constrained temporal connections, such as local time windows neighborhoods, to justify the current design and clarify the contribution of temporal structure.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive feedback. Below we address the concerns. Q1(R1-1, R2-1): Novelty. CaDGNN and dFCExperts follow fundamentally different paradigms. dFCExperts decouples spatial state from temporal state aggregation on zero-lag dBFC; CaDGNN jointly models spatiotemporal coupling in lag-aware dBFC networks. The key distinction is the CCE module, which couples the spatiotemporal features by tracking each node’s switching history across communities over time, a mechanism absent in dFCExperts. Ablation (Fig.2) confirms removing CCE causes larger performance drop than removing Transformer encoder, validating that improvements stem from spatiotemporal community modeling rather than standard operators. We acknowledge Transformer/GAT are established components; our contribution is their principled composition for spatiotemporal brain network modeling. Q2(R2-2, R3-1): Lag Robustness. Three-point parabolic interpolation mitigates the discrete TR sampling limitation for lag estimation. It refines the CCF peak using only its two neighbors, avoiding noise-prone broader CCF regions while requiring no extra hyperparameters. ADNI, ABIDE, and * are processed with the same DPARSF pipeline. Results on the single-site * dataset further indicate lag effects are not solely driven by multi-site acquisition. Following prior work, we discount delays >4s and convert to TR-specific shifts, reducing artifact-prone long delays while keeping lag estimation comparable across datasets. Q3(R3-2,4): Temporal Community. CaDGNN does not detect communities per segment and artificially merge them. Instead, Temporal Community Detection (TCD) treats time windows as layers and links the same node across adjacent layers via coupling parameter ω. Community assignments are inferred through a single joint optimization, inherently encouraging temporal consistency while allowing network-driven switching. This design reduces the risk of artificial merging due to label switching. For the community-level graph, the all-ones adjacency enables flexible cross-window information exchange; GAT then learns nonuniform temporal attention, so windows are not equally aggregated. Ablation (w/o CG, Fig.2) validates this design’s contribution. Q4(R1-3,4): Fairness & Baselines. Two types of baselines are included, spanning dynamic brain activity models (ST2GCN, BISTFormer) and modularity-prior GNNs (BMR, similar to dFCExperts in its decoupled modeling way). We use strict subject-wise 5-fold cross-validation, ensuring that all samples from the same subject are assigned to the same fold to prevent subject-level leakage across train/test splits. No demographic or clinical variables are used as input features. As shown in Table 1, most compared methods achieve relatively high performance on ADNI, especially for CN vs. EMCI, indicating intrinsic separability of the diagnostic tasks rather than an artifact of our method. Q5(R3-3): Atlas Resolution. Schaefer-500 is widely adopted in brain network studies. Its finer parcellation captures functional boundaries coarser atlases may miss, important for detecting subtle disorder alterations. CaDGNN’s consistent performance across four datasets with varying acquisition suggests results are not driven by atlas resolution alone. Moreover, TCD naturally groups ROIs into communities, providing built-in regularization against overfitting at higher resolutions. Q6(R1-2,5,6): Clarifications. For Fig.1(d), the concatenation combines complementary information: X_{fc}^t preserves current synchrony, H^t encodes lag-aware community dynamics. Fig.3(a) shows sensitivity of k (KNN neighbors) and w (window length), color denoting ACC. For Sec.3.3, Grad-CAM is applied to ROI-level embeddings from intra-level graph learning; importance scores are computed from class-score gradients and averaged across subjects. Q7(R1-7, R2-3): Paper Readability. We apologize for the ‘Grpah’ typo. We will regroup Fig.2 by metrics and correct the typos.

title: DD-INR: Dynamics-Driven Implicit Neural Representation for Accelerated Whole-Brain Functional MRI Reconstruction
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in accelerated fMRI. The basic modeling choice is appropriate for this setting: the dominant signal is largely static, whereas the quantity of interest is a much smaller dynamic component. Estimating the background separately and reserving the INR for the dynamic residual is therefore a reasonable design. The method is organized clearly at a high level, and the regularization imposed on the dynamic term is appropriate for task fMRI. The simulation results are encouraging, and within the comparison set included in the paper, the proposed method improves the reported activation maps and time-series metrics.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The paper gives the impression of introducing a new reconstruction framework for accelerated fMRI, but the underlying ideas are closer to existing work than the manuscript acknowledges. The separation of slowly varying background structure from a smaller dynamic component is already established in accelerated fMRI and dynamic MRI reconstruction. Petrov et al. used a low-rank plus sparse model for accelerated fMRI, including prospective experiments, and Chiew et al. incorporated task-related temporal information directly into highly accelerated fMRI reconstruction through a constrained low-rank model. More broadly, INR-based reconstruction for dynamic MRI is already an active direction. I would therefore encourage the authors to position the paper more narrowly, as an INR-based implementation of a background-plus-dynamic strategy for accelerated fMRI. Several key quantities are introduced with less precision than one would expect in a methodological paper. The notation around (f_\theta) is not defined carefully enough when first introduced, and the construction of the background estimate (\hat{x} {bg}) through (A {1:T}^{\dagger}y_{1:T}) remains largely intuitive. The idea itself is acceptable, but the operator, the temporal aggregation step, and the underlying assumptions should be stated more explicitly. The numerical results are favorable, but the qualitative evidence is more limited than the wording suggests. In Fig. 3, the recovered curves are improved relative to the noisier baselines, but they still do not follow the expected response especially closely in an absolute sense. I would therefore encourage the authors to moderate the stronger claims about the accurate recovery of amplitude and phase. The paper would benefit from a more direct discussion of downstream fMRI inference. In this area, image quality alone is not the decisive criterion. Prior work has already noted that nonlinear reconstruction can affect temporal correlations, effective degrees of freedom, and statistical sensitivity. That point deserves more careful treatment here.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.Heuristically, modeling fMRI data as a static background component plus a temporally varying dynamic component makes a lot of sense, similar to residual learning, or the low-rank plus sparse (L+S) reconstruction approach. The authors argue that such a decomposition allows the INR to focus its capacity on modeling the dynamic component as opposed to repeatedly learning the static background component. 2.The authors provide a strong justification for their choice to do Fourier feature embedding separately in space and time. Specifically, their justification for this is two-fold, i.e., reducing number of total parameters and the ability to allocate different bandwidths for spatial versus temporal features. 3.The authors perform extensive evaluation on both simulated data where a ground truth is available, and on data acquired in vivo. This includes quantitative (Table 1) and qualitative (Figs. 2 and 3) evaluations against ground truth when using the simulated data, and also qualitative evaluation when using in vivo data. 4.Finally, it is non-trivial that the proposed regularization works well. The proposed regularization does NOT explicitly assume a hand-crafted model for the temporal signals across dynamics. It only encourages neighboring voxels to have similar temporal patterns.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The paper is already very clear and well-written although additional details can be incorporated during revision to further improve the clarity and highlight the contribution of this work. 1.For readers not familiar with INR, it might be unclear (until later in the paper) that the method does not require training on a carefully curated dataset but instead works on a single subject. Consider clarifying or maybe briefly highlighting this in the abstract and introduction so that the readers can better appreciate this work. 2.At the bottom of page 3, it is unclear how \hat{x} {bg} is estimated. Later in the paper, the authors explain that \hat{x} {bg} is obtained from temporally aggregated measurement. Is the (k, t)-space data temporally aggregated first into 3D k-space without the temporal dimension? Or is it the case that a least-squares problem is solved assuming the underlying image to be reconstructed is temporally static? 3.At the top of page 4, the authors presents two regularizers in (3) but only introduces the latter one, i.e., “spatially regularize the temporal derivative”. It might be helpful to at least briefly describe the former one as well. 4.Why does the image contrast differ across different methods in Fig. 2? Is it because of scaling during visualization? 5.In Table 1, it might be helpful to also compute and report tSNR. It helps to make the claim that the proposed method improves temporal stability. 6.In Fig. 4, the reconstructed image for PnP looks over regularized in the spatial domain. Is the regularization parameter for PnP properly tuned? 7.In the discussion, the authors attempt to explain the different behaviors of spatiotemporal vs spatial regularizations. However, the discussion does NOT explain why R_{xyz} results in more temporal smoothing whereas R_{xyz, t} results in less temporal smoothing in Fig. 3.It might be helpful to include more in-depth discussion about this behavior in the discussion section. There is one technical question though. When using INR for 3D+t MRI reconstruction, it is reasonable (and in fact common) to assume that the underlying 3D+t data satisfies certain regularity condition in both space and time, e.g., spatiotemporally continuous. In the current formulation (static background + dynamic), does the regularity condition still holds after removing the static background. There is no issue with regularity in the temporal domain because temporally a constant is removed and adding/subtracting a constant doesn’t change the regularity of the underlying function. However, there might be an issue in the spatial domain. Say the static background reconstruction is not perfect and there are artifact in the estimated static background \hat{x} {bg} which introduces spatial discontinuities. In this case, even if it is assumed that the 3D+t fMRI data is continuous, the dynamic component to be modeled using INR is NOT spatially continuous because of the spatial discontinuity in \hat{x} {bg}. One small limitation of the work is that joint reconstruction is performed across all dynamics, making it hard to apply this method for real time fMRI applications.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The problem framing is sharp and well-motivated: BOLD signals are 2–5% intensity fluctuations superimposed on a strong static background, and dedicating INR capacity exclusively to the dynamic residual is a principled design choice. The use of autodifferentiation to compute the temporal derivative for regularization is elegant and technically clean. The comparison against PnP-fMRI (a strong domain-specific baseline) strengthens the evaluation. Both simulation with ground-truth activation maps and in vivo results are provided, with appropriate fMRI-specific metrics (F2-score, GLM z-score maps, BOLD time-series correlation). The performance gap over baselines is large and consistent — Corr of 0.909 vs. 0.84 for PnP and 0.40 for generic INR is a meaningful improvement.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Single subject in vivo evaluation. The in vivo experiment involves one healthy volunteer with a single task paradigm (visual block design). This is insufficient to assess generalizability across subjects, tasks, motion levels, or scanner variability. The simulation compensates partially but uses a simplified phantom (white/gray matter/CSF only), which may not capture the full complexity of real fMRI noise. 2.Static background assumption is fragile. The background is estimated once from temporally aggregated measurements and frozen throughout reconstruction. This is violated by head motion, physiological noise (cardiac/respiratory fluctuations), and slow scanner drifts — all common in fMRI. The discussion acknowledges motion but dismisses it without quantitative analysis. No experiment tests robustness under varying motion levels. 3.Reconstruction time is prohibitive for practical use. ~2 hours per scan on an RTX 6000 GPU is noted as “comparable to traditional methods” — but this is not accurate for clinical or large-scale research use. Standard CS fMRI reconstruction is typically minutes, not hours. This severely limits the practical appeal of the method, and no analysis of the computational bottleneck or potential speedups is provided beyond attributing cost to NUFFT. 4.Hyperparameter sensitivity is uncharacterized. The regularization weights (λ = 10⁻² and 2×10⁻³), warm-up schedule, Fourier embedding dimensions (Bxyz ∈ R²⁵⁶ˣ³, Bt ∈ R⁶⁴), and network width (512) are all fixed without ablation. Given the sensitivity of SIREN-based methods to initialization and frequency parameters, and the critical role of λ in balancing data fidelity vs. regularization for weak BOLD signals, this is a significant gap. 5.No resting-state fMRI evaluation. The method is evaluated only on task-based fMRI with a simple block design — the easiest possible activation pattern to recover. Resting-state fMRI (functional connectivity, default mode network) involves weaker, less structured temporal fluctuations and represents the majority of clinical and research fMRI use. No discussion of applicability to this setting is provided.

title: Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Mapping for EEG-to-fMRI Synthesis via Gaussian-Guided Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
reviewer_1_strengths: -The method has a certain degree of novelty. The authors propose using a Gaussian function with mean and variance parameters to model ROI-specific hemodynamic functions, and apply this function as a temporal mask in the message-passing mechanism, reflecting the authors’ unique insights into neural signal analysis and deep learning. -The method description is relatively clear, and the correspondence between formulae and symbols is good. -The experimental design is relatively complete, including comparisons with baseline methods, ablation experiments covering the basic modules, and additional validation on an independent dataset. -The dataset split is handled reasonably, and comparisons are made under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: -The authors mention two main challenges in the Introduction, among which 2) Spatial Ambiguity is not addressed in a particularly unique way in the paper. -The authors emphasize the subject specificity of the HRF in the cited literature, but the Gaussian mask modeled in the paper seems to have only region specificity. -The HRF usually does not follow a unimodal Gaussian distribution, and a single pair of $\mu$ and $\sigma$ parameters may not fully capture the region specificity of the HRF. Moreover, this modeling choice is not well supported by the experiments. -In Section 2.1, the authors mention that the constructed heterogeneous graph has directed Electrode-to-ROI edges $\epsilon_{ER}$ and undirected Functional edges $\epsilon_{FC}$. The definitions of these two variables should be explained there; otherwise, they may confuse readers. -The authors state that the constructed heterogeneous graph is dynamic, but this dynamic property seems to depend only on the time-varying attention parameters in message passing. Therefore, the dynamic graph structure should be more clearly distinguished from dynamic message passing. -The third term in Equation (5) refers to the neighborhood of node $k$. If FC is not sparsified, this almost means that the neighborhood of $k$ contains all other nodes. The expression of the formula could be simplified here to reduce symbolic redundancy. -Why is the edge weight in Equation (3) obtained by using the fMRI ROI node state at the previous time step $(t-1)$ and the electrode features at the current time step (after hemodynamic Gaussian masking)? What is the physiological basis for this design? How does the formula behave at $t=0$? -Some references do not follow the required format. -The main acquisition parameters for EEG and fMRI are not provided. -Some important information is missing, which reduces the reproducibility of the paper, such as the atlas used for fMRI ROI signal extraction, the time window length $L$, the feature dimension $d$, and the latent dimension. -This citation is inappropriate: Unlike methods relying on static network structure [2], our graph structure dynamically evolves [20, 19, 4, 13], allowing the model to capture time-varying dependencies between the electrodes and ROIs. -There is inappropriate bolding in Table 2: for the intra-subject setting and ConnMSE, DSTP (Ours) is not the best result.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The method has a certain degree of novelty, especially the combination of a dynamic heterogeneous graph and Gaussian-guided message passing, which is broadly consistent with the underlying physiological mechanism. The learnable Gaussian mask is used to simulate region-specific hemodynamic responses and serves as a weighting factor in message passing, helping the model identify the EEG history segments most relevant to fMRI generation. 2.A multi-objective optimization strategy is adopted, taking into account temporal correlation loss and FC matrix reconstruction loss in addition to reconstruction accuracy. This design is well aligned with the main application scenarios of fMRI. 3.The overall experimental results are strong. From the reported results, DSTP achieves the best overall performance relative to the baselines under both intra-subject and inter-subject settings. 4.The ablation study is relatively complete and covers the effectiveness of the main modules.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.There is a lack of direct validation of physiological plausibility. At present, the effectiveness of the Gaussian mask design for simulating ROI-specific HRFs is only validated through fMRI reconstruction performance, without directly examining whether the learned \mu and \sigma are physiologically interpretable. 2.Some experimental results are not fully consistent with the description in the paper. In Table 2, the proposed method does not achieve the best Conn MSE under the intra-subject setting, and this trade-off is not discussed in the manuscript. 3.Some important details are missing. The specific dimensionalities of parameters in the model structure, as well as the time-window length L and feature dimension d, are not reported explicitly, which limits the reproducibility of the paper. 4.The manuscript does not clearly define the reported mean and variance values. It is unclear whether these statistics are computed across time points or across cross-validation results.
reviewer_2_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Strengths and Contributions Physiologically Grounded Problem Formulation: The manuscript correctly frames EEG-fMRI synthesis as a dynamic spatial-temporal mapping problem rather than a static regression task. This perspective directly addresses the core challenges of volume conduction and regional HRF heterogeneity, reflecting sound theoretical insight. Interpretable and Rational Methodological Design: The learnable Gaussian mask elegantly incorporates HRF priors as a soft constraint, balancing data-driven flexibility with physiological interpretability. The DHGNN, with its heterogeneous nodes and dynamic edges, effectively models the non-stationary cross-modal spatial correspondence. The multi-objective loss function is appropriately designed to preserve functional connectivity topology. Promising Direction for Generalizability Assessment: The paper presents preliminary evidence of zero-shot generalization across tasks (resting-state to auditory task) and spatial resolutions (DiFuMo 64 to 512), suggesting that the model may capture intrinsic physiological mapping principles rather than merely overfitting to dataset-specific distributions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Lack of Statistical Rigor in Experimental Evaluation: The performance comparisons presented in Tables 1 and 2 entirely omit statistical significance testing (e.g., paired t-test, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). Given the reported standard deviations (e.g., Intra-subject Tcorr: 0.458±0.173 vs. 0.416±0.166), superiority based solely on mean rank ordering cannot be confidently distinguished from random variation. This omission substantially undermines the credibility of the reported empirical gains for a MICCAI submission. Internal Inconsistency in Methodological Design: The functional connectivity weights in Equation (5) are pre-computed from the training set and remain fixed during both training and inference. This design choice appears at odds with the central premise of “dynamic evolution” and may introduce systematic bias in the presence of domain shifts (e.g., inter-subject evaluation). The authors do not provide sufficient justification for this static prior. Insufficient Detail in Generalization Experiments: The description of the zero-shot generalization experiments in Section 3.4 is overly cursory. Critical details regarding the source-domain training and target-domain testing protocols, as well as whether baseline methods (e.g., UnEBOLT) received equivalent pre-training and data splits, are absent. This lack of detail prevents independent assessment of the reported findings. Relatively Limited Sample Size: The primary experiments rely on resting-state data from 22 subjects (29 scans) and task-based data from 10 subjects (16 scans). For a model architecture incorporating Transformer-based temporal modules and dynamic graph structures, this sample size poses a non-trivial risk of overfitting and limits the generalizability of the conclusions. Incomplete Writing and Compliance Statements: The manuscript lacks an Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval statement concerning data usage, as well as any indication of data availability or code release intent. Furthermore, a dedicated Limitations section is absent.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the meta-reviewer and reviewers for their constructive feedback and for recognizing the novelty of our dynamic heterogeneous graph framework and Gaussian-guided temporal modeling for EEG-to-fMRI synthesis, as well as the physiologically motivated design and the multi-objective loss. We have carefully considered the major concerns and grouped them into the following categories for clarification Physiological interpretation and scope (R1-C1/R1-C2/R1-C3/R1-C7, R2-C1, Meta-C3). Our goal is not to suggest that a single Gaussian can fully characterize the complete HRF or all subject-specific hemodynamic variability. Instead, the Gaussian mask is intended as a compact ROI-conditioned temporal gating mechanism that highlights the most relevant EEG history during message passing, while broader temporal dependencies are further modeled by the downstream temporal module. We also recognize that the current evidence for the Gaussian mask remains primarily empirical and reconstruction-based, while a more direct physiological interpretation of the learned μ and σ parameters remains an important direction for future investigation. Dynamic graph clarification and methodological consistency (R1-C4/R1-C5/R1-C6/R1-C11, R3-C2). We appreciate the reviewers’ comments on the distinction between dynamic graph construction and dynamic message passing. In the current model, the main time-varying component lies in the Gaussian-guided electrode-to-ROI interaction together with the evolving ROI states, whereas the functional-connectivity term in Eq. (5) is used as a fixed prior estimated from the training data. We recognize that the present wording may leave room for ambiguity, and the role of dynamic cross-modal interaction versus fixed structural prior could be more clearly articulated Experimental rigor and result interpretation (R1-C12, R2-C2/R2-C4, R3-C1/R3-C3/R3-C4, Meta-C1). We appreciate the reviewers’ thoughtful comments regarding statistical rigor, protocol clarity, and the calibration of the reported conclusions. Regarding Table 2, we recognize that under the intra-subject setting the full model does not achieve the lowest ConnMSE in the ablation study, and this trade-off could have been described more carefully in the manuscript. At the current stage, we view the results as showing the strongest overall empirical trade-off across major metrics and settings, rather than uniform superiority on every ablation entry. We also acknowledge that formal statistical significance testing is not included in the present manuscript, such analysis could provide additional perspective on the reported comparisons, and we appreciate this as a valuable consideration for subsequent refinement. As for the data sample issues, given that paired EEG-fMRI is extremely rare, we have to follow the existing works’ usage of the available dataset with a limited sample size. Reproducibility, reporting, and compliance (R1-C8/R1-C9/R1-C10, R2-C3, R3-C5, Meta-C2). We appreciate the reviewers’ concerns regarding reproducibility and reporting completeness. The manuscript already specifies several parts of the training setup, including the optimizer, training epochs, batch size, learning rate schedule, Gaussian-mask initialization, loss weights, but we recognize that some implementation and dataset details are not stated as explicitly as they could be, including certain acquisition and dimensional settings. We also recognize that the present submission does not include an explicit code-availability or limitations statement, and we are positively considering making implementation details and configuration settings publicly available in the future.

reviewer_1_strengths: This method incorporates frequency-domain coherence and time-domain correlations, which may capture a more comprehensive representation of neural communication compared to single-domain approaches.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1）Most of the comparison models chosen by the authors were published in/before 2022.The article lacks comparisons with more recent technologies. Furthermore, the lack of comparisons with cross-domain (or domain-adaptive/generalization) methods raises concerns about the robustness and reliability of the reported results, especially when distributions shift. It is recommended to enhance this aspect of the paper by incorporating comparisons with state-of-the-art techniques to improve the overall innovativeness of the study. 2) The authors compute coherence between ROIs only within the 0.01–0.1 Hz frequency band. author_feedback: We thank reviewers for constructive comments. We are encouraged that they recognized strong motivation(R4,R5), clarity(R1), novelty(R4), thorough evaluation/ablations(R4,R5) & clinical relevance of equity-aware diagnosis with biologically meaningful results(R5). Q1:Baseline. GCDA[24] & CoRE-BOLD[22] are both 2025 SOTA. GCDA is an SOTA SSL benchmark designed for cross-site generalization. RESOLVE outperforms both in utility & FATE under cross-site distribution shift & Gaussian noise. Prior generalization-based approaches don’t explicitly address fairness. Q2:L_DP loss. Section 3.1 provides 3 quantitative validations of L_DP: (i)Table 1 shows RESOLVE is the only method achieving positive FATE on both cross-site protocols, reducing demographic parity difference more effectively than baselines.(ii)In Fig.2(c),RESOLVE w/o L_DP shows a clear rise in ΔDP, showing its contribution to reducing subgroup disparity.(iii)Fig.2(b) shows RESOLVE preserves best utility-fairness tradeoff across labeled-data fractions. Q3:Dataset. MDD is used as a proof-of-concept due to established gender bias. However, RESOLVE is disease/cohort agnostic. Our cross-site validation (S20→S14 & S20→S21) already evaluates realistic distribution shifts & demographic composition, where RESOLVE achieves SOTA performance. The OT alignment performs non-parametric matching between two subgroup distributions, making it applicable to arbitrary binary subgroup populations. We also validated RESOLVE on ABIDE dataset with consistent improvement. Due to rebuttal policy,results will be detailed in GitHub repo upon acceptance. Q4:Novelty. RESOLVE is, to our knowledge, 1st equity-aware multi-domain SSL framework for connectomes without task labels, a setting previously unaddressed in neuroimaging. It delivers 3 connectome specific contributions: (a)Representation-level fairness in SSL: since diagnostic labels are unavailable during pretraining, RESOLVE enforces demographic invariance in fused latent space via OT alignment, unlike prior methods that mainly operate in supervised prediction space (b)Joint multi-domain reconstruction: RESOLVE reconstructs both correlation & coherence based connectomes from a fused embedding, rather than a single connectivity view, introducing a novel SSL pretext (c)Graph-level cross-domain SSL: Jointly modeling time & frequency domain connectivity while preserving ROI interactions. No prior method unifies SSL pretraining, multi-domain connectome learning, & equity-aware latent representation learning. Q5:Frequency. The 0.01–0.1 Hz range is widely established as Low-Frequency Fluctuation(LFF) band in seminal rsfMRI literature, capturing dominant spontaneous BOLD fluctuations while attenuating low frequency drift(<0.01Hz) & physiological noise(>0.1Hz)[C1,C2]. The same filter is applied during preprocessing to isolate this signal. RESOLVE’s frequency encoder captures phase synchronization within this band, which a time-domain encoder doesn’t explicitly model. This will be clarified in camera ready. Q6:k & threshold. Following prior literature, we tuned k∈[5,15] & threshold∈[0.1,0.6] via grid search on validation data. Due to page limit we didn’t provide the analysis. Q7:READOUT. READOUT (Global mean pooling,in Sec.3) aggregates ROI(node)-level embeddings into a subject(graph)-level vector. Q8:CV split. We use standard 5-fold CV where each fold holds 20% for testing; rest 80% is split as 90:10 into training and validation, yielding a 72/8/20 split. We will correct it in camera ready. Q9:Fusion. RESOLVE aim to derive its gains from objectives in Eq. 9 rather than fusion complexity, yet outperforms SOTA baselines including transformer-based architectures. Exploring attention-based fusion is a promising future direction. Q10:Presentation. RESOLVE acronym is expanded in Introduction; we will additionally include it in Abstract. We will rename Problem 1 to Problem Statement. C1: Cordes et al.,AJNR, 2001 C2: Biswal et al.,Magn Reson Med. 1995

reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The geodesic distance to the baseline cluster is an interesting way of representing the group-level response to the different conditions in the task. 2.The proposed approach does not assume linearity in the BOLD response and doesn’t depend on defining a hemodynamic response to retrieve task-related activation maps.
