author_feedback: Thank all reviewers for valuable comments. Our responses are presented as follows. 1.Quantitative comparison vs GLM (MR-Q1, R1-Q2, R2-Q1, R3-Q3) We thank the reviewers for requesting quantitative evidence. We had computed Dice and sensitivity between MGS and GLM group maps for the five motor conditions (Dice: 0.61, 0.66, 0.82, 0.72, and 0.79 for l/r hand, l/r foot, and tongue; sensitivity: 1 for all). Still, we think using GLM as absolute ground truth is not fully appropriate, since our goal is to examine whether task-activation information encoded in looped manifold trajectories can be translated into vertex-wise activation statistics under possible HRF mismatch. Thus, the experiment is not merely a qualitative comparison with GLM, but an evaluation of the activation information carried by the looped manifold trajectory. The GLM comparison further confirms that MGS recovers canonical motor activation patterns. 2.Effectiveness of individual components (MR-Q1, R1-Q1, R2-Q2) We agree that a weightless-MGS control is a meaningful ablation. In Eq. (2), w(dG) transfers manifold-trajectory information into the vertex-wise activation statistic. Replacing it with an all-one vector would reduce MGS to a normalized block-average BOLD summary and discard the baseline-departure/return profile learned through UMAP, DBM clustering, and geodesic distance estimation. Thus, the geodesic weighting is the component that separates MGS from simple block averaging. Task condition blocks were used to provide the same design basis as GLM, where condition blocks are convolved with an HRF, enabling direct comparison while avoiding HRF fitting in MGS. Future work can further reduce task-label dependence by defining task-related segments from the unsupervised loop trajectory. 3.Parameter setting (MR-Q2, R2-Q3&4, R3-Q4) The 6-frame shift equals 4.32 s at the HCP TR of 0.72 s and falls within a physiologically plausible range for motor/sensorimotor BOLD timing. Chen et al. (2023), “BOLD Response is more than just magnitude: Improving detection sensitivity through capturing hemodynamic profiles”, reported motor-cortex HRF peaks around 3–4 s, while canonical HRF models peak around 5 s. Fig. 2A also supports this choice, as the 6-frame shift gives clearer condition-coherent petals than 0-frame labels. The shift was fixed before MGS computation. For UMAP, n_neighbors=40, 2D embedding, and standardized Euclidean distance were fixed before activation inference as moderate settings to preserve the smooth group-level trajectory and reduce vertex-wise scale effects. We agree that broader sensitivity analysis would be useful, but these parameters were not tuned to optimize the final activation maps. 4.Dataset scope and selection (R1-Q3, R3-Q1&2) Fig. 3 reports individual-level ΔMGS maps, showing subject-level motor patterns. We agree that direct individual-level comparisons with GLM or deconvolution methods would further strengthen the evaluation. We also tested HCP Emotion and Relational tasks and observed consistent MGS behavior, but omitted them due to the MICCAI page limit. For subject selection, we used the official HCP 100-unrelated subset to reduce family-structure dependence and evaluate the method on a diverse independent cohort. We expect the same conclusion to hold on the full HCP-YA 1113-subject dataset. 5.Code availability (MR-Q3) We apologize for not preparing open-source code at submission. We have prepared an Anonymous GitHub repository named /r/MGS-0B07/. If accepted, the repository will be moved to GitHub and linked in the final paper. 6.Minor clarifications (R1) We thank R1 for the careful reading and detailed suggestions. We agree on Fig. 2 color consistency. Rest pseudo-blocks followed the same order as task blocks. Each frame was projected along the estimated geodesic path. Fig. 3 indeed shows ΔMGS. We will clarify these points if accepted. We hope these responses clarify key points. Thanks again for all the thoughtful evaluations.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Reject Justification(s): Perhaps the most pervasive approach to perform segregational analysis in neuroimaging, inc. fMRI, is by using a characterization of the response function as a factor in the general linear model. Although less popular due to their inherent complexity, topological and geometrical approaches can also carry out such analysis with some collateral benefits over the plain statistical counterparts (although of course, strictly speaking the GLM is a manifold, but we hardly think of it as such). This paper is one good example of topological and/or geometrical approaches. The manuscript presents a framework to characterize brain activation at group level that exploit the geometry of the underlying manifold, where the actual modelling occurs, to make statements about task-related effects that would otherwise be missed by the GLM. All reviewers coincide in highlightin the novelty of the approach, and whilst perhaps for me this is less so (I happen to work very closely to this field), but I do coincide that there is novelty here. Among the weaknesses, the lack of quantitative evidence (R1/R2/R3) and the arbitrary decisions over the parameterization (R2/R3) have dominated the reviews. Coupled with the lack of direct access to the code (R1/R3), hence limiting the reproducibility, these shortcomings have somewhat limit the potential that the drat could have had. Nevertheless, given the two more senior reviewers, and I concurr, in supporting acceptance, but the split decision, I recommend inviting a rebuttal. Specifically, the rebutall must address: Affording quantitative evidence inc. comprehensive comparison (R3) e.g. vs classical GLM, and about the effectiveness of the individual components (R2). Provide rationale and/or empirical evidence to justify parameter setting. Disclose code details | The pre-rebuttal meta-review identified three major issues: (1) lack of quantitative evidence and comparison against classical methods such as the GLM; (2) unjustified parameter choices; (3) unavailability of source code. The rebuttal only partially addressed these points with Reviewer #2 explicitly maintaining the Reject score after the rebuttal. Quantitative benchmarking and ablation studies remain absent, and advantage over the gold standard (GLM) has been attempted but not clearly evidenced. Despite genuine novelty, the evidentiary basis for acceptance is insufficient at this time. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Despite some lingering concerns, the authors have done a good job addressing the main critiques to extent allowed by MICCAI (i.e., no new experiments). This work would be of interest to the community. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): All reviewers are satisfied with the quality of the rebuttal responses and have voted to accept the paper. I think the authors have done a good job addressing all concerns raised during the review and plan to address the comment on reproducibility upon acceptance by releasing their Github repository.

title: H2GT: Hub-enhanced Hierarchical Graph Transformer for Explainable Diagnosis of ASD with Functional Brain Networks
reviewer_1_strengths: The proposed method enables the capture of features related to modular organization and hub nodes, which may be important for classifying brain networks.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The major weaknesses of the paper: 1.The absence of multi-fold cross-validation in the classification experiments raises concerns about the reliability of the reported performance metrics of the proposed methos, as a single train-test split may yield overly optimistic or pessimistic results due to data partitioning variance. 2.The model is explained in terms of hub nodes, connections within modules, and coordination between modules. However, it may not incorporate explanations based on key brain connectivity patterns (or to identify critical subgraphs) , which are commonly used in previous studies. The modular organization and hub nodes are important but may not be sufficient for graph classification models.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: (1)The proposed H2GT effectively combines topological priors with Graph Transformer architecture. The hierarchical design that separately models intra-module (via provincial hubs) and inter-module (via connector hubs) interactions is biologically motivated and technically sound. (2)Unlike many “black box” deep learning methods, H2GT provides interpretable results at three levels: (a) hub nodes identification, (b) critical ROIs within functional modules, and (c) discriminative functional modules. The findings align with established neurobiological evidence (e.g., importance of DMN, DAN, and Limbic system in ASD). (3)The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on both ABIDE I and ABIDE II datasets, outperforming 9 baseline methods including recent Transformer-based approaches
reviewer_2_weaknesses: (1)The evaluation is conducted only on ABIDE datasets (I and II). While these are standard benchmarks, additional validation on independent, multi-site datasets would strengthen the generalizability claims. (2)The paper does not compare with very recent methods that may have reported better results on ABIDE. For instance, some recent self-supervised learning approaches for brain networks are not included. (3)The paper does not provide code availability information (anonymized link or planned release). Details about hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation strategy, data split, and computational resources are limited. (4)On ABIDE II, while achieving high specificity (87.5%), the sensitivity (51.3%) is relatively low compared to some baselines. This imbalance could limit clinical utility where missing ASD cases (false negatives) has significant consequences. (5)The paper does not analyze cases where the model fails, which could provide insights into its limitations and potential improvements. (6) The paper presents a module in the figure that is never mentioned in the text. In Fig.1 (“Inter-Module Coordination Modeling”), a component named “Deep Embedding Clustering Pooling” is shown, yet no related content is found anywhere in the manuscript.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed model achieves favorable performance on the ABIDE I and ABIDE II datasets, and the effectiveness of the presented method is further validated through insightful analyses and discussions.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The proposed method lacks substantial novelty. Although it reports high performance metrics, the paper does not specify the number of subjects or other detailed information of the ABIDE I dataset used, which casts doubt on the reliability of the reported results. In addition, the number of comparative methods is insufficient and the methods adopted for comparison are relatively outdated, while the explanation of the model methodology is not sufficiently clear and comprehensive.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: N/A
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Provisional Accept Justification(s): I recommend an early accept for this paper. Reviewers highly praised the biologically motivated H2GT framework and its multi-scale interpretability for ASD diagnosis. The integration of topological priors into a hierarchical graph Transformer is technically sound. Although one reviewer gave a borderline score (3) citing minor concerns over baseline recency and dataset subject details, these do not undermine the core methodological novelty, solid experimental results, and strong clinical relevance of the work.

title: Image-mediated fMRI-to-caption generation with visual pathway tokens and hyperbolic alignment
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The research introduces a novel geometric formulation by performing alignment in the hyperbolic Poincaré ball, which more effectively captures the complex, non-uniform hierarchical structure of brain representations compared to traditional Euclidean metrics. 2.The model employs an original data utilization strategy through visual pathway tokenization, which bypasses the information loss of standard regional averaging by converting fine-grained, vertex-level activations into query tokens. 3.The work demonstrates strong neurobiological interpretability, as the model’s regional activations align with known functional brain specialization for specific parts of speech without requiring any explicit word-type supervision during training.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.The proposed method relies on a frozen image-to-caption pipeline as a teacher, which potentially caps the fMRI decoding performance by the inherent biases and linguistic limitations of the pre-trained CLIP and LLaMA3 models. 2.The Visual Pathway Tokenization utilizes a high-dimensional vertex input (V=12535 vertices) that significantly increases the parameter count and computational overhead compared to standard regional parceling.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper has several notable strengths. First, the overall problem is interesting and timely: generating captions directly from fMRI is challenging due to the large modality gap between brain activity and language, and the proposed image-mediated formulation is well motivated. Second, the method is technically coherent and combines three meaningful design choices: hyperbolic embedding alignment, TPDA-based teacher-student distillation, and visual pathway tokenization using fine-grained vertex-level features from visual cortex. Third, the empirical results are strong: on NSD, the method reports the best CIDEr score among the compared methods, and the gains are supported by ablation studies that isolate the impact of the alignment loss, TPDA, stage-1 pretraining, and visual pathway tokenization. Fourth, the paper is generally well organized and includes both quantitative and qualitative analyses, including neuroscientific attribution analysis that improves interpretability. Finally, the submission provides an anonymized code link, which is a positive signal for reproducibility.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The main weaknesses are as follows. First, the relevance to core MICCAI themes is somewhat limited: although the paper uses fMRI, the task is natural-scene brain captioning rather than a medical imaging or clinically grounded problem, and the clinical significance remains indirect. Second, the experiments are limited to NSD and appear to focus on only the first subject who completed all trials, which raises concerns about subject-level generalization and broader robustness. Third, while the combination is interesting, some components are incremental relative to the recent brain decoding and multimodal literature cited by the authors, including BrainCap, BrainChat, UMBRAE, and MindLLM; therefore, the paper would benefit from a clearer discussion of what is fundamentally new beyond a strong integration of existing ideas. Fourth, the evaluation is centered on automatic captioning metrics, and stronger evidence such as cross-subject validation, statistical significance testing, or a more explicit analysis of failure modes would further strengthen the claims. Finally, the interpretability analysis is interesting, but at present it remains more suggestive than conclusive.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper tackles an ambitious problem across neuroimaging, representation learning, and language generation. The two-stage design is clear and easy to follow. Results on NSD are strong, beating several prior baselines. The ablation study is reasonable, and the authors also make an effort to link their model’s behavior to known brain organization, which is a nice addition beyond just reporting benchmark scores.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The evaluation is limited to caption generation. It remains unclear whether the proposed method generalizes to other tasks such as VQA, which have been explored in concurrent work like MindLLM. The advantages of this approach in broader task settings are therefore not established. 2.The evaluation relies primarily on automatic NLG metrics (CIDEr, BLEU, etc.). For a generation task of this nature, human evaluation or semantic analysis would provide stronger evidence of caption quality. 3.The claimed neuroscientific interpretability seems to be overstated. The observation that the model activates known visual regions without explicit word-type supervision is interesting, but it does not demonstrate that the model has learned neurobiologically meaningful representations. A more plausible explanation is that the model simply picks up on statistical regularities in the data. For example, nouns and adjectives may correlate with different types of visual features, which in turn map to distinct fMRI patterns. To support the claim, the authors would need to show cross-subject generalization of these activation patterns or test whether perturbing specific regions degrades corresponding word-type predictions. As it stands, the analysis remains correlational. 4.The motivation for using hyperbolic geometry is not sufficiently justified. Figure 3 only shows that hyperbolic alignment yields smaller embedding distances, which is an auxiliary metric. The paper would benefit from a direct qualitative comparison of captions generated with and without hyperbolic alignment. For instance, whether hyperbolic alignment leads to better preservation of hierarchical or fine-grained semantic relationships. Additionally, a visualization of the embedding space (e.g., using horoPCA) comparing hyperbolic vs. Euclidean representations could provide intuitive evidence of why the hyperbolic space is better suited for aligning fMRI and image embeddings.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers for valuable comments. Below we address concerns. Q1 (R1-1,2): Architectural design rationale. A: The frozen image-to-caption pipeline is an intentional anchor for stable Stage 2 alignment despite the known bias. The high-dimensional vertex input feeds only a single MLP, not a large computation burden by recent standards. We will clarify this. Q2 (R2-1): Clinical significance & MICCAI relevance. A: Brain decoding has been published in MICCAI (Huang et al., MICCAI 2022; Shen et al., MICCAI 2025), placing the task within core MICCAI themes. Studying the healthy brain is important to gauge the diseased brain. Our method treats the healthy brain as a normative reference to interpret simulated regional impairments. We generate captions with each visual region’s input zeroed at inference (see Q6) and note that impairment varies by region and meaning. Fusiform face area lesion distorts the gender for an image of a woman standing on a tennis court, the lesion of early visual regions misinterprets type of food for an image of pizza (Fig 2). The region perturbation results are similar to the caption generation without visual pathway tokenization (Fig 2), which can be interpreted as how the brain would decode fMRI if some visual pathway regions are impaired. We will clarify this. Q3 (R2-2, R3-3;Meta#1): Cross-subject validation. A: We had cross-subject results, but chose not to include them for fair comparison since existing studies only reported Subject1.We train a separate model for each subject and present cross-subject results. Vertex-level visual-pathway attribution maps (Fig 4b across four subjects in NSD) yield intra-class correlation of 0.607/0.578/0.653 (noun/verb/adjective, 0.6+ is “Good” range). All 6 (4 choose 2) pairwise correlations are significant (mean r=0.478, all FDR p<0.001). We will briefly mention these results. Q4 (R2-3;Meta#2): Novelty relative to recent brain decoding works. A: Three contributions are fundamentally new among cited methods (BrainCap/BrainChat/UMBRAE/MindLLM): (1) non-Euclidean (hyperbolic) alignment for fMRI-image. (2) vertex-level visual pathway tokenization — UMBRAE uses subject-specific voxel-subset tokenizer, MindLLM region-level attention, neither at vertex granularity. (3) post-hoc neuroscientific verification: prior works report captioning metrics only. We will clarify this. Q5 (R3-1): The possibility of task extension. A: Our method generates embeddings that can generate captions from fMRI. Thus, zero-shot extension to VQA or retrieval tasks is possible by interfacing the output embedding with off-the-shelf image-conditioned VLMs without any retraining. This will be added. Q6 (R3-2,3;Meta#3,4): Region perturbation as semantic evaluation. A: To test whether perturbing specific regions degrades corresponding word-type predictions, we generate captions with each visual region’s input zeroed at inference. Disruptions are region-specific and differ across meanings. For an image of a woman standing on a tennis court, fusiform face area lesion distorts the gender. For pizza, early visual regions yield within-category changes (compare with examples in Fig 2). This provides both (i) model-level perturbation evidence beyond correlation and (ii) semantic analysis complementary to automatic NLG metrics. This will be added. Q7 (R3-4;Meta #5): Hyperbolic alignment justification. A: We examine whether the learned geometry encodes interpretable semantic structure with horoPCA-style visualization comparing hyperbolic vs. Euclidean representations. A horoPCA-style projection using tangent-space approximation provides intuitive evidence: PC1 correlates with the average noun concreteness per caption for hyperbolic (|r|=0.153, p<0.001), not for Euclidean PCA (|r|=0.051, p_FDR=0.165). Thus, the radial coordinate encodes word concreteness only in the hyperbolic case. We will briefly mention these results.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper proposes a two-stage fMRI-to-caption framework using image embeddings as an intermediate representation, with hyperbolic alignment, TPDA, and visual pathway tokenization. Reviewers appreciated the strong NSD results, clear ablations, and the attempt to connect model behavior with functional brain specialization. However, the rebuttal should address the reviewers’ concerns through clarification and appropriate qualification of claims, including, but not limited to, the narrow single-subject NSD evaluation and lack of broader robustness evidence, the novelty relative to recent brain decoding and multimodal captioning methods, the reliance on automatic captioning metrics without stronger semantic evaluation, the correlational nature of the neuroscientific interpretability claims, and the need to better justify why hyperbolic alignment is appropriate beyond improved embedding distance. | The submitted manuscript presents a technically solid fMRI-to-caption framework with strong NSD results and meaningful ablation evidence, and the combination of hyperbolic alignment, TPDA, and visual pathway tokenization is sufficiently interesting. However, the evaluation remains narrow and the neuroscientific interpretation should be moderated, given the single-subject setting and largely correlational analysis. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a technically coherent fMRI-to-caption framework, with strong benchmark results and well-designed ablation studies that isolate the contributions of each component. The initial reviews raised legitimate concerns about single-subject generalization, the neuroscientific interpretability claims, and the justification for hyperbolic alignment. The authors’ rebuttal provided substantive additional evidence that directly addressed these weaknesses, including cross-subject reliability of attribution maps, region perturbation analyses demonstrating semantic specificity, and a horoPCA-style comparison showing that hyperbolic space better encodes concreteness. Two reviewers ultimately recommended acceptance, recognizing the work’s novelty and the strength of the response. The paper’s contributions and the rebuttal’s effective resolution of major concerns justify acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors directly addressed key concerns including cross-subject validation with significant inter-subject reliability, region perturbation analysis demonstrating semantic specificity, horoPCA visualization validating hyperbolic geometry, clarification of clinical relevance to brain decoding for normative reference, and articulation of novelty relative to prior methods.

title: Inflated Performance in fMRI-Based ASD Diagnosis: A Reproducibility Study of Data Leakage in Feature Selection Pipelines
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper highlights a critical methodological issue that directly affects the credibility of findings in neuroimaging-based machine learning research. The study follows a convincing and transparent workflow of reproduction, correction, and comparative re-evaluation, with clearly quantified results. This enhances the paper’ s persuasiveness. The authors make their corrected code publicly available, which improves the reproducibility and practical value of the work.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The level of methodological novelty is somewhat limited. The study mainly verifies and applies already recognized methodological principles, rather than introducing a fundamentally new concept or technique. The evidence supporting the generality of the conclusions remains insufficient. Although the warning raised by the authors is reasonable and important, drawing broad implications for the field from only two case studies leaves the empirical basis somewhat limited. Stronger support for claims of broader prevalence would require a wider survey or more systematic analysis. Some experimental details and analyses need to be described more thoroughly. In particular, the setup of the corrected experiments, especially the treatment of hyperparameters, is not sufficiently detailed, which weakens the rigor of attributing the observed performance drop solely to data leakage. The current work focuses primarily on correcting and comparing two published cases. The paper would be substantially strengthened by either screening a larger number of potentially affected studies or providing a deeper analysis of the interaction between data leakage and hyperparameter choices.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The paper addresses a critical yet often overlooked issue in neuroimaging-based machine learning research, namely data leakage, which is essential for improving the reliability and reproducibility of results. 2.Beyond identifying the problem, the authors distill a generalizable checklist that provides practical guidance for similar fMRI classification studies. 3.By re-evaluating existing pipelines, the study reveals potential sources of performance inflation, offering valuable insights for the community. 4.The idea of integrating AI tools into the code review process aligns well with current trends toward reproducibility and automated auditing, and shows a degree of forward-looking thinking.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.After correcting the data leakage issues, model performance drops noticeably. However, it is unclear whether a systematic hyperparameter search and re-optimization were conducted on the revised pipelines, making it difficult to assess whether the reported results reflect their best achievable performance. 2.The paper lacks a comparative analysis of discriminative features (e.g., key brain regions) before and after correction. In particular, it remains unclear whether the neurobiological interpretations reported in prior work are preserved, which is important for validating the method. 3.The discussion on AI-assisted code review remains largely conceptual. It would benefit from more concrete details, such as general prompt templates or semi-automated review workflows, to improve practicality and reproducibility. 4.The experiments are primarily conducted on a single dataset (e.g., ABIDE I). Additional cross-dataset validation (e.g., ABIDE II) would strengthen the robustness and generalizability of the findings. 5.While the proposed checklist appears general, empirical validation is limited to ASD tasks. Including case studies on other psychiatric disorders or similar classification problems would further support its broader applicability. 6.There are several formatting issues in the submission, such as tables and text exceeding page boundaries (e.g., table sizes and content on page 3), as well as inconsistent header formatting. These should be corrected in the final version.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: Relevance: Data leakage and overestimation of performance are well-recognized issues in the machine learning literature. Addressing these problems in the context of rs-fMRI-based ASD classification and providing concrete recommendations makes the contribution valuable. Transparency and reproducibility: The authors provide corrected implementations of the evaluated methods, enabling a clearer assessment of their true performance and supporting reproducibility.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Limited novelty: While the paper addresses an important issue, the methodological novelty is limited. The proposed contributions consist primarily of relatively minor corrections to previously published pipelines, without introducing new analytical frameworks or substantially extending prior approaches. Inconsistent and incomplete reporting of results: The presentation of results lacks consistency. For example, Table 1 reports performance as decimal values, whereas Table 2 uses percentages. In addition, although both analyses employ cross-validation, standard deviations are only reported for the corrected results in the second case study. This inconsistency makes it difficult to interpret variability and compare results across experiments. Limited depth of discussion: The discussion does not fully explore the broader implications of the findings. For instance, the claim that leaderboard results are often above 90% and likely overestimated is important, but its impact on the field is not sufficiently analyzed. Similarly, while the authors suggest that data leakage may affect previously reported biomarkers, they do not provide additional analyses to support or quantify this claim. Weak integration of the clinical context: The introduction of the medical domain is somewhat superficial and occasionally imprecise. For example, statements such as describing ASD as a “prevalent condition” or implying that rs-fMRI directly measures “whole-brain functional connectivity” would benefit from more careful wording and stronger grounding in the neuroimaging literature.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for their constructive feedback. We address each major concern below and commit to concrete revisions. [R1, R2, Meta] Hyperparameter treatment We intentionally retained the original hyperparameters in the corrected experiments. Re-tuning after removing leakage would introduce a second source of variation, making it difficult to attribute performance changes specifically to leakage. Our goal is to isolate the effect of leakage, which requires holding all other factors constant. We will clarify this rationale explicitly in the revision. Importantly, the corrected accuracies (66.35% and 65.02%) are not anomalously low. Dong et al. (Human Brain Mapping, 2025), an independent study on ABIDE I using a standardized framework with per-fold tuning across multiple architectures, reports test accuracies in the roughly 65–72% range. Our results fall within this interval, supporting the interpretation that they reflect realistic generalisation rather than under-optimised models. [R1, R3, Meta] Scope of case studies and strength of claims We agree that two case studies alone are insufficient to establish field-wide prevalence. Accordingly, we will moderate our claims in the abstract and conclusion, replacing broad generalisations with more precise, evidence-backed statements. At the same time, independent corroboration strengthens this point. Dong et al. (2025) explicitly state in Section 2.5.2 that they adapted EV-GCN from Huang and Chung (2020), resolved an information leakage issue in the EV-GCN model, and performed fold-wise model selection using validation performance. Under this corrected setup, EV-GCN drops to about 68%, far below the originally reported 81%. Together with our two case studies, this provides converging evidence that leakage-induced inflation recurs across distinct ABIDE I pipelines. We will incorporate this reference and adjust our framing to reflect this broader but still carefully scoped evidence. [R2, Meta] AI-assisted code review The workflow is described in Section 6.2: we use structured prompts derived from the checklist in Section 6.1, such as identifying supervised feature selection applied outside cross-validation loops, forming a reusable QA protocol. We emphasise that AI review is intended as a first-pass diagnostic tool, not a substitute for expert validation. To improve clarity, we will add a table of example prompts and explicitly scope the role of AI in the revision. [R2, Meta] Neurobiological interpretability This concern is already addressed in Section 7 (“Broader implications for reported biomarkers”): the XAI-for-ASD interpretability analysis identifying visual-cortex markers was performed on a model whose feature space was pre-optimized using test-set labels, meaning those biomarker attributions lose statistical validity after correction. While recomputing feature importance under leakage-free pipelines exceeds the scope of this reproducibility study, we note that Dong et al. (2025) report leakage-free reanalysis and feature-importance results in broadly comparable regions. We will expand this into a dedicated discussion paragraph, clearly scoping interpretability as future work. [R3] Clinical framing and terminology We will revise the introduction to use precise neuroimaging terminology, clarify that rs-fMRI measures BOLD-derived functional connectivity, replace imprecise prevalence statements with the cited WHO figure, and ensure consistent ABIDE citation throughout. [R2, R3, Meta] Table reporting consistency The differing formats in Tables 1 and 2 are intentional: Table 1 uses point estimates to match MADE-for-ASD’s original single-run reporting, while Table 2 reports mean ± std to match XAI-for-ASD. This design enables direct, like-for-like comparison with each paper’s reported results. We agree this was not sufficiently explained and will add clarifying notes in the table captions.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Data leakage is an important issue that can be overlooked and is often ignored. It leads to overestimation of the results and questionable exagerations of clinical impact. This is the starting point and motivation for this proposal and, this motivation itself, is one of the strengths of the paper that all reviewers agree with. Not just that, but the authors provide corrected implementations and a checklist of good practices. This is also underscored by all the reviewers. However, there are also clear limitations in the current version of the manuscript. In what follows are a list of potentially adressable weaknesses informing my decision. The number of case studies is limited (2) which does not guarantee the broad implications presented by the authors [R#1]. This should be backed up by a larger set of examples and a more systematic approach (probably impractical without new experiments) or toned down conclusions. Related to that, there should be a more in-depth discussion [R#3] with more details on hyperparameters [R#1 and 2] and AI-use [R#2] and ideally some details on how the methodology fixes impact neurobiological interpretations [R#2]. The format should be carefully checked. There are clear inconsistencies between the results tables that should not be present in a final draft [R#2 and 3]. This not only difficults comparison but also detracts from the final presentation, making the whole manuscript feel unpolished. Nonetheless, this is a non-exhaustive list of things to address and I would advise the authors to check all the specific requests from each reviewer. | I think the authors did a really good job of being transparent and open to downplay some of the claims which were the things I was looking forward with the rebuttal. This is not just my opinion but also the opinion of reviewers #1 and #3 (there was no justification given by reviewer #2). In that sense, as long as the authors include all the information and promises from the rebuttal in the final manuscript, I see no issues with the submission. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): Based on the clarifications provided in the rebuttal, a majority of the reviewer’s concerns have been addressed. I believe this is a timely and interesting contribution which addresses an important gap in reporting pipelines and studies contributing factors systematically and adds value to the broader neuroimaging community Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a reproducibility evaluation of ASD classifiers under data leakage and explores changes in performance after correcting this leakage using AI-based code review in two studies. The reviewers pointed out the limited novelty of the results, a point with which I partially disagree, especially if we consider this an application study. Secondly, the reviewers raised several weaknesses, including the absence of hyperparameter tuning in the reproduction after leakage correction, and requested more details on the AI-based code analysis used to detect leakages. The authors’ rebuttal addresses these two points perfectly. The reviewers seem satisfied with the authors’ responses to their concerns and acknowledge that the authors are particularly aware of the paper’s limitations and are willing to make appropriate changes to address them. Given the quality and rigor of this study, especially given the complexity of reproducing published findings, I recommend acceptance.

title: Latent Pathology–Age Decoupling in Functional Connectivity Graphs for Multi-task Schizophrenia Assessment
reviewer_1_strengths: Introduces a novel and principled framework (LPAD) addressing a key challenge in schizophrenia FC analysis: confounding between age and pathology. Clinically-informed gated modulation (CIGM) thoughtfully reintroduces age as a contextual factor, preserving aging-sensitive cognitive signals. Extensive experiments across multiple symptom and cognitive domains demonstrate statistically significant improvements over strong baselines. External validation on an independent clinical dataset supports cross-site generalizability, which is critical for clinical translation. Comprehensive interpretability analyses, including linear probes and spatial ROI mapping, provide biological plausibility and insight into the pathology-age decoupling.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The impact of preprocessing choices (e. g. , denoising, parcellation scheme) on model performance is not clearly discussed, limiting reproducibility and understanding of robustness. Sample size is relatively small. The study design and dataset usage, particularly which dataset serves as external validation, could be described more clearly to improve transparency.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: Main strength of the paper is the explicit reuse of age-related features after disentanglement, rather than discarding them. Additionally, the overall orchestration of the modules appears coherent, suggesting a well-designed pipeline.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: There are several concerns, mainly related to the clarity and completeness of methodological descriptions: 1 ) The description of the GPSConv-GINE layer is unclear and requires substantial clarification. Unlike widely established models such as GCN or GAT, this combination is not standard and cannot be assumed to be familiar to the reader. The GPS model is essentially a Graph Transformer framework that integrates local message passing with global attention, along with various encoding strategies while GINE model extends GIN by incorporating edge features into the aggregation process. It is not clear from the paper whether these two models are combined, and if so, how the integration is implemented, which components of the GPS framework are actually used and the motivation for choosing a Graph Transformer-based approach. 2 ) The baseline models lack sufficient explanation. For example, the abbreviation “MT” is introduced without definition. Some relevant prior works on disentangling age as a covariate (e.g., cited in [33]) are mentioned in the text but not included in the main comparison table. This makes it difficult to assess the fairness and completeness of the experimental comparison. 3 ) The paper states that two datasets are used, but it is not clear whether the datasets are merged and if merged, what are differences acquisition protocols etc..
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The paper tackles the age confounding issue in schizophrenia, which is very relevant. The idea of removing age first and then reintroducing it as context is intuitive and aligns well with clinical reasoning. 2.The ablation study is thorough and shows each part actually helps. 3.The Interpretability analysis is thorough.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The cosine orthogonality penalty only removes linear dependencies, whereas the aging process is inherently nonlinear. It is therefore possible that z^p still encodes age-related information or z^a encodes pathological information in a nonlinear form that this constraint cannot capture. 2.The node-level scalar gate g_i is computed solely from h^p. However, after being constrained by L_ortho, h^p is supposed to be free of age-related information, so how can it reliably decide how much contextual information from v_i should be injected? 3.The linear probe shows that z^p no longer contains age-related information, but there is no corresponding evidence that z^a is free of SZ-related pathological features.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and AC. We accept the meta-reviewer’s two limitations—no theoretical guarantee of nonlinear age removal, and limited sample size—and will state both in the camera-ready. Nonlinear decoupling and bidirectionality (R3-1, R3-3). L_ortho enforces only linear orthogonality and cannot guarantee removal of nonlinear age–pathology coupling. The linear probe shows z^p does not predict age (R²=-0.176) but does not symmetrically test whether z^a predicts pathology. Both will be listed as limitations, with bidirectional probing and nonlinear extensions as future work. Existing analyses still jointly support bidirectional separation: (1) Fig. 3(b) shows zero overlap (Jaccard=0.000) between top-10% ROIs; age-stream ROIs concentrate in subcortical/temporal regions consistent with normal aging, while pathology-stream ROIs anchor in SZ-related DMN—if z^a retained pathological information, its ROIs would more likely overlap with SZ-related DMN. (2) z^a is driven by explicit age regression supervision, which with L_ortho exerts directional pressure toward age representation. (3) Fig. 3(a) shows clear t-SNE cluster separation, indicating separation persists in nonlinear spaces. Gating on h^p (R3-2). The asymmetric gate g_i=σ(w_g^T h_i^p) is intentional. Under L_ortho the pathology branch suppresses age-related shortcuts while retaining pathology-severity information. The gate does not recover age from h^p; it determines, based on pathological representation, whether a node needs age-context modulation. Clinically, age–SZ pathology interactions are more pronounced in pathology-affected regions [20,8], so stronger-pathology nodes need more age modulation. Table 2 confirms this: removing CIGM yields the largest cognitive drop on WM (Δcorr=0.023), the task most sensitive to aging–pathology interactions. GPSConv-GINE (R2-1). We will clarify in Sec. 2.1.GPSConv [25] is a hybrid graph transformer layer combining local message-passing with global attention. We instantiate the local module with GINE [12,32], which naturally exploits continuous FC edge weights w. GPSConv-GINE is thus a GPSConv layer using GINE as its local MPNN, motivated by GINE preserving continuous FC weights (often weakened in GCN/GAT) and GPSConv’s global attention modeling cross-network long-range dependencies disrupted in SZ. Dataset usage (R2-3). Datasets are not merged. COBRE (n=135) is used solely for five-fold cross-validation in Table 1; the local dataset (n=35) serves only as independent external validation in Fig. 2.They differ in protocols and cognitive batteries (MCCB T-scores vs. BACS raw scores), so no merged training was performed. We will explicitly label the local set as held-out external validation in Sec. 3.1 and Fig. 2 caption. Baseline coverage (R2-2). MT denotes Multi-Task; the full term will appear at first occurrence. [33] is built on sMRI-derived structural graphs with explicit covariate disentanglement; its modality, graph construction, and supervision differ from our FC-based subject-wise prediction, making fair reproduction under identical FC inputs infeasible. For comparability, Table 1 includes two directly corresponding FC-based age-deconfounding baselines: MT-SZ_ar (regression residualization [4]) and MT-SZ_adv (adversarial deconfounding [6,1]), reimplemented under identical FC inputs and task setup. Preprocessing and sample size (R1). We agree preprocessing and parcellation affect FC modeling and that the paper underdiscusses this. Experiments use fMRIPrep [7] with FC on the Power-264 atlas [24]; the camera-ready will discuss denoising, parcellation, and FC construction. We acknowledge sample size as an important limitation; COBRE (n=135) and the external set (n=35) are comparable to recent multi-site SZ studies.

title: Learning Geometry-Aware Bundles with Spectral Heat Kernel Diffusion for fMRI-based Brain Disease Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: The formulation is genuinely interesting. Using vector bundle theory for brain networks is a novel move in this space. Rather than pushing all ROIs into a shared feature space, each region gets its own subspace with a learned orthogonal transformation — which is a principled and meaningful way to handle inter-regional heterogeneity. Standard GNN assumptions don’t really account for this, so the departure feels well-motivated. Heat kernel augmentation is a smart choice. Swapping out random edge/node dropping for heat kernel-based perturbations is one of the more thoughtful design decisions in the paper. Brain graph topology carries physical meaning, so more structured, less destructive augmentations make real sense here. Results are solid. The method consistently outperforms baselines on both datasets (Table 1), including recent GCL methods. The gains aren’t dramatic, but they’re stable across metrics. The ablation and interpretability work is a real plus. Table 2 does a reasonable job supporting each component’s contribution, and the ROI-level interpretability analysis is a strong point — the identified regions align with known disease-related areas, which matters a lot for clinical relevance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: The theoretical side is thin. The geometric motivation is appealing, but the paper provides no formal analysis or evidence that the proposed formulation actually reduces geometric misalignment or improves representation quality over standard GNNs. The heat kernel approximation used for augmentation also feels somewhat heuristic without further justification. Reproducibility is a concern. Several important implementation details are missing — diffusion time parameters, specifics of the orthogonality constraint, architectural choices. There is also no mention of code availability.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: S1.The paper explores a geometry-aware formulation for brain connectivity modeling, aiming to account for heterogeneous functional structure across regions. S2.The integration of diffusion-based representations with contrastive learning is a reasonable design choice. S3.The method is evaluated on the ADNI dataset and an in-house dataset, and shows improved performance over several baselines, suggesting potential empirical effectiveness.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.The paper claims to “introduce a Bundle Laplacian,” but this construction appears to have been already proposed in prior work, most notably in Bundle Neural Networks (Bamberger et al., ICLR 2025). The current manuscript does not cite this paper, despite the substantial overlap in the core formulation. This weakens the novelty claim and makes the positioning with respect to prior work unclear. W2.Several key motivations and claims in the paper are stated rather strongly, but are not sufficiently supported by evidence. In particular, the introduction argues that conventional GNNs fail because different brain regions reside on heterogeneous functional manifolds with distinct local geometric properties, yet the cited references [1,26] do not seem to directly substantiate this claim, and the paper does not provide its own empirical evidence for it. Likewise, the paper claims that the proposed multiscale spectral diffusion preserves the coherence of the vector bundle and ensures “strict physical and geometric consistency across views,” but this notion is neither clearly defined nor experimentally validated. As a result, the rationale behind the proposed method is not fully convincing beyond the observed performance gains. W3.The paper also lacks sufficient explanation and citation for heat kernel and heat diffusion, even though these are core components of the proposed method. W4.The paper mentions a first-order approximation of the heat kernel but does not present the corresponding equation or theoretical justification. In addition, Section 2.3 is difficult to interpret due to undefined variables (e.g., X_B, X_spec) and unclear module interactions (e.g., the shared backbone). W5.The implementation details of the spectral perturbation module are incomplete (\tau_1, \tau2). W6.The term “CI” is used without definition, making the interpretability analysis unclear.
reviewer_2_rating: (2) Reject — should be rejected, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The application of vector bundle theory for ROI-level orthogonal feature projection and between-node feature alignment is innovative and well-motivated. The proposed contrastive learning strategy is both straightforward and highly effective. The method is rigorously validated across multiple datasets, demonstrating consistent state-of-the-art results.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Ambiguity in Figure 1: Part 2 of Figure 1 is somewhat confusing. Because the bundle transformation should not introduce new topological connections that do not exist in the original functional graph, the graph connectivity shown in panel B (the bundle subspace) should align with panel A. However, they appear visibly different. The authors should clarify this discrepancy or revise the figure accordingly to avoid misleading the readers. 2.Missing Complexity Analysis: The bundle transformation increases the size of the Laplacian matrix by a factor of $d$. Consequently, the authors should provide an explicit discussion regarding the computational complexity and memory overhead of VB-GCL, particularly in comparison to standard GNN baselines.
reviewer_3_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their constructive feedback. All clarifications will be incorporated into the final version. [R1 & R2: Relation to BuNN (Bamberger et al., ICLR 2025)] We will cite this work. The bundle Laplacian L_B = O^T (L ⊗ I_d) O traces back to Singer & Wu (2012, Vector Diffusion Maps and the Connection Laplacian) , and both BuNN and VB-GCL build on it. However, VB-GCL differs from BuNN in three aspects. First, BuNN is a general-purpose GNN for heterophilic and long-range graph tasks targeting over-smoothing, over-squashing, and limited expressivity. VB-GCL is the first to apply vector bundle theory to fMRI-based brain disease diagnosis, to model ROI manifold heterogeneity. Second, BuNN relies on the full heat kernel, often requiring costly spectral methods, to enable global node communication. By contrast, VB-GCL employs a localized K-order polynomial filter with residual connections for efficient structural feature aggregation, which is well suited to brain networks. Third, our spectral contrastive learning module is an independent contribution. BuNN does not include a contrastive mechanism, whereas VB-GCL uses a first-order heat-kernel expansion specifically to generate weak and strong contrastive views. This design avoids computationally expensive matrix exponentials while providing noise regularization for small clinical fMRI cohorts. In addition, ROI-level saliency analysis for disease biomarkers, as shown in Fig. 3, is also unique to our work. [R2-W2: Insufficiently supported claims] We will replace [1,26] with Bijsterbosch et al. (eLife, 2018) on region-specific spatial configurations and Vidaurre et al. (PNAS, 2017) on region-specific hierarchical temporal dynamics, supporting manifold heterogeneity. We will formalize these as a mathematical property. Two views are generated by (I - τ_t L ̂_B) driven by the same bundle Laplacian, sharing the eigenbasis of L ̂_B and remaining on the manifold induced by (O, L ̂_B), unlike edge dropping which destroys topology. [R2-W5: Perturbation parameters] τ_1, τ_2 are not fixed but sampled per batch from two non-overlapping ranges corresponding to weak and strong diffusion scales. This stochastic sampling acts as built-in augmentation, exposing the contrastive objective to multi-scale perturbations. [R2-Q1: Are W_k shared across layers?] W_k are not shared. Within a layer, each polynomial order k ∈ {0, …, K} has its own W_k. Across layers, each layer maintains an independent set {W_0, …, W_k} to capture distinct geometric scales. [R2-Q2: In-house dataset availability] Due to IRB constraints, public release is not permitted. Qualified researchers may contact the corresponding author and obtain authorized access for non-commercial research after a data-use agreement. [R4-2: Complexity] VB-GCL has 13K parameters, 397 MB peak memory, and 5 ms inference per subject on a V100 GPU with batch size 32, compared with 3K parameters, 69 MB, and 3 ms for the GCN backbone. Despite the 3.8-fold parameter and 5.8-fold memory increase from bundle Laplacian operations, the absolute cost remains lightweight and clinically practical. [R1: Reproducibility] To clarify the missing reproducibility details, we use d=8, K=3 polynomial filter, QR-based orthogonality enforcement, and Focal Loss with adaptive class weighting. Due to the double-blind policy, code is currently private; the full implementation will be released upon acceptance. [Additional clarifications: R2-W3, R2-W4, R2-W6, and R4-1] We will define H(τ) = exp(−τ L̂_B) ≈ I − τ L̂_B. X_B denotes the bundle-transformed feature in Sec. 2.1, and X_spec^(i) denotes the contrastive views in Eq. 3.The shared backbone is the bundle diffusion encoder applied across streams. CI denotes Cognitive Impairment, consistent with Sec. 3.Fig. 1 will be revised to ensure that the bundle subspace preserves the original graph connectivity.
meta_review: Meta-review #1 Initial recommendation: Invite for Rebuttal Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): This paper proposes a vector bundle-based graph contrastive learning framework for fMRI analysis, and reviewers acknowledge the conceptual novelty and promising empirical performance; The overall assessment is highly mixed (scores: 3 / 2 / 5). While the geometric formulation is interesting, several reviewers raise concerns about unclear novelty relative to recent work, insufficient theoretical justification, and lack of proper citation and positioning. In addition, important methodological details are missing, key claims are not fully supported by evidence, and reproducibility and clarity issues make the approach difficult to assess. The authors are encouraged to address these concerns in the rebuttal, particularly by clarifying novelty, strengthening theoretical and empirical justification, and improving methodological transparency. | Based on the reviewer votes, acceptance is recommended. However, the authors should properly acknowledge that the core bundle Laplacian formulation and vector-bundle-based heat diffusion framework are closely related to prior works regarding bundle neural networks and other Laplacian literature. Meta-review #2 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): After carefully reviewing the authors’ rebuttal, I have revised my initial assessment to Accept. The authors directly addressed key concerns including clarifying novelty relative to BuNN (ICLR 2025) with three distinct differences, replacing insufficient citations with evidence supporting ROI manifold heterogeneity, providing computational complexity and hyperparameter details, and committing to code release upon acceptance. Meta-review #3 Post-rebuttal recommendation: Accept Justification(s): The paper presents a conceptually interesting geometry-aware graph contrastive learning framework for fMRI-based disease diagnosis, with promising empirical results and useful ablation and interpretability analyses. The reviewers were mixed, mainly due to concerns about novelty, missing methodological details, reproducibility, and insufficient positioning relative to prior vector-bundle and heat-kernel diffusion work. After rebuttal, most concerns were reasonably addressed, including code release, implementation details, complexity analysis, and clarification of the relation to prior work. I recommend acceptance, but the final version must include proper citations and a clear scholarly positioning with respect to Bundle Neural Networks, connection Laplacian, vector diffusion maps, and heat-kernel diffusion literature.

title: Learning the Hierarchical Organization in Brain Network for Brain Disorder Diagnosis
reviewer_1_strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation. The paper clearly articulates a genuine limitation of atlas-based approaches: predefined sub-network boundaries are rigid and cannot accommodate the well-documented phenomenon of cross-network functional interactions that are disease-relevant. The motivating example, that Frontal_Inf_Oper_L and Temporal_Sup_L are hard-coded into separate Yeo7 communities despite known ASD-related connectivity between them, is concrete and well-supported by neuroscience literature. This makes the transition from fixed to learnable sub-networks a natural and compelling direction. Principled hierarchical design. The three-level hierarchy (node → subgraph → graph) is architecturally clean and mirrors the known modular-hierarchical organization of the brain. The use of Sparsemax at the node-to-subgraph level is a thoughtful choice: it enforces sparsity in the attention distribution, which both aids interpretability (each subgraph attends to a limited subset of nodes) and provides a natural mechanism for discovering discrete-like community structure. This is more principled than simply applying Softmax, which would produce diffuse attention weights. Complementary regularization strategy. The combination of orthogonality constraint (encouraging diversity among subgraph tokens) and hierarchical consistency (distilling graph-level semantics back to node features) is well-designed. The orthogonality loss formulated as a cross-entropy over the cosine similarity matrix (Eq. 4) is elegant and differentiable. The teacher-student setup for hierarchical consistency (Eq. 5) with temperature-scaled KL divergence is a standard but effective mechanism for ensuring that local node features are informed by global context. The ablation study convincingly shows that each component contributes to performance. Interpretability analysis. The paper goes beyond classification accuracy to provide meaningful neuroscientific interpretation. Figure 3 shows that some learned sub-networks align with predefined functional networks (e. g. , No. 7 for MDD overlapping 66.7% with SMN), while others span multiple predefined networks, capturing the very cross-network interactions the method was designed to find. The disease-related sub-networks identify regions consistent with prior literature (e. g. , fusiform gyrus and amygdala for ASD, hippocampus and anterior cingulate for MDD), which strengthens the clinical relevance claims. The method is tested on two distinct disorders (ASD and MDD) with different datasets, demonstrating generality. On both datasets, BrainHO achieves the best accuracy among the compared baselines, and notably does so using only the static PCC matrix while several competitors also require raw BOLD signals as additional input.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Narrow and potentially non-representative baseline selection. This is the most significant concern. Table 1 compares BrainHO exclusively against a narrow set of recent Transformer/GNN-based methods (BNT, Com-BrainTF, ALTER, DHGFormer, LHDFormer), all from roughly the same methodological lineage. However, the broader literature on ABIDE classification includes numerous methods that report substantially higher accuracy. For example, Subah et al. (2021) reported 88% accuracy using DNNs [Subah et al. A deep learning approach to predict autism spectrum disorder using multisite resting-state fmri. Applied Sciences (2021)]; Chen et al. (2024, DeepASD) reported 87–88% accuracy using adversarial-regularized graph learning with multimodal data [Chen et al. Deepasd: a deep adversarial-regularized graph learning method for asd diagnosis with multimodal data. Translational Psychiatry (2024)]; Saponaro et al. (2024) achieved 85% using a joint fusion approach [Saponaro et al. Deep learning based joint fusion approach to exploit anatomical and functional brain information in autism spectrum disorders. Brain Informatics (2024)]; Epalle et al. (2021) reported 78.1% with hinge-loss-trained deep architectures [Epalle, Thomas Martial, et al. “Multi-atlas classification of autism spectrum disorder with hinge loss trained deep architectures: ABIDE I results. “ Applied soft computing 107 (2021): 107375]; and even simpler methods such as DFS+GCN (Shao et al. , 2021) achieved 79.5% on ABIDE with the C-PAC pipeline [Shao, L. , Fu, C. , You, Y. , & Fu, D. (2021). Classification of ASD based on fMRI data with deep learning. Cognitive Neurodynamics, 15(6), 961]. Against this broader landscape, BrainHO’s 69.68% accuracy appears modest rather than state-of-the-art. At minimum, the paper should acknowledge these higher-performing methods and explain why they were excluded from the comparison or why the comparison set is restricted to the Transformer/GNN family. The same concern likely applies to REST-meta-MDD, where recent work such as Liu et al. (2024) reported 77.6% accuracy using GCN on this dataset [Liu S. , & Gui, R. (2024). Fusing multi-scale fMRI features using a brain-inspired multi-channel graph neural network for major depressive disorder diagnosis. Biomedical Signal Processing and Control, 90, 105837], and a recent LGMF-GNN approach (2024) achieved 78.75% on a comparable MDD cohort [Liu S. , et al. (2024). An objective quantitative diagnosis of depression using a local-to-global multimodal fusion graph neural network. Patterns, 5(12)]. The paper’s claim of state-of-the-art performance is therefore overstated relative to the full literature. Potential data leakage and insufficient methodological detail on evaluation. The paper uses 5-fold stratified cross-validation with 25% of the training set reserved for validation (early stopping). However, several aspects of the experimental setup raise concerns about data leakage: (a) Site effects in multi-site data. ABIDE is collected across 17 sites with heterogeneous scanner parameters, protocols, and demographics. REST-meta-MDD similarly aggregates data from 25 sites. If subjects from the same site appear in both training and test folds, the model may learn site-specific confounds rather than disease-related features. The paper does not describe whether site-aware splitting was performed, nor whether any harmonization was applied. This is a critical omission for multi-site neuroimaging studies, where site correction done outside the cross-validation loop can itself constitute leakage. (b) Mixup augmentation. The paper states that Mixup augmentation was adopted following prior works. Mixup is applied during training and generates synthetic examples by interpolating between pairs. If not carefully implemented within folds, interpolation between training and validation samples could introduce subtle leakage. The paper provides no details on this. (c) Hyperparameter selection. The paper reports specific values for α=1.3, K=8, d=384, τ=2.0, and a sigmoid-scheduled β, but does not describe how these were selected. If hyperparameters were tuned by observing test-fold performance (even indirectly through iterative experimentation), this constitutes another form of leakage. Absence of nested cross-validation. Related to the previous comment, the standard recommendation for neuroimaging classification studies, especially those with complex models and multiple hyperparameters, is nested cross-validation, where an inner loop handles hyperparameter optimization and an outer loop provides unbiased performance estimates (Varoquaux et al. , 2017, NeuroImage). BrainHO has numerous hyperparameters (α, β, K, d, τ, learning rate, weight decay, batch size, scheduler parameters, number of layers, number of heads) yet uses flat 5-fold CV. As shown in the methodological literature, flat CV can produce positively biased accuracy estimates when hyperparameters are tuned. Given that the accuracy margins over baselines are relatively small (1–2%), such bias could account for the observed improvements. A nested CV protocol, or at minimum a sensitivity analysis over hyperparameters, is needed to establish that the reported gains are robust. Limited statistical analysis of results. While the paper reports mean ± standard deviation across 5 folds, it does not perform statistical significance testing (e. g. , paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests) against baselines. Given the overlapping standard deviations in Table 1 (e. g. , BrainHO 69.68±2.11 vs. Com-BrainTF 67.69±3.09 on ABIDE), it is unclear whether the improvements are statistically significant. For MDD, the margins are even tighter (BrainHO 64.71±2.01 vs. ALTER/LHDFormer 63.95). Without significance tests, the claim of outperformance is not rigorously supported. Scalability and sensitivity to K not explored. The number of subgraph tokens K=8 is fixed throughout experiments. However, the optimal number of latent sub-networks likely varies across disorders and datasets. The paper provides no sensitivity analysis for K, which is arguably the most important architectural hyperparameter. How does performance degrade for K=4, 6, 10, 12? Does the interpretability of learned sub-networks change qualitatively? Similarly, the paper does not discuss computational complexity or runtime compared to baselines. Minor issues. (a) The term “intrinsicly” on page 2 is a typo (should be “intrinsically”). (b) The interpretability analysis in Section 3.2 is based on mapping CC200 regions to AAL116, but this mapping itself introduces approximation errors that are not discussed.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The motivation is clinically grounded and well-illustrated: Fig. 1(a) concisely demonstrates that significant inter-subnetwork correlations exist that fixed atlases systematically discard, providing a clear empirical justification for the learnable aggregation design. The interpretability analysis in Fig. 3 is a genuine strength—showing that learned subgraphs partially recover known functional networks (e.g., SMN, DAN) while also spanning cross-network regions provides meaningful validation beyond classification accuracy alone.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: W1.Insufficient Novelty Positioning Against Prior Hierarchical Brain Network Literature. The paper frames fixed-atlas methods as the dominant paradigm to overcome, but several recent works already achieve data-driven or atlas-free hierarchical brain network learning without predefined subnetwork constraints—including SW-HGL (MICCAI 2024), and hierarchical GNN approaches in the brain network analysis literature (e.g., 10.1109/TNNLS.2023.3282961). DHGFormer, which is used as a baseline in Table 1, itself performs hierarchical learning with dynamic graph structures. The paper does not discuss how BrainHO’s learnable subgraph token design is methodologically distinct from these contemporaries, leaving the novelty claim inadequately substantiated. Furthermore, the core mechanism—using learnable latent tokens as queries in cross-attention to pool node features into higher-level representations—is structurally identical to the Perceiver architecture (Jaegle et al., ICML 2021) and closely related to DiffPool (Ying et al., NeurIPS 2018); neither is cited or discussed. W2.The Hierarchical Consistency Loss Lacks Theoretical Justification and Has a Structural Conflict.Lhc​ (Eq. 5) uses the graph-level token X^g​ as a teacher to supervise node-level features X^n​ via KL divergence. However, X^g is itself derived by hierarchically aggregating from X^n through the same shared encoder, meaning teacher and student are computed from the same parameter set within the same forward pass. This creates a circular dependency in the gradient signal: improving node features changes the teacher simultaneously, making the optimization target non-stationary in a way that is neither theoretically motivated nor empirically analyzed. The paper provides no justification for why global-to-local distillation in this self-referential setting should produce stable or meaningful supervision, and no ablation isolates the effect of distillation direction (graph→node vs. node→graph). W3.Interaction Between LOC​ and Lhc​ Is Unanalyzed. LOC pushes subgraph tokens toward mutual orthogonality in the representation space, while Lhc pulls node representations toward alignment with the graph token derived from those same subgraph tokens. These two objectives operate on overlapping parts of the representation space and may conflict: orthogonality encourages subgraph diversity, but consistency encourages node features to converge toward a single global summary. The paper neither analyzes this potential tension theoretically nor provides training curve or gradient norm diagnostics to confirm stable joint optimization. The sensitivity analysis for α and β is absent. W4.The “w/o HA” Ablation Is Inadequately Defined. Table 1 reports a “w/o HA” variant described only as replacing the hierarchical attention with “an attention module,” yielding 61.74% accuracy. This description is too vague to be scientifically meaningful—it is unclear whether the replacement is a standard self-attention over all nodes, a mean pooling, or another architecture. Without a precise definition, this ablation cannot confirm that the performance gap is attributable to the hierarchical structure specifically rather than to incidental architectural differences such as parameter count or depth.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: This study introduces the Brain Hierarchical Organization Learning (BrainHO) framework, which aims to capture the inherently hierarchical dependencies within brain networks by leveraging their intrinsic features instead of relying on predefined sub-network labels. The proposed approach incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism that enables the model to aggregate nodes into a structured hierarchical organization. The analysis reveals cross-network interaction patterns characterized by strong Pearson correlations, which are insufficiently represented by conventional rigid, prior-based organizational models. In contrast, some existing methods predominantly depend on predefined functional sub-networks to define relationships between sub-networks.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: The major weaknesses of the paper: 1.There are numerous studies that have utilized the static PCC connectivity matrix (or brain functional networks) for classifying brain disorders. However, the paper compares only two such methods; including a comparison with a broader range of representative approaches would enhance the evaluation and more comprehensively demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. 2.I agree that cross-network interaction patterns with high Pearson correlation are significant. However, recent studies classifying brain functional networks—especially those employing graph neural networks based on static Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) connectivity matrices—often do not depend on predefined functional subnetworks, although some methods do. To present a more comprehensive overview of the current research, the paper should clarify this distinction.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
