Although one reviewer gave a borderline score (3) citing concerns over the breadth of baseline comparisons and cross-validation protocols, these do not undermine the core methodological novelty, solid experimental results, and strong clinical relevance of the work.

title: MARBLE: Lightweight EEG-to-fMRI Translation via Mamba-Attention and ROI-Conditioned Decoding
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The architecture proposed here is novel in the incorporation of temporal Mamba and ROI-wise cross-attention, which reduces the number of parameters of the model and makes projecting attention weights to the brain possible, respectively. 2.The proposed model performs better than state-of-the-art models that it was compared with across most of the metrics presented here.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.There are implementation details missing (data split and sizes of model inputs and outputs). 2.The authors do not discuss any limitations of the model. 3.FC can have negative values too. Authors should either include negative correlations in to the FC matrix, or justify the use of connections that are positive only. 4.Authors do not report statistical significance of their proposed model being better than the state-of-the-art approaches. 5.The authors do not describe how they adapt the LaBraM model (EEG-specific foundation model) to perform the EEG-to-fMRI task, which undermines the validity of using it as a baseline. The authors should better motivate its use. 6.The sample size is limited to 22 subjects, which warrants a generalizability study of the proposed model to out of distribution data.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The method improves synthesis performance while reducing the number of parameters and memory usage, which enhances its practical value. 2.The evaluation simultaneously demonstrates signal reconstruction quality and functional connectivity preservation. 3.The ablation study highlights the effectiveness of two key modules, namely the ROI-CA decoder and tMamba. 4.The paper provides an attention-based interpretability analysis, revealing corresponding relationships between brain functional networks and EEG electrodes.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The evidence supporting the main innovation claims is insufficient. The authors argue that tMamba is better suited than a Transformer for modeling HRF-driven delays and unidirectional dependencies, but they do not provide direct evidence for this claim, such as further analysis of whether the temporal dependencies learned by Mamba are consistent with the physiological characteristics of the hemodynamic response. 2.Some results do not support a blanket claim that the proposed method outperforms the baselines. For example, FC-Corr is slightly lower than that of NeuroBOLT and UnEBOLT, so the use of the term “superior performance” in the main text is not fully appropriate. 3.Some implementation details are still missing, such as the specific structures of the encoder and decoder.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The proposed solution—with the choice of architecture, along domain-specific enhancements (encoder with state-space model and decoder with ROI-conditioning)—provides improvement in performance as a reduction in model size. The model also includes interpretability as an inherent feature.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Several conceptual and methodological aspects need more clarification: (a) Resting state fMRI corresponds to spontaneous BOLD fluctuations that are slow, continuous oscillations that reflect intrinsic network activity. So, the use of state-space model for capturing HRF-driven temporal dynamics seems like a conceptual mismatch. (b) EEG has poor sensitivity to deep subcortical structures (hippocampus, thalamus, basal ganglia). Performance comparison of the ROI-conditioned heads on subcortical vs. cortical ROIs would have given more credit to “whole-brain” activity estimation from EEG. (c) Several works have already proposed combining Mamba with Transformers. So major contribuitions are ROI-conditioned decoding heads and the cross-modal EEG-to-fMRI translation objective specifically. (d) An ablation study to observe the contribution of Transformer blocks in addition to the tMamba would have been more insightful. (e) Cross-attention topographies revealing network-specific electrode contributions in Figure 5 would have been more meaning when compared with topographies generated without ROI-CA module.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank the reviewers and the Area Chair for their constructive feedback. We are encouraged that the reviewers recognize the practical value, efficiency, and interpretability of MARBLE, and we address the main concerns below. (1) Statistical significance (R1-1), superiority claims (R2-2). Table 1 reports mean ± std across 6 held-out scans under a subject-independent protocol consistent with prior studies [16,18]. The standard deviation reflects inter-subject variability, the main source of variation in this setting. MARBLE showed consistent improvements across metrics and Yeo networks (Fig. 2), indicating stable rather than isolated gains. Ablations further support component-specific contributions (ROI-CA: FC-Corr −0.061, tMamba: Corr −0.010). While formal statistical testing could further strengthen the evaluation, we believe the reported trends are meaningful within the benchmark setting used in prior work. Regarding claims, we agree that “superior performance” is too strong given that FC-Corr is slightly lower than [16,18]. We instead claim a balanced trade-off between reconstruction quality, efficiency, and interpretability. (2) Positive-only FC matrices (R1-2). FC was computed using Pearson correlation without thresholding or sign filtering. FC values are predominantly positive in our data. As stated in Sec. 3.2, FC-Corr is computed on the full signed correlation matrix (upper-triangular); the 25% top-edge threshold is applied only to the rightmost panels of Fig. 4 for visualization and does not affect any quantitative metric. (3) Generalization concerns (R1-3). We acknowledge the 22-subject cohort is limited, constraining generalization. The subject-independent protocol follows standard practice [16,18], and we used cross-subject splits to evaluate generalization within available data. We will state the single-site n=22 cohort and eyes-closed-only condition as explicit limitations in Sec. 4.(4) HRF interpretation (R2-1, R3-a), novelty (R3-c), additional ablations (R3-d, R3-e). tMamba was not intended to model hemodynamic responses, but to capture temporally extended EEG dependencies from 16-second EEG windows for regression to slow-varying BOLD signals. The contribution of tMamba is supported by ablation. We will soften “captures HRF dynamics” to “provides inductive bias for HRF-relevant structure” in the revision. The Mamba–Transformer encoder is a deliberate efficiency choice for this domain-specific application. Our central novelty is ROI-CA, which is the largest contributor in our ablation, enabling ad-hoc interpretability via attention topographies (Fig. 5), absent in adapter-based decoders. ROI-specific topography (Fig. 5) is intrinsically defined by the ROI-CA mechanism: without ROI queries, no ROI-conditioned attention map exists to compare against. (5) Missing implementation details (R1, R2). MARBLE uses embedding dim 64, depth 4, Mamba state size 16, conv width 4, dropout 0.2.The ROI-CA employs 64 ROI queries with the same embedding dim. The 3:1:1 split is over subjects, with no subject in multiple splits. Each input is a 16-s, 26-channel EEG window at 200 Hz; the target is the BOLD signal across 64 ROIs at the corresponding fMRI time point. Training for 20 epochs was selected based on monitored validation loss, which plateaued well before termination. (6) LaBraM motivation (R1-4). LaBraM [13] is included as a foundation-model-only control. We initialize from LaBraM-base and replace its classification head with the same multi-ROI regression head used across baselines, under identical training conditions. This isolates the contribution of EEG-to-fMRI specific design over a generic large-scale EEG foundation model. (7) Subcortical sensitivity (R3-b). We acknowledge EEG limitations in subcortical regions. The DiFuMo atlas includes cortical and subcortical ROIs, and results are reported across all regions. A separate cortical-versus-subcortical evaluation is an interesting direction for future work.

title: MEASURE: Multi-Task Slice Selection and Regression for Neonatal Brain Biometry
reviewer_1_strengths: Although the motivation and clinical importance of the proposed method are clear, and the methodology is well formulated through a two-stage approach, first detecting the optimal measurement slice and subsequently estimating the measurements on those slices (thus avoiding the more challenging task of directly estimating 2D measurements from 3D data), while also incorporating different components in the network to improve estimation accuracy, the main strength of the paper lies in its strong end-to-end evaluation. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation, including the required statistical analysis for biometric measurement assessment (Pearson correlation, MAE, ICC, Bland-Altman), intra-rater analysis, ablation studies on different parts of the model, and comparisons with state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the method is also applied to the FeTA dataset to demonstrate its generalization performance.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Since the Kidokoro scoring system for assessing brain abnormalities is highly mentioned throughout the manuscript, being used to present the clinical motivation of the work, a more explicit connection between the results of the paper and this scoring system should have been provided. The Kidokoro scoring system does not necessarily rely on the specific biometric measurements extracted in this work, while also considering additional MRI findings. In fact, the Kidokoro score relies on a combination of MRI findings, such as signal abnormalities, structural alterations, and developmental features, where some of them can be inferred from the biometric measurements. Therefore, the paper could be more explicit about how the retrieved measurements can be used, or how the proposed methodology could be extended, to support the computation of a Kidokoro score.
reviewer_1_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The paper addresses a clinically important problem with strong alignment to real-world measurement workflows and eliminates the need for dense annotations, improving practical applicability. The proposed two-stage architecture is well motivated and thoughtfully designed. The work is supported by comprehensive and rigorous experimental evaluation, including cross-validation, multi-metric analysis, ablations, and comparison against human variability, with clear and reproducible presentation. In addition, Fig. 2 demonstrates high interpretability, where attention maps reflect the underlying biometry of interest.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The evaluation of thick-slice conditions relies on simulated data rather than real clinical acquisitions, limiting practical validation. The study depends on single-expert annotations without inter-rater analysis, and comparisons with 3D methods may be biased due to explicit slice supervision. Furthermore, interpretability claims are only qualitatively supported, cross-domain generalization evidence is limited, and some architectural components (e.g., SAFA, AAR) show inconsistent gains.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.Clinically well-motivated and annotation-efficient design. The proposed framework requires only slice indices and scalar measurements as supervision, avoiding voxel-level annotations entirely. This is a practically meaningful advantage for neonatal brain MRI, where expert annotation is costly and time-consuming. 2.Rigorous and transparent evaluation protocol. The paper presents a strong and well-structured evaluation, including 5-fold cross-validation, multiple complementary metrics (ICC, Pearson r, MAE), and statistical testing with Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction. Notably, the authors explicitly mark ablation cases where variants outperform the full model but are not statistically significant (◦), demonstrating a commendable level of transparency that is often lacking in similar works. 3.Inclusion of clinically relevant evaluation (Bland–Altman analysis). The use of Bland–Altman analysis provides additional clinical context beyond standard ML metrics, which is often missing in similar work. While not novel, this analysis helps interpret model performance relative to intra-rater variability and improves the practical relevance of the evaluation.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.Cross-domain experiment does not support — and in fact weakens — the generalization claim. The FeTA evaluation is presented as evidence of architectural transferability, but the results are not convincing. The image-only configuration fails to converge, and even when combined with GA, image features provide only limited and inconsistent improvements, with no gains for some structures (e.g., HV, LCC). While the authors attribute this to limited data, the results more strongly indicate sensitivity to domain shift and data scale. As such, this experiment reads less as supporting evidence and more as a demonstration of the method’s limitations, weakening the overall claim of generalizability. 2.Single-site, single-protocol dataset severely limits generalizability. All experiments are conducted on a single dataset (dHCP) acquired under controlled conditions. This does not reflect real clinical variability, where neonatal MRI often involves lower resolution, thick slices, and motion artifacts. 3.Limited empirical contribution of SAFA and AAR. Although the authors explicitly mark non-significant results (◦) and provide partial explanations (e.g., interpretability trade-offs for AAR), the empirical evidence supporting these modules remains weak. In particular, SAFA shows statistically significant improvement only in a small subset of metrics, while AAR does not yield significant gains. The provided explanations are largely qualitative and do not sufficiently justify their inclusion as key components of the method. 4.The fine/coarse routing mechanism relies on under-justified heuristic gating. The mixing weight 𝑟 is defined using a Sobel-derived edge complexity map, a fixed threshold 𝜏, and a learnable temperature, but the paper does not adequately explain how the fixed threshold is chosen or how sensitive performance is to this design. This makes the routing mechanism appear heuristic rather than well-validated, especially given the low contrast and noise characteristics of neonatal MRI. 5.The proposed “attention” mechanism is closer to spatial weighting than relational attention. The measurement-specific attention operates as a spatial weighting (i.e., weighted pooling) over feature maps, rather than modeling interactions between spatial locations (e.g., via query-key-value attention). While effective in practice, this limits its ability to capture global dependencies and reduces the conceptual novelty of the module.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: ##### We apprecia all reviewers for recognizing the overall framework, clinical relevance, comprehensive evaluation, and transparent reporting. #### [R1] Kidokoro scoring connection. Full Kidokoro scoring also requires signal abnormalities, structural alterations, and qualitative findings beyond biometry. We will clarify that MEASURE automates the quantitative biometric component, is a module that can be integrated with quantitative detectors toward comprehensive automated scoring. [R1] Clarifications. (a) Input: 6ch = 3 slices (2.5D) + 3 coordinate channels (x,y,radial). (b) Selector returns top-2; predictor randomly samples one as center slice. (c) Base = ResNet-34 + GAP + prediction heads. (d) GA-only is a univariate linear regression baseline per FeTA challenge protocol, not an input to our pipeline. [R2] 3D comparison framing. This comparison tests clinical workflow-based decomposition benefits and plane-aware supervision, not intrinsic 2D-vs-3D superiority. We will revise wording. [R2] Interpretability. Measurement-wise pooling maps directly determine predictions via measurement-specific weighted pooling, providing spatial explanations of which regions contribute to each biometric. We agree this is demonstrated qualitatively (Fig. 2) rather than via quantitative localization. [R2] Single-expert annotations. Table 2 compares model–expert with intra-rater variability (>3-month re-measurement) via Bland–Altman LoA ratios. We acknowledge inter-rater analysis will strengthen the validation. [R2&R3] Simulated thick-slice. Our simulation provides preliminary robustness evidence, not a substitute for real clinical MRI. We will make this limitation explicit. [R2&R3] FeTA cross-domain. This was not intended as proof of broad generalizability, but as a transparent transfer test under substantial domain shift (term neonatal to younger fetal, N=470 to N=70). In context, most FeTA challenge methods did not outperform GA-only regression, our Image+GA improves MAE for 3/5 targets with clear gains for sBIP and TCD. We will clarify this as limited but non-trivial evidence of architectural adaptability. [R2&R3] Role of SAFA and AAR. We will clarify the component hierarchy: measurement-specific pooling is the main performance driver (Table 1, largest ablation gap). SAFA provides selective, statistically supported benefits (FDR-corrected for BPW and IHD, p=0.036), consistent with its through-plane context role. AAR only works with the presence of measurement-specific pooling (Table 1, w/o pooling ablation is also excluding AAR), and is not intended as an independent component to improve regression accuracy, Rather, it regularizes pooling maps via symmetry/smoothness/distinctiveness, consistent with the structured behavior qualitatively illustrated in Fig. 2.We will revise framing accordingly. [R3] Attention terminology. We agree that our module is not relational query–key–value attention, but measurement-specific spatial attention pooling. We will clarify this terminology and emphasize that its contribution is target-specific spatial aggregation for constructing distinct biometric representations in multi-measurement neonatal biometry. [R3] Fine/coarse routing threshold. We want to clarify that Sobel complexity map c is normalized per-sample to [0, 1], τ is fixed as the midpoint of [0,1] complexity range. Setting τ = 0.5 intuitively means that locations with normalized edge complexity above 0.5 are preferentially routed toward the fine branch. Routing sharpness is controlled by temperature t, learned end-to-end, allowing the model to adapt how aggressively it differentiates regions. We will clarify the Sobel complexity map normalization, τ justification explicit in Section 2.3. [R3] Dataset limitation. dHCP is the largest publicly available standardized neonatal MRI cohort for controlled method development. We will state explicitly that multi-site validation remains future work. We appreciate all reviewers for their efforts.

title: Multi-Expert Representation Learning with Dynamic Routing for Brain Captioning
reviewer_1_strengths: 1.The method has a reasonable motivation. Combining low-level geometric experts with high-level semantic experts is broadly consistent with the hierarchical vision mechanism described in this paper. 2.The empirical results are promising. As shown in Table 1, MERPA outperforms the listed baselines in both single-subject and multi-subject joint-training settings, with particularly clear improvements on semantic metrics such as CIDEr, SPICE, CLIP-S, and RefCLIP-S. 3.The paper provides useful ablation studies. They at least preliminarily show that the routing strategy, alignment objective, and expert grouping all contribute to the final performance. 4.The framework appears to be extensible. Using multiple pretrained vision experts as structured supervision sources can potentially be extended to other perceptual attributes or modalities.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: 1.There is a mismatch between the main claim and the actual evaluation setup. The paper repeatedly emphasizes cross-subject generalization, but the reported “cross-subject” experiment jointly trains on S1/S2/S5/S7 and evaluates on held-out images. This is much closer to multi-subject joint training than to genuine generalization to unseen subjects. Therefore, the central claim on cross-subject generalization is not well supported. 2.The novelty boundary remains insufficiently clear. Based on the paper’s own related work and references, MEVOX has already introduced multi-task vision experts into brain decoding and brain captioning. BrainOT already uses optimal transport for brain-image alignment, and VINDEX discusses the effects of different visual feature spaces in multimodal neural decoding. The current manuscript does not clearly identify whether the real novelty lies in brain-conditioned dynamic routing, the progressive OT+Fair scheduling, or only in the specific combination of these components. 3.The technical description contains several critical ambiguities that affect reproducibility. For instance, the paper mentions that “RoBERTa serves as the frozen language decoder” but does not explain the concrete implementation of caption generation. In addition, the granularity of routing weights (sample-level / ROI-level / token-level), ROI feature processing, adapter structure, and module interfaces are not clearly specified. The paper also repeatedly uses terms such as “interpretable” and “brain-inspired” without providing direct evidence on whether the expert preferences learned by the routing mechanism are consistent with the functional specialization of the cerebral cortex. 4.The experimental evidence remains limited. The paper uses only a single dataset and evaluation protocol, and does not provide the mean and standard deviation from multiple random seeds, significance testing, qualitative or failure-case analysis, nor training and inference cost analysis. For modest improvements in some metrics, these omissions severely weaken the reliability of the conclusions.
reviewer_1_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: 1.The idea of aligning brain activity with multiple structured visual experts rather than a single embedding is interesting and potentially meaningful for brain decoding. The hierarchical decomposition (e.g., depth, edges, segmentation, OCR) provides interpretable intermediate representations and may better reflect the multi-level processing of visual information. 2.The combination of optimal transport for global distribution alignment and robust regression for local refinement is reasonable and well-motivated for handling noisy fMRI signals.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: 1.The visual tokens produced by different experts are not inherently in a shared representation space, and their distributions may vary significantly. Moreover, these expert features are not explicitly aligned with the text token space of the LLM, which may limit the effectiveness of cross-modal alignment and ultimately constrain the performance of the proposed framework. 2.The selection of vision experts appears heuristic. The paper does not justify why these specific experts were chosen, nor does it analyze the impact of different expert combinations or the number of experts. 3.The paper refers to ROI-conditioned routing but does not clearly define the ROI regions. Since the design is motivated by neuroscience, additional analysis would strengthen the claim, such as region-wise routing visualization, ROI-specific performance, or evidence demonstrating neuro-inspired hierarchical alignment. 4.Despite the increased model complexity, the performance improvements over BrainOT appear relatively modest. More discussion is needed to clarify where the gains originate, as well as to acknowledge potential limitations and outline future directions. 5.Figure 2 could be improved by explicitly separating the training and inference pipelines, which would help clarify the workflow and improve readability.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: The paper is overall well-written, and the motivation and visualization of the usage of multiple vision experts, and plugging them into the brain-captioning framework, I think, is well communicated. It is easy to see how the methodology in this aspect differs from other works, especially in the “vision brain understanding” problem. Both the distribution alignment of brain captioning and visual expert tokens, and the robust feature refinement are well-motivated with regards to the architectural choice made by the authors. This is shown to be a simple contribution but one that performs well compared to the current works. BrainHub captioning experiments (Table 1) show that across all metrics and compared against many past works, MERPA performs better or at least comparably. This shows that incorporating multiple streams of visual information does hold weight and is a research direction that could merit further investigation. Ablation experiments (Table 2) also demonstrate how all MERPA components combined contribute to performance gains.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: Vision-brain understanding is not my main field, but I do not see blatant, major, flaws in this work. I do have several points I wish for the authors to clarify. 1) While the alignment of brain tokens with heterogeneous vision tokens makes sense to me, can the authors clarify how MERPA uses the brain tokens or the weighted vision tokens to pass on to the LLM for caption generation? This step should be essential to clarify both in the formulation and in the figure, which does not explicitly show the data flow into the LLM/decoder block to generate captions. This is also not clarified in the manuscript it seems; apologies if I missed this. 2) Can the authors elaborate on their choice of the Roberta LLM? Was this standard across comparable works, or is it a good compromise between low-cost and effectiveness? Just a little discussion on this would be helpful, as well as what other works (in the experiments shown) use to make the comparisons more transparent. 3) Additionally, how sensitive is Roberta (or any applicable LLM for that matter) to the new tokens it is taking in? I ask this on the basis that the distribution of the tokens from MERPA vs what LLMs like Roberta expect may be different, so it would strengthen the paper if the authors can provide insight on this, if it is an issue at all. 4) Can the authors clarify how well the actual generated/decoded captions via MERPA compare with respect to visual stimulus images? I assume since ablations were done, the authors would have the response-image stimulus pairs already. All to say, while Tables 1 and 2 may suggest quantitatively that MERPA is performant in comparison to other methods, how does it compare qualitatively? Showing this inference output along with input images would be beneficial since much of the scores check for overlap of n-grams, but readers are not able to see full image-generated caption pairs. 5) For the mix of vision experts, since multiple feature extractor look at the same image, there may be an overlap of features across (b,w) pairs, i.e., there may be redundant features. Can the authors provide insight as to how this may affect downstream modules? This could potentially be an insight in future work. 6) Minor comment: The best results in Table 2 should be in bold. Additionally, any abbreviations in Table 2 should be defined in the caption, increasing readability when a reader just looks at the table.
reviewer_3_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the reviewers and meta-reviewer for the constructive feedback and positive assessment of our method. 1.Cross-subject terminology We agree that the wording “cross-subject generalization” may overstate the experimental setting. This terminology follows prior methods such as MindEye/MEVOX/BrainOT/VINDEX, which also describe similar multi-subject joint training. We agree that the current setup corresponds more precisely to multi-subject joint training rather than unseen-subject zero-shot generalization. We will replace “cross-subject generalization” with “multi-subject joint training” and remove any implication of zero-shot transfer. Importantly, our contribution is not unseen-subject transfer, but a structured representation learning framework that improves multimodal alignment through: (1) hierarchical expert supervision, (2) brain-conditioned dynamic routing, and (3) progressive OT-based alignment optimization. 2.Novelty and relation to prior work Unlike the static aggregation (uniform weights) in MEVOX, MERPA introduces brain-conditioned routing that adaptively modulates expert contributions using ROI-dependent neural representations (Tab 2 Routing row: static 49.89 -> dynamic 71.91, +44.1%). In addition, while BrainOT uses OT for structural alignment, MERPA addresses the dual challenge of distributional alignment and neural noise robustness through progressive combination of OT-based global alignment with Fair loss-based local refinement, achieving consistent improvements across metrics (Tab 1-2). 3.Implementation details During training, frozen vision experts produce structured visual tokens dynamically aggregated via brain-conditioned routing as alignment targets for brain encoder. During inference, only optimized brain tokens are projected to frozen RoBERTa’s input space and decoded for caption generation. Vision expert features may be partially redundant; however, the brain-conditioned router dynamically selects complementary information across experts (Tab 2: removing any expert degrades performance). The learned adapter aligns brain tokens with the language model input. We will revise Fig. 2 to explicitly separate training/inference pipelines, clarify routing granularity and module interfaces, and provide implementation details in the appendix. Code and models will be released. 4.Expert selection and neuroscience motivation The selected experts were not chosen arbitrarily but to reflect complementary visual hierarchy, covering low-level geometric (depth / surface normals / edges) and high-level semantic (segmentation / object detection / OCR) cues. This design is motivated by the hierarchical organization of the visual cortex and supported by ablations (Table 2), where low-level-only and high-level-only experts both underperform the combined configuration. We will include neuroscience-oriented analyses and studies on different expert combinations in the revision. 5.Evaluation Although improvements over BrainOT are modest on some metrics, MERPA consistently improves performance across metrics in both single-subject and multi-subject settings, especially on semantic-sensitive metrics (CIDEr +5.1%, SPICE +3.8%), which are particularly relevant for semantic consistency in brain captioning. Statistical analysis across 5 runs further demonstrates stable performance with statistically significant improvements (p<0.05) in both single-subject (BLEU-4 20.94±0.19, CIDEr 71.91±0.42, and SPICE 14.55±0.31) and multi-subject (BLEU-4 23.13±0.22, CIDEr 77.46±0.48, and SPICE 15.65±0.35) settings. 6.Ethics Our work uses the publicly available NSD dataset, which is anonymized and distributed under established research protocols. We do not collect new human-subject data, and all experiments are conducted on anonymized publicly available data for research purposes. We will also include an ethics and privacy discussion, qualitative caption comparisons, and failure cases in the revised manuscript.
