reviewer_2_strengths: The major strength of the paper is the fact that the proposed method allows longitudinal modeling, unlike cross-sectional approaches of the past. Furthermore, the way that the method was developed allows it to simulate transitions between ages, rather than disconnected timepoints. The model does so while preserving subject-level individual properties.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The model makes assumptions about certain neurodevelopmental patterns for the sake of stability and implementation of model, such as the fact that the brain development takes on a monotonic, plateauing curve pattern. While this may be accurate for healthy infant aging, if the model were to be adopted for other patterns such as aging across human life span, such as events that may lead to regression or nonlinear shifts, such assumption may become a limitation of the model.
reviewer_2_rating: (4) Weak Accept — marginally above the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if rejected, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1.The formulation is technically sound, especially the FiLM-conditioned residual transition module that models how brain dynamics evolve with age while preserving subject identity. This is a nice way to separate subject-specific structure from developmental effects. 2.The paper goes beyond prediction and explicitly targets causal interpretability, using Jacobian-based effective connectivity and causal distillation. This makes the model more aligned with neuroscience questions. 3.The counterfactual developmental knobs is a strong idea, as it allows simulation of how perturbing specific regions affects future connectivity.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1.The whole framework depends on training separate surrogate models per (subject, age) and then learn transitions between them, but from a computational perspective, it seems that it is data inefficient and could scale poorly. There is no discussion of how stable these surrogates are with limited timepoints. 2.The comparisons are weak with respect to other competing methods, since Table 1 only compares against standard models like (baseline surrogate, RNN, CNN, ablations) rather than established longitudinal models like [1]. Given that [1] is already discussed in the introduction, it would have been more convincing to include it in the evaluation. 3.The FiLM-based residual transition in the paper assumes that the developmental changes are additive corrections from the source surrogate (Eq. 4–5), which is a fairly strong assumption? In early brain development where dynamics could change nonlinearly, this residual formulation might be too restrictive but this is not discussed. [1] A few-shot learning graph multi-trajectory evolution network for forecasting multimodal baby connectivity development from a baseline timepoint, MICCAI 2021
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We sincerely thank the Area Chair and reviewers (R) for their constructive comments and for recognizing NDE as a “novel and promising framework” with “strong methodological contributions,” including its “causal/individualized formulation”, “rigorous validation”, and counterfactual developmental knobs as a “strong idea”. Below, we clarify the main concerns. Comparison with longitudinal FC prediction methods (R1, R4): We agree that longitudinal FC prediction methods are relevant. However, they are not directly target-matched to NDE: existing methods primarily forecast FC matrices, whereas NDE can model developmental transitions as a causal surrogate system. In NDE, effective connectivity (EC) and counterfactual sensitivity are primary outputs, while FC only serves as a static summary of the generated dynamics. To test whether NDE’s performance can be explained by optimizing FC matching alone, we included NDE-FC, a within-framework variant trained with FC-similarity loss. Table 1 shows that although NDE-FC achieves reasonable FC prediction, it degrades EC preservation and developmental fidelity, supporting our central claim that NDE captures causal surrogate dynamics beyond conventional FC matching. We will clarify this scope distinction and discuss direct FC-forecasting comparisons as a future extension in the revision. Assumption on residual formulation and developmental pattern (R3, R4): We would like to clarify that NDE does not impose monotonic, plateauing, linear, or additive developmental trajectories on FC edges. Eqs. 4-5 operate at fMRI signal level rather than directly on FC. Specifically, Eq. 4 adds an age-conditioned signal residual to the source-age neural surrogate to predict target-age fMRI state evolution, while FC is derived afterward from the generated time series. Thus, the residual formulation does not constrain FC trajectories. Moreover, the residual is produced by nonlinear FiLM-conditioned networks, allowing nonlinear transitions. Similarly, the age-gap gate in Eq. 5 regularizes the residual magnitude at signal level to stabilize training, without forcing FC to be monotonic or plateauing. We will clarify this distinction between signal- and FC-level constraints, while noting that the age-gap gate may reduce sensitivity to abrupt dynamical shifts. Details on FC_free generation and developmental knob (R1): We will better define FC_free and developmental knob in the revision. As stated in Sec. 3.2, FC_free in Table 1 is computed from BOLD dynamics generated by autoregressive “free rollouts span 200 steps across four random seeds”. Regarding the developmental knob g, it is not optimized. As introduced in Sec. 2.2 through Eq. 9 and the leverage score (Imp_k) definition, g is inserted into the trained NDE with fixed parameters, and the leverage score of each region k on a targeted FC edge is computed via automatic differentiation. Top FC drivers in Fig. 3c-e are ranked by |Imp_k|, while the sign of Imp_k indicates modulation direction. Scalability, surrogate stability, PDE fine-tuning, and statistics (R1, R4): Regarding scalability, the individualized surrogates are lightweight and trained independently, making this stage parallelizable. Although this design preserves scan-specific dynamics, we will acknowledge surrogate stability under limited timepoints as a limitation. For PDE fine-tuning, we understand the concern that limited TD samples may increase the overfitting risk. We have mitigated the risk by 1) matching scan protocol and age range between BCP and PDE data; 2) using 68 longitudinal scans from 18 TD infants; and 3) conservative fine-tuning with the identity encoder frozen and a reduced learning rate. We will clarify these and acknowledge the need for larger TD samples in the revision. Moreover, using the existing cross-validation outputs, a paired permutation test confirmed that NDE significantly outperformed competing methods across tasks (p < 0.001). We will include this in the revision.

title: UniFCHarm: Unified Prompt-Guided Harmonization of fMRI Functional Connectivity Across Scanners and Atlases
reviewer_1_strengths: . As far as I know, prompt-guided connectome harmonization is a novel idea. Whether novel or not, it is definitely a promising approach. . The method can handle multiple atlases / connectome resolutions, which is very interesting for applications . Strong method validation, involving a large data set (44,493 connectomes from 14 databases) and a comparison with 4 SOTA alternatives . The manuscript is well written and easy to follow.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: major weakness . The need for a coarse-to-fine strategy to generate the harmonized connectomes is a main weakness of the approach. This issue required a more complex approach, and raises questions about the atlas used for the refinement: would the authors get better results with a different atlas, particularly if there were greater similarity between the atlas and the target connectome atlases? Since additional experiments cannot be conducted to assess this point during the rebuttal phase, I would suggest mentioning this issue as a method limitation in the conclusion. minor weaknesses . The author should provide more details about the datasets and the implemented methods. For instance, the most important dataset for the validation, the SRPBS traveling-subject benchmark used to derive the entire Table 1, is not described at all. How many scans does it contain? The downstream analysis is not described either: which classifier was implemented? How many NC/MCI/AD scans were used? . The authors should report the training time, not just the number of epochs and hardware settings.
reviewer_1_rating: (5) Accept — should be accepted, independent of rebuttal
reviewer_2_strengths: The proposed method consistently outperforms the selected baseline methods across the reported evaluation metrics. An ablation study is also conducted to assess the contribution of individual components within the framework.
reviewer_2_weaknesses: The motivation for the proposed framework is not sufficiently justified. It remains unclear why this specific model design is appropriate for the problem. There are important missing technical details. For example, no loss function is explicitly defined in Section 2.1 (GraphCLIP pre-training for prompt–FC alignment). Key variables, such as N_a, N_c, d, and k, are introduced without clear definitions. The descriptions of the text and graph encoders are also insufficient. The manuscript lacks essential details required for experiments. In particular, it does not clearly describe how the models, including baseline methods, were trained, how hyperparameters were selected (e.g., the choice of lambda=0.2), or which fMRI preprocessing pipeline was used. The data information is insufficiently described. It is also unclear how the ground-truth functional connectivity (FC) is defined in this study. The selection of baseline methods (e.g., [3][15][26]) is not sufficiently justified, and the relationships between these methods and the proposed approach are not clearly explained. Furthermore, several related works discussed in the Introduction (e.g., [8][19][21][25]) are not included in the experimental comparisons without justification.
reviewer_2_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
reviewer_3_strengths: 1) Successfully deals with variability of scanners and atlases, a major problem in multi-center fMRI analysis. 2) Proposes a flexible harmonization model that is conditional on prompts rather than having predetermined mappings. 3) Employs a hierarchical model starting from large scales (networks) down to small scales (regions). 4) Attains state-of-the-art results, significantly outperforming other models. 5) Highlights the contribution of different components such as hierarchy, prompts, and atlas. 6) Enhances clinical diagnosis between subjects using data from different scanners. 7) Preserves individual differences while minimizing scanner effects. 8) Verifies model reliability by testing on various atlases and using qualitative assessments.
reviewer_3_weaknesses: 1) Limited novel contribution, since the framework is a combination of current paradigms (such as contrastive alignment and graph representation) but with some changes. 2) Lack of credit is given to GraphCLIP or dilated GCN-based alignment, leading to ambiguity on novelty and its connection to other literature. 3) Lack of detailed discussion on prompt design and model design, specifically on the impact of FC graphs on prompts and performance. 4) Not investigated how sensitive the model is to perturbations to prompts, which might impact the performance. 5) Little discussion on interpretability, especially in terms of neuroscientific evidence that can help interpret the results. 6) Introduction of critical terms (for instance, InfoNCE loss) without necessary explanation or citations.
reviewer_3_rating: (3) Weak Reject — marginally below the acceptance threshold, but would not mind if accepted, dependent on rebuttal
author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for recognizing the novelty and practical value. We address the main concerns below. 1) R1/R2/R3: innovation, novelty, and attribution. UniFCHarm’s key innovation is target-conditioned FC harmonization: text prompts specify the target scanner/protocol and atlas-defined FC, and hierarchical graph editing performs harmonization under this target prompt. Unlike previous harmonization methods tied to a fixed site and atlas, UniFCHarm handles arbitrary site and atlas FCs. We will also clarify that GraphCLIP denotes our FC-specific graph-text alignment rather than a new contrastive paradigm, and add corresponding citations. 2) R1/R2: coarse-to-fine rationale and Yeo-7 scaffold. Coarse-to-fine harmonization is motivated by the multi-scale nature of acquisition-induced heterogeneity, which affects both subnetwork-level and ROI-to-ROI connections. A single-step correction treats these scales equally, so ROI-level changes may remove subject-specific FC patterns with site effects. UniFCHarm first harmonizes subnetwork-level connectivity and then refines residual ROI-to-ROI biases under this coarse constraint, reducing over-correction. Table 1 (A2) supports this design: removing coarse-to-fine weakens age MAE from 4.10 to 4.95.Yeo-7 is used only as a shared cross-atlas functional scaffold, mapping ROIs from different atlases to the same seven subnetworks before ROI-level refinement. We will discuss atlas-matched or learnable scaffolds as future work in the Conclusion. 3) R1/R2: data and ground-truth FC. We use 14 datasets in total: 44,493 FC-prompt pairs for model training, SRPBS traveling-subject scans for validation, and ADNI Siemens-to-GE subset for downstream diagnosis task validation. SRPBS contains 411 rs-fMRI scans from 9 healthy males across 3 scanners. The ground-truth target FC is the same subject’s FC under the target scanner, protocol, and atlas. ADNI diagnosis task validation uses BrainGNN as classifier with 360 Siemens training FCs (NC/MCI/AD = 120/120/120) and 150 GE testing FCs (50/50/50). 4) R2/R3: loss formulation and encoder details. GraphCLIP employs symmetric InfoNCE over normalized graph/text embeddings, averaging graph-to-prompt and prompt-to-graph losses. We will clarify this loss in the revised manuscript. The notation used in the paper will be clarified as: Na is the number of ROI in atlas a, Nc=7 is the Yeo subnetwork number, d is the input feature dimension, k is the latent dimension, and L is the prompt token length. In Stage 1, the text encoder maps structured prompts to prompt embeddings, and a three-layer GCN maps FC graphs to graph embeddings. In Stage 2, the Resampler and dilated GCN handle atlas-dependent ROI dimensions for ROI-level harmonization. 5) R2/R3: training details and prompt design. We will expand Sec. 3.1 with GRETNA preprocessing, ROI extraction, Pearson FC construction, and training details. λ=0.2 is selected from {0.1,0.2,…,1.0} using validation Corr/MAE. Training takes 6.4/6.1 days for Stage 1/2 on one A100.Prompts include scanner identity, TR, TE, TI, flip angle, voxel size, and FC atlas. A1 confirms prompt design: replacing prompts with scanner-specific one-hot embeddings drops ACC from 91.2 to 72.4 and degrades Corr/MAE from 0.82/0.03 to 0.78/0.04.6) R2: baseline selection. Due to space limits, the original submission reports representative baselines. Each baseline is trained separately for each source-target harmonization task under the same setting. We further include the previously obtained DeepCombat comparison (Corr 0.78, MAE 0.04, target ACC 50.20%, age MAE 4.70), indicating that nonlinear fitting helps but still lacks prompt-conditioned multi-target control. 7) R3: interpretability. Due to space limits, the original submission only briefly discussed interpretability through Fig. 3(A). UniFCHarm yields target-consistent connectivity patterns with localized and moderate modifications, indicating controlled harmonization without widespread distortions.

title: URLCF: Universal Representation Learning for Cross-Domain Few-Shot Autism Spectrum Disorder Detection
reviewer_1_strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem in multi-site neuroimaging, and the evaluation protocol is well aligned with the motivation. The leave-one-site-out setting is appropriate for studying unseen-site generalization, and the additional five-shot setting is also clinically relevant. The overall framework is coherent and the reported empirical gains over the included baselines are encouraging. The paper is also generally well organized and includes ablation analysis and qualitative visualization.
reviewer_1_weaknesses: Global limitation: The paper does not truly establish “universal” representations in a strong scientific sense; it mainly shows improved performance on the ABIDE benchmark. The biological and interpretability claims are also overstated. The presented FC visualization, t-tests, and t-SNE plots are post-hoc and correlational, and do not justify claims about reliable biomarkers or mechanistic interpretability. ￼ Method-induced limitation: The main concern is limited novelty. Once unpacked, the method is a relatively standard combination of teacher-student distillation, masked reconstruction, domain discrimination, and a lightweight adapter. In addition, the framework is fairly heavy, requiring multiple teacher models, generators, and a discriminator, yet the paper provides little analysis of computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, or training stability. The ablation study is useful but still not enough to show why this specific combination is necessary. ￼ Dataset-induced limitation: The empirical validation is restricted to ABIDE only. Although leave-one-site-out is stronger than random splitting, it is still internal validation on a single benchmark. This is not sufficient to support strong claims about robust cross-domain generalization. In addition, the five-shot setting is inherently fragile in medical imaging due to substantial subject-level and site-level heterogeneity. ￼ Another concern is reproducibility. Although the paper provides an anonymized code link, the anonymous repository does not yet appear sufficiently complete for full verification. These missing details should be explicitly addressed in the rebuttal. In particular, the authors should clarify what exactly is included, whether the full training and evaluation pipeline can be reproduced, and whether all implementation details, scripts, and dependencies needed for leave-one-site-out and few-shot experiments are available.

author_feedback: We thank all reviewers for their comments and enthusiasm for our work. R#1 Q1: Global limitation A1: In this work, the term “universal representation” is intended to describe representations that are transferable across heterogeneous imaging domains, rather than biologically universal representations in a strict neuroscientific sense. We will revise the manuscript to avoid overly broad interpretations. Also, we agree that the current visualization analyses are post-hoc and correlational. These analyses were used to provide qualitative insight into the learned feature structure and cross-domain consistency. We will revise the manuscript to present these findings as preliminary observations that may motivate future neuroscientific validation. Q2: Method limitation A2: Although the individual modules are inspired by existing techniques, the main contribution of this work lies in the principled integration of these modules into a unified framework for cross-domain few-shot fMRI representation learning under severe site heterogeneity. Importantly, ablation results indicate that these components play complementary roles within the framework, as removing any individual module leads to degraded unseen-domain generalization performance. Regarding computational costs, we would like to mention that multi-teacher training is performed only once in an offline stage. During inference and target domain adaptation, only the student model and a lightweight adapter are used, making the framework computationally efficient for few-shot fine-tuning. Q3: Generalization A3: The current study primarily focuses on ASD-related analysis and evaluation. We will further validate our method on additional multi-site datasets (e.g., MDD and ADHD) in future work. Q4: Reproducibility A4: As suggested, we have updated the anonymized repository to clearly present the full training and testing pipeline, ensuring the reproducibility of our implementation. R#2 Q1: Calculating of performance score A1: For each non-held-out site, we split the data into training and validation sets, and compute the validation accuracy as the performance score using a single fully connected layer. To prevent overfitted teacher models, we apply a temperature scaling parameter τ in Eq. (1), which smooths the weight distribution, ensuring that no single teacher model dominates the distillation process. Q2: Architecture of baselines A2: For a fair comparison, all few-shot learning and domain-invariant methods were implemented using the same three-layer MLP architecture as our feature extractor. Q3: Missing citation A3: We apologize for the typo error, and will revise it in the revised version. R#3 Q1: Deficiencies of MLP A1: We agree that shallow MLPs are insufficient to fully capture the complex topological structure of FCs. In this study, we use shallow MLPs to avoid over-parameterization and ensure stable optimization, especially under limited neuroimaging data. This lightweight backbone also allows us to better evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework itself, independent of sophisticated network architectures. Q2: Masking A2: Masking is a feature corruption strategy that hides parts of the input to promote robust representation learning, whereas dropout is a regularization technique that randomly drops neural activations during training to reduce co-adaptation and prevent overfitting. Compared with directly masking raw FC matrices, masking semantically enriched high-level latent representations enables more robust feature learning and improves downstream clinical prediction performance. Q3: Generalization A3: A similar concern was also raised by R#1.A detailed response is provided in our reply to Q#3 of R#1.Q4: Comparison methods A4: We have already compared against 3 categories and 9 baseline methods. In future work, we will further expand the comparisons by incorporating additional SOTA methods to provide a more comprehensive evaluation.
